levels.title: Market Forces
levels.subtitle: Supply, demand & elasticity
briefing: Price moves toward equilibrium: excess demand bids it up, excess supply pushes it down, until Qd = Qs.
A change in the good's own price moves you ALONG a curve. Anything else (costs, technology, incomes, other prices) SHIFTS the curve.
Elasticity = % change in quantity ÷ % change in price. It is not the slope: on a straight demand line it changes at every point.
Time matters: demand for nondurables and supply of commodities are more elastic in the long run; demand for durables is more elastic in the short run.
A binding price ceiling turns a temporary excess demand into a lasting shortage, so something other than price does the rationing.

levels.title: Taste Test
levels.subtitle: Preferences, budgets & optimal choice
briefing: Four assumptions: completeness, transitivity, more is better, diminishing MRS (convex indifference curves).
MRS = how much Y you would give up for one more X and stay equally happy = |slope of the indifference curve| = MUx/MUy.
Budget line: I = Px·X + Py·Y, slope −Px/Py. Income changes shift it; price changes rotate it.
Interior optimum: MRS = Px/Py, or MUx/Px = MUy/Py. If no tangency exists, you get a corner solution.
Choices reveal preferences (WARP). Laspeyres overstates cost-of-living increases; Paasche understates them.

levels.title: Demand Unpacked
levels.subtitle: Income & substitution effects, market demand
briefing: Price-consumption curve (PCC): optimal bundles as Px changes → read off the individual demand curve.
Income-consumption curve (ICC): optimal bundles as income changes → Engel curves (necessity 0 < E < 1, luxury E > 1, inferior E < 0).
A price change = substitution effect (always opposite to price) + income effect (depends on normal vs inferior).
Giffen good: inferior AND the income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so demand slopes up. Very rare.
Market demand = horizontal sum of individual demands. Network effects make demand more elastic (bandwagon) or less elastic (snob).

levels.title: The Factory Floor
levels.subtitle: Production functions & returns to scale
briefing: Production function q = F(K, L): the most output that each input combination can give, with today's technology.
Short run: at least one input (usually capital) is fixed. Long run: every input can change. The length depends on the industry.
MP > AP pulls the average up, MP < AP pulls it down, so MP cuts AP at AP's maximum.
Diminishing marginal returns: with other inputs fixed, extra labour eventually adds less output. Output still rises, just more slowly.
Isoquant slope = MRTS = MPL/MPK. Returns to scale ask what happens when ALL inputs grow together.

levels.title: Counting Costs
levels.subtitle: Economic cost, short & long run
briefing: Economic cost = opportunity cost: it includes implicit costs, such as the owner's time, the firm's own building and the owner's capital.
Sunk costs cannot be recovered, so they must not affect forward-looking decisions.
TC = FC + VC. MC = ΔTC/Δq = ΔVC/Δq. MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minimum points.
Cost minimisation: MRTS = w/r, or MPL/w = MPK/r — the last dollar spent on each input yields the same output.
LAC is the envelope of SAC curves. Economies of scope: joint production is cheaper. Learning curve: cost falls with cumulative output.

levels.title: Price Takers
levels.subtitle: Perfect competition
briefing: Three conditions: price taking, a homogeneous product and free entry and exit.
Every firm maximises profit at MR = MC. For a price taker MR = P, so it produces where P = MC.
In the short run, shut down only if P < AVCmin. Fixed costs are paid either way, so they do not matter for this choice.
Firm supply = the MC curve above AVCmin. Producer surplus = profit + fixed cost = TR − VC.
In the long run, entry and exit drive economic profit to zero: P = MC = LACmin.

levels.title: Hands on the Market
levels.subtitle: Price controls, taxes, subsidies, tariffs
briefing: Efficiency: a competitive market maximises total surplus (CS + PS). Deadweight loss is surplus that nobody gets.
Price ceiling: consumers gain A and lose B, producers lose A and C, so the deadweight loss is B + C.
Price supports and quotas help producers, but at a far higher cost to society than handing them the same money in cash.
Tariff: consumers lose A + B + C + D, producers gain A, the state collects D, so the deadweight loss is B + C. A quota whose rents go abroad also loses D.
Tax incidence depends on elasticities, not on who pays the tax office: buyers bear Es/(Es − Ed) of the tax.

levels.title: One Seller, One Buyer
levels.subtitle: Monopoly & monopsony
briefing: MR = P·(1 + 1/Ed). MR is below price, and it is positive only where demand is elastic.
A monopolist sets MR = MC, then charges the highest price the demand curve allows at that output. It never operates on the inelastic part.
Lerner index L = (P − MC)/P = −1/Ed: the more elastic the firm's demand, the smaller its markup.
Sources of market power: elasticity of market demand, number of firms, how firms interact. Barriers: patents, licences, scale economies.
Monopsony: marginal expenditure lies above average expenditure, so the buyer purchases less and pays less than under competition.

levels.title: Pricing Power
levels.subtitle: Price discrimination, two-part tariffs, bundling
briefing: A single price leaves surplus on the table: buyers who would pay more, and buyers who would pay above MC but below the price.
First degree: charge each buyer their reservation price. Output rises to the competitive level, and the firm captures all surplus.
Second degree: different prices for different quantities (block pricing). Buyers sort themselves.
Third degree: separate groups, MR₁ = MR₂ = MC, higher price where demand is less elastic.
Two-part tariff: entry fee + usage price. Bundling pays when reservation prices are negatively correlated. Tying meters usage.

levels.title: The Few
levels.subtitle: Monopolistic competition & oligopoly
briefing: Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, free entry. In the long run demand is tangent to LAC: zero profit, but P > MC.
Excess capacity: output stays below the minimum of LAC — the price of product variety.
Cournot: firms choose quantities, each taking the rival's output as given. The Nash equilibrium lies between competition and monopoly.
Bertrand with identical goods: price falls to MC even with two firms. Stackelberg: the firm that commits first wins.
Kinked demand explains sticky prices. A dominant firm prices off residual demand. Cartels need inelastic demand, inelastic outside supply and discipline.

levels.title: Game On
levels.subtitle: Game theory, strategy & auctions
briefing: Dominant strategy: best whatever the rival does. Nash equilibrium: each does its best, given what the other actually does.
Every dominant-strategy equilibrium is a Nash equilibrium, but not every Nash equilibrium uses dominant strategies.
Prisoners' dilemma: individually rational choices lead to a worse result for both. Repetition (tit-for-tat) can sustain cooperation.
Sequential games are solved by backward induction. Only credible threats count, and irreversible commitments can deter entry.
Auctions: English, Dutch, first-price and second-price sealed-bid. In common-value auctions, beware the winner's curse.

levels.title: Hired Inputs
levels.subtitle: Labour & factor markets
briefing: Input demand is derived from demand for the output. A firm hires until the marginal revenue product equals the input price.
MRP_L = MP_L × MR. With competitive output MR = P, so MRP = VMP = MP × P. With output monopoly, MRP < VMP.
Industry input demand is steeper than the sum of firms' MRPs, because the output price falls when all firms expand.
Labour supply bends backward if the income effect of a higher wage outweighs the substitution effect.
Economic rent = pay above what is needed to keep the input in use. Unions, monopsony and bilateral monopoly change wages.

levels.title: Time Is Money
levels.subtitle: Capital, interest & risk
briefing: Stocks are measured at a point in time (machines, capacity); flows per period (investment, depreciation, revenue).
PDV = Σ FVₜ/(1 + R)ᵗ. A dollar today beats a dollar tomorrow because today's dollar can earn interest.
Perpetuity: PV = C/R. Bond prices move opposite to interest rates.
NPV rule: invest if NPV > 0. Discount nominal cash flows at a nominal rate and real flows at a real rate.
Only nondiversifiable risk earns a premium (CAPM beta). Hotelling: the net price P − MC of an exhaustible resource rises at the rate of interest.

levels.title: The Big Box
levels.subtitle: General equilibrium & efficiency
briefing: Partial equilibrium looks at one market; general equilibrium follows the feedback between related markets.
Edgeworth box: if MRS_A ≠ MRS_B, both can gain by trading. The contract curve is the set of allocations where MRS_A = MRS_B.
First welfare theorem: a competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient. Efficiency says nothing about fairness.
Production efficiency: equal MRTS across industries, which traces the PPF. Output efficiency: MRS = MRT = MCx/MCy.
Trade lets a country consume outside its PPF, even if a partner has an absolute advantage in everything.

levels.title: When Markets Fail
levels.subtitle: Externalities & public goods
briefing: Four sources of market failure: market power, incomplete information, externalities, public goods.
Negative externality: MSC = MC + MEC, so the market overproduces. Positive externality: MSB = D + MEB, so it underproduces.
Fixes: a Pigouvian fee equal to MEC at the efficient output, standards, tradable permits, or Coase-style bargaining.
Common property (rival, non-excludable) is overused: the tragedy of the commons.
Public goods (non-rival, non-excludable) invite free riders. The efficient level is where the VERTICAL sum of marginal benefits equals MC.

questions.question: The market price of copper is above its equilibrium level. What brings it back to equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Above equilibrium Qs > Qd, so there is excess supply. Competition among sellers pushes the price down, which raises Qd and lowers Qs until they meet. Nothing shifts — the adjustment is a movement along both curves.

options.text: Excess supply builds up, so sellers cut prices until Qd = Qs
Buyers bid prices higher because they fear the surplus will soon run out
Producers raise output until the extra supply clears at the higher price
The demand curve shifts right until it crosses supply at the current price

questions.question: A strike unexpectedly closes several large copper mines. In a competitive world market, what happens?
questions.explanation: Lost mine output is a supply shift, not a price-driven movement. At the old price buyers want more than is available; the excess demand is temporary because the price rises until the market clears at a higher P and lower Q.

options.text: Demand shifts right because buyers stock up, so both price and quantity rise
Supply shifts left; at the old price there is excess demand, so price rises and quantity falls
Supply shifts left, but the price stays put because a world market absorbs the shock
Supply moves along the curve to a lower quantity while the price stays the same

questions.question: What separates the excess demand after a supply disruption from the shortage caused by a binding price ceiling?
questions.explanation: In a free market, excess demand is self-correcting — the price rises and closes the gap. A legal maximum price blocks that mechanism, so the shortage lasts as long as the ceiling does.

options.text: They are the same thing: both last until the government ends the crisis
With a ceiling the price is not allowed to rise, so the gap between Qd and Qs persists
A ceiling raises quantity supplied, while a disruption reduces it
After a disruption the gap is larger, so it takes longer for the market to clear

questions.question: Which events SHIFT the world supply curve of crude oil, rather than causing a movement along it?
questions.explanation: Supply shifts when something other than the oil price changes producers' willingness to sell: costs, technology, capacity, war. Higher Asian incomes shift DEMAND, not supply. When producers react to a change in the oil price itself (up or down), they move along the existing supply curve.

options.text: A fall in the oil price makes producers cap some marginal wells
Strong demand from China raises the world oil price and producers pump more
A war shuts down pipelines in a major producing region
Fracking technology lowers the cost of extracting shale oil
Higher incomes in Asia raise demand for crude oil

questions.question: Higher world crude prices lead US shale firms to drill and complete more wells. How is this shown on a supply diagram?
questions.explanation: The trigger is the good's own price, so output rises along the existing curve. An outward shift would need a non-price change — for example, cheaper drilling technology letting firms supply more at every price.

options.text: A movement up along the existing supply curve
An inward shift of the demand curve
An outward shift of the supply curve
A pivot of the supply curve to make it steeper

questions.question: Which formula defines the price elasticity of demand?
questions.explanation: Elasticity compares percentage changes, so it has no units. ΔQ/ΔP is the inverse slope, which depends on units. The last option is income elasticity.

options.text: (ΔQ/Q) ÷ (ΔI/I)
ΔQ ÷ ΔP
(ΔQ/Q) ÷ (ΔP/P)
(ΔP/P) ÷ (ΔQ/Q)

questions.question: Why is price elasticity not the same thing as the slope of a straight-line demand curve?
questions.explanation: On a linear demand curve ΔQ/ΔP never changes, but P/Q is high near the price axis and low near the quantity axis. So demand is elastic at high prices and inelastic at low prices, even though the slope is the same everywhere.

options.text: They are the same, measured in different currencies
E = (ΔQ/ΔP)·(P/Q): the slope term is constant, but the ratio P/Q changes along the line
Elasticity is constant along a straight line, while the slope keeps changing
The slope uses percentages, elasticity uses absolute units

questions.question: Why do economists use the arc (midpoint) elasticity when measuring elasticity between two price points?
questions.explanation: With the simple formula, going from P=4 to P=5 gives a different percentage change than going from 5 to 4. The arc formula uses the midpoint of P and Q, so the result is symmetric. Point elasticity is the version used at one point on the curve.

options.text: It always gives a value closer to −1 than point elasticity does
It measures elasticity at a single point, which is more precise
It is the only formula that works for curved demand curves
Using average P and Q gives the same answer whether the price rises or falls

questions.question: Where on a straight-line demand curve is total consumer expenditure (P·Q) highest?
questions.explanation: Above the midpoint demand is elastic, so cutting the price raises spending. Below it demand is inelastic, so cutting the price lowers spending. Spending peaks where |E| = 1, which on a straight line is exactly halfway.

options.text: At the lowest price, where the most units are sold
Where the curve meets the price axis
Where demand is most inelastic
At the midpoint, where demand is unit elastic

questions.question: Demand for a medicine is inelastic (E = −0.3). The price goes up 10%. What happens to total spending on it?
questions.explanation: When |E| < 1, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so P·Q goes up. This is why sellers of goods with few substitutes can raise revenue by raising prices.

options.text: It rises: quantity falls only about 3%
It falls, because quantity falls by about 30%
It stays the same, because spending never depends on price
It falls, because any price rise reduces revenue

questions.question: Demand is P = 10 − Q. Put these points in order from the most elastic to the least elastic.
questions.explanation: For this curve E = −P/(10 − P): −9 at P = 9, about −2.3 at P = 7, −1 at the midpoint and −0.25 at P = 2. Moving down a straight demand line, demand becomes less and less elastic.

options.text: At P = 2
At P = 7
At P = 9
At P = 5 (the midpoint)

questions.question: The cross-price elasticity between imported electric vehicles and domestic gasoline cars is +0.8. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: A positive cross-price elasticity means a higher price of one good raises demand for the other — the definition of substitutes. For carmakers it means price moves by rivals selling the other technology directly affect their sales.

options.text: EVs are a luxury: a 10% rise in income raises EV demand by about 8%
They are substitutes: a 10% rise in gasoline-car prices raises EV demand by about 8%
They are complements: a 10% rise in gasoline-car prices lowers EV demand by about 8%
The goods are unrelated, because the value is below 1

questions.question: The income elasticity of demand for luxury EVs is +2.2. What does that tell a global carmaker?
questions.explanation: An income elasticity above 1 marks a luxury: a 1% rise in income raises demand by 2.2%. Such firms do well in fast-growing, high-income markets but suffer most in recessions, so they diversify across countries whose cycles differ.

options.text: Sales grow faster than incomes and are very sensitive to the business cycle
Higher incomes reduce sales, because rich buyers switch to other brands
Sales do not respond to income, only to the price of fuel
Sales grow more slowly than incomes, so they are recession-proof

questions.question: Which pairings of elasticity value and meaning are correct?
questions.explanation: Inferior goods have negative income elasticity; necessities rise with income, but by less than income; luxuries rise more than proportionally (above 1). A negative cross-price elasticity means complements (substitutes have a positive one). A cross elasticity of 0 means the goods are unrelated.

options.text: Income elasticity above 1 — an inferior good
Cross-price elasticity of exactly 0 — perfect substitutes
Cross-price elasticity below 0 — substitutes
Income elasticity between 0 and 1 — a necessity
Income elasticity below 0 — an inferior good

questions.question: Which good's demand is more elastic in the long run than in the short run, and why?
questions.explanation: For a nondurable like gasoline, consumers are locked into their current car in the short run, so demand is inelastic. Given time, they change the stock of cars and habits, so long-run demand is much more elastic.

options.text: Commercial aircraft — airlines can only postpone orders for a few months
Gasoline — in the long run drivers stop noticing price changes
Gasoline — over time drivers switch to fuel-efficient cars and transit
Both have equal short-run and long-run elasticities because both are traded globally

questions.question: Why is demand for durable goods such as commercial aircraft MORE elastic in the short run than in the long run?
questions.explanation: For durables, annual purchases replace a large existing stock. When prices rise, buyers can keep flying old planes for a while, so purchases drop sharply at first. In the long run the stock has to be maintained, so the percentage fall in demand is smaller.

options.text: Durable goods are luxuries, and luxuries always have elastic demand
Manufacturers cut prices over time, so long-run demand does not need to respond
Buyers can delay replacing old units, but the fleet must eventually be replaced
In the long run airlines lose interest in price because aircraft are a small share of their costs

questions.question: Why is the long-run supply of aluminium or wheat much more elastic than its short-run supply?
questions.explanation: Supply elasticity reflects how easily output can expand. In the short run firms can only run existing capacity harder. In the long run new mines, smelters and planted acreage come on stream, so the response to a price change is much larger.

options.text: Producers ignore prices in the short run and only react once prices are reported
Short-run supply is limited by price controls that expire in the long run
Capacity is fixed short-run; new mines and land take time
In the long run demand becomes more elastic, which makes supply more elastic too

questions.question: Copper is also supplied from recycled scrap. How does this secondary supply behave?
questions.explanation: High prices quickly pull old wiring and pipes into recycling, so secondary supply jumps in the short run. Over time the available stock of scrap runs down, so the long-run response is smaller. In Pindyck's copper example this raises the short-run elasticity of total supply.

options.text: More elastic in the short run: high prices pull scrap out, but the stock runs down
It has a negative elasticity, because high prices make people hoard old metal
It is perfectly inelastic, because the amount of scrap is fixed by past consumption of copper
It is more elastic in the long run, because recycling plants take years to build

questions.question: World copper demand is QD = 32 − 0.20P. Demand rises by 20% at every price. Which equation describes the new demand?
questions.explanation: "20% more at every price" means multiplying the whole function by 1.2, so both the intercept and the slope term scale: 1.2·(32 − 0.20P). Adding 20% only to the intercept would be a different (parallel) shift. Then set the new demand equal to supply and solve for P and Q.

questions.question: Demand for copper rises while supply is fairly inelastic. What is the likely result?
questions.explanation: When demand shifts right along a steep (inelastic) supply curve, most of the adjustment shows up in price. In the copper example, a 20% rise in demand raises the price by about 30% but quantity by only about 7%.

options.text: Quantity rises by a large percentage, price by a small one
Price and quantity rise by exactly the same percentage
Price falls, because producers expand to meet the extra demand
Price rises by a large percentage, quantity by a small one

questions.question: A government caps the price of an imported fertiliser below the market-clearing level. Which outcomes should you expect?
questions.explanation: Below equilibrium, quantity supplied falls while quantity demanded rises. Farmers can only buy what is supplied, so total purchases fall. With price no longer rationing, something else does: queues, coupons, favouritism or illegal resale.

options.text: Queues, waiting lists or coupons decide who gets the fertiliser
Importers bring in less, because the capped price no longer covers their costs
Imports rise, because foreign suppliers want to win market share
Farmers buy more fertiliser than before, because it is cheaper
A black market appears where it sells above the legal price

questions.question: Who gains from a binding price ceiling on an essential import?
questions.explanation: Lucky buyers who get the good pay less and gain. Buyers who are rationed out lose, and so do sellers, who sell fewer units at a lower price. A ceiling raises no revenue — it is a transfer plus a deadweight loss.

options.text: All buyers, because everyone pays less
The government, because it collects the price difference as revenue
Only buyers who actually obtain the good at the lower price
Importers, because they sell more units

questions.question: On the graph, the price ceiling is Pmax. What quantity do consumers actually buy?
questions.explanation: Trade cannot exceed what sellers offer. At Pmax firms supply only Q₁, even though buyers want Q₂. Q₂ − Q₁ is the shortage, and Q₀ is the free-market quantity.

options.text: Q₂
Q₀
Q₁
Q₂ − Q₁

questions.question: Which are standard assumptions about consumer preferences in Pindyck & Rubinfeld?
questions.explanation: Consumer theory needs only an ordinal ranking. Utility numbers just order bundles; their size has no meaning. The four listed assumptions give downward-sloping, non-crossing, convex indifference curves.

options.text: Completeness — the consumer can rank any two bundles
Diminishing MRS — indifference curves are convex
More is better — goods are desirable
Cardinality — utility can be measured in fixed units
Transitivity — if X beats Y and Y beats Z, then X beats Z

questions.question: Why can two indifference curves never cross?
questions.explanation: If curves U₁ and U₂ crossed at A, then A ~ B (on U₁) and A ~ D (on U₂), so by transitivity B ~ D. But one of B or D contains more of both goods, so by "more is better" it must be preferred. That contradiction rules out crossing.

options.text: Because the budget line can only be tangent to one indifference curve at a time
One of two equally good bundles would contain more of both goods
Because indifference curves must be parallel by definition
Because utility cannot be measured, so curves cannot meet

questions.question: A consumer prefers tea to coffee and coffee to juice, but juice to tea. Which assumption is violated?
questions.explanation: Transitivity requires that if tea beats coffee and coffee beats juice, tea must beat juice. Circular rankings make a consistent "best" choice impossible.

options.text: More is better
Completeness
Transitivity
Diminishing MRS

questions.question: What is the marginal rate of substitution of X for Y?
questions.explanation: MRS is a preference concept: the absolute slope of the indifference curve. The market exchange rate is the price ratio Px/Py (slope of the budget line). The two are equal at an interior optimum.

options.text: The most Y the consumer would give up for one more X and stay equally happy
The extra utility from one more unit of X
The rate at which the market lets the consumer swap Y for X, given by the price ratio
The ratio of the price of X to the price of Y

questions.question: Why is MRS = MUx/MUy?
questions.explanation: Moving along an indifference curve, the utility gained from extra X must exactly offset the utility lost from less Y. Rearranging gives the MRS as the ratio of marginal utilities.

options.text: Because MRS is defined as the ratio of total utilities
Because the budget line slope equals the marginal utility of income
Utility is constant, so MUx·ΔX = −MUy·ΔY
Because consumers always equate marginal utility to price

questions.question: What does a diminishing MRS mean?
questions.explanation: As X becomes plentiful and Y scarce, X is valued less relative to Y. That makes indifference curves flatten as you move right — they are convex to the origin, which reflects a taste for balanced bundles.

options.text: The consumer's total utility falls as they buy more X
The price of X falls as the consumer buys more of it
The consumer will always give up the same amount of Y for each extra X
The more X a consumer already has, the less Y they will give up for an extra unit of X

questions.question: Two goods are perfect substitutes (one-for-one). What do the indifference curves look like?
questions.explanation: If the consumer always trades one unit of X for one of Y, the MRS is constant at 1. The optimum is usually a corner: buy only the cheaper good, unless the price ratio equals the MRS.

options.text: Straight lines with a constant MRS
Curves convex to the origin with diminishing MRS
Upward-sloping lines
L-shapes with a corner on a 45° ray

questions.question: Left and right shoes are perfect complements. What follows for consumer choice?
questions.explanation: An extra left shoe without a right one adds nothing, so utility depends on the number of pairs (Leontief preferences). The optimum is at the kink, and a price change only has an income effect, never a substitution effect.

options.text: L-shaped curves; shoes are bought in pairs and prices cause no substitution
Indifference curves slope upward; extra shoes reduce utility
Indifference curves are straight lines; the consumer buys only the cheaper shoe
Indifference curves are vertical lines; only right shoes matter

questions.question: X is industrial pollution (a "bad") and Y is a normal good. What shape do the indifference curves have?
questions.explanation: Keeping utility constant while adding a bad requires more of the good, so the curves slope upward. Utility increases toward the upper-left (less pollution, more Y). A rational consumer chooses zero of the bad when possible.

options.text: Horizontal: pollution does not affect utility
L-shaped: pollution and Y are consumed in fixed proportion
Upward-sloping: more pollution must be compensated with more Y
Downward-sloping and convex, as with normal goods

questions.question: X on the horizontal axis is a neutral good — the consumer does not care about it. What do the indifference curves look like, and what is chosen?
questions.explanation: Utility depends only on Y, so any bundle with the same Y is equally good — a horizontal line. The MRS of X for Y is zero, so the consumer buys no X and puts all income into Y.

options.text: Vertical lines; the consumer spends the whole budget on X
L-shapes; the consumer buys X and Y in fixed proportion
Straight downward lines; the consumer buys equal amounts
Horizontal lines; the consumer spends the whole budget on Y

questions.question: What is the slope of the budget line I = Px·X + Py·Y, with X on the horizontal axis?
questions.explanation: Solving for Y gives Y = I/Py − (Px/Py)·X. The slope is the market rate at which Y can be traded for X. −MUx/MUy is the slope of an indifference curve.

options.text: −I/Px
−Py/Px
−Px/Py
−MUx/MUy

questions.question: All prices rise by 20% while nominal income stays the same. How does the budget line change?
questions.explanation: The price ratio Px/Py is unchanged, so the slope is the same. But real income falls: the intercepts I/(1.2Px) and I/(1.2Py) move toward the origin. Only if nominal income also rose by 20% would the line stay where it was.

options.text: It shifts outward, because nominal income now buys more
It rotates around the Y-intercept and becomes steeper
Parallel inward shift: the slope is unchanged, the intercepts fall
It does not change, because relative prices and the price ratio are still the same

questions.question: A 10% import tariff is applied only to imported good X (on the horizontal axis). How does the budget line change?
questions.explanation: The most Y you can buy (I/Py) is unchanged, so the Y-intercept stays. The most X falls to I/(1.1·Px), so the line pivots inward and gets steeper, because X is now relatively more expensive.

options.text: It rotates around the X-intercept and becomes flatter
It pivots inward around the Y-intercept and gets steeper
It rotates outward around the X-intercept
It shifts inward in parallel, because the consumer is poorer after the tariff

questions.question: At the consumer's current bundle, MRS > Px/Py. What should the consumer do?
questions.explanation: MRS > Px/Py means the consumer values one more X (in units of Y) more than the market charges for it. Swapping Y for X raises utility, and as X rises the MRS diminishes until it equals Px/Py.

options.text: Buy less X and more Y, until the MRS rises to the price ratio
Nothing — any bundle on the budget line is optimal
Buy more X and less Y, until the MRS falls to the price ratio
Spend more than their income on X

questions.question: Which condition is equivalent to MRS = Px/Py at an interior optimum?
questions.explanation: Since MRS = MUx/MUy, the tangency condition becomes MUx/MUy = Px/Py, or MUx/Px = MUy/Py: the last dollar spent on each good must give the same extra utility (the equal marginal principle).

options.text: Px·X = Py·Y
MUx/MUy = Py/Px
MUx/Px = MUy/Py
MUx = MUy

questions.question: Which bundle on the graph maximises utility given the budget line?
questions.explanation: A is affordable and lies on the highest reachable indifference curve (U₂). B and C are affordable but only reach U₁. U₃ lies entirely outside the budget set.

options.text: C, because it has the most of good X
A, where the indifference curve is tangent to the budget line
B, because it has the most of good Y
Any point on U₃, because it gives the highest utility

questions.question: At point B the MRS is Y/X = 16/2 = 8, while Px/Py = 2. What should this consumer do?
questions.explanation: At B the consumer would give up 8 units of Y for one more X, but the market asks only 2. Trading Y for X raises utility, and as the consumer moves toward A the MRS falls until it equals 2.

options.text: Stay at B, because it is on the budget line
Give up some X to buy more Y, moving up the budget line
Give up some Y to buy more X, moving down the budget line toward A
Cut total spending so the MRS falls to 2

questions.question: Which statements about the graph are correct?
questions.explanation: B and C lie on the same indifference curve U₁, so the consumer is indifferent between them. A, B and C all lie on the budget line, so they cost the same. At C the MRS is 4/8 = 0.5, which is below the price ratio of 2.

options.text: C is preferred to B because it contains more of good X
At C the consumer values X less than its market price, so should buy less X
Bundles on U₃ are preferred but not affordable
A costs more than B because it is on a higher indifference curve
Bundle B gives the same utility as bundle C

questions.question: What is a corner solution?
questions.explanation: If the consumer values X less than its price at every bundle (MRS < Px/Py even with zero X), no tangency exists and they spend everything on Y. Corner solutions are typical with perfect substitutes or when one good is strongly preferred.

options.text: An optimum with zero of one good
An optimum at the kink of an L-shaped indifference curve
A bundle where the consumer spends exactly half of income on each good
Any bundle where the budget line is tangent to an indifference curve

questions.question: A traveller sees domestic and foreign airlines as perfect substitutes. A domestic ticket costs $300 and a foreign one $250. What does the traveller choose?
questions.explanation: With straight-line indifference curves (MRS = 1), the consumer compares the MRS with the price ratio. Since the foreign ticket is cheaper, every dollar buys more flights there — a corner solution. Only if prices were equal would any mix be optimal.

options.text: Pick any combination, because both airlines give exactly the same utility per flight
Split flights evenly to equalise marginal utility
Fly only the foreign airline, since it is cheaper and a perfect substitute
Fly only the domestic airline, because quality is the same

questions.question: A consumer buys bundle A when bundle B was also affordable. What does the theory of revealed preference conclude?
questions.explanation: If you could have bought B but chose A, you have shown that you prefer A (at least weakly). Revealed preference builds indifference maps from observed choices instead of asking people about their utility.

options.text: The consumer is indifferent between them
A is revealed preferred to B
B is revealed preferred to A
Nothing, because preferences cannot be observed

questions.question: In period 1 a consumer buys A when B is affordable. When would buying B in period 2 violate the Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP)?
questions.explanation: WARP says that if A is revealed preferred to B, then B must never be chosen when A is also affordable. Choosing B when A is out of reach is consistent; choosing B while A is still affordable contradicts the earlier choice.

options.text: If the consumer's income rises in period 2
If B is cheaper in period 2 than in period 1
If A is no longer affordable in period 2
If A is still affordable in period 2

questions.question: Why does a Laspeyres price index overstate the rise in the true cost of living?
questions.explanation: Laspeyres asks what the old basket costs at new prices. Consumers can do better by substituting toward relatively cheaper goods, so they need less extra income than the index suggests — an upward substitution bias.

options.text: It uses current-period quantities, which overweight expensive goods
It includes taxes, which are not part of the cost of living
It fixes base-period quantities and ignores substitution
It measures income rather than prices

questions.question: Prices change and consumers substitute toward cheaper goods. Rank the measured increase in the cost of living from highest to lowest.
questions.explanation: Laspeyres overstates the increase (it ignores substitution away from goods that got dearer). Paasche understates it (it assumes the new basket was also bought in the base period). The true index lies between them. Chain-weighted indexes try to get close to it.

options.text: Paasche index (current-period quantities)
Ideal cost-of-living index
Laspeyres index (base-period quantities)

questions.question: Which factors are usually cited as sources of upward bias in a consumer price index?
questions.explanation: Fixed-weight indexes miss substitution, count quality improvements as pure price rises, and add new products late (after their prices have already fallen). Using current-period weights is the Paasche method, which biases the index down rather than up.

options.text: Excluding imported goods from the basket
Substitution toward goods whose relative prices fell
Quality improvements that are not fully reflected in prices
New goods entering the basket only years after launch
Using current-period quantities as weights

questions.question: How is an individual demand curve derived from indifference curves?
questions.explanation: Each price of X gives a new budget line and a new optimum. Linking these optima traces the PCC; plotting each price against the quantity chosen gives the demand curve. Varying income instead traces the ICC and Engel curve.

options.text: Plot the marginal utility of X against the quantity of X
Change income with prices fixed and plot income against the chosen X
Add up the quantities chosen by all consumers at each price of the good
Vary Px, find each tangency (the PCC) and plot Px against the chosen X

questions.question: Y is "all other goods" (Py = 1). As Px falls, the price-consumption curve slopes downward. What does that reveal?
questions.explanation: With fixed income, spending on X = I − Y. A downward-sloping PCC means Y falls as Px falls, so spending on X rises — elastic demand. A horizontal PCC means unit elasticity; an upward-sloping PCC means inelastic demand.

options.text: Demand for X is elastic: spending on other goods falls, so spending on X rises
Demand for X is inelastic: spending on X falls as its price falls
X is a Giffen good, because less Y is bought
Demand for X is unit elastic: spending on X does not change

questions.question: What does an Engel curve show?
questions.explanation: Engel curves come from the income-consumption curve: as the budget line shifts out in parallel, each new optimum gives one income–quantity pair.

options.text: Quantity bought at each level of income, with prices held fixed
The quantity demanded at each price, with income and other prices held fixed
How spending on a good changes as its price falls
The combinations of two goods that give equal utility

questions.question: Rank these goods from the highest to the lowest income elasticity of demand.
questions.explanation: Luxuries have income elasticity above 1 (spending share rises with income), necessities between 0 and 1 (share falls), and inferior goods below 0 (people buy less as they get richer).

options.text: A necessity, such as electricity
An inferior good, such as instant noodles
A luxury, such as long-haul holidays

questions.question: What happens to a necessity as a household's income rises?
questions.explanation: Necessities have income elasticity between 0 and 1: quantity rises, but less than proportionally, so the budget share shrinks (Engel's law for food). Buying less as income rises would make it inferior.

options.text: The household buys less of it, so the Engel curve slopes backward
Consumption stays exactly the same
Its budget share rises faster than income
The household buys more of it, but its share of the budget falls

questions.question: On the income-consumption curve, what shows that X is an inferior good?
questions.explanation: For a normal good, both goods increase as the budget line shifts out, so the ICC slopes up and to the right. If X is inferior over some income range, the ICC turns back toward the Y axis there, and the Engel curve slopes backward.

options.text: The ICC bends back toward the Y axis as income rises
The ICC is a straight line from the origin
The ICC slopes upward more steeply at higher incomes, so X grows faster
The ICC is horizontal, because only X is bought

questions.question: What is the substitution effect of a price change?
questions.explanation: The substitution effect moves along the original indifference curve to the bundle that would be chosen at the new price ratio. The income effect is the remaining move, caused by the change in real income.

options.text: The change in consumption caused by the change in purchasing power, with relative prices fixed
The total change in quantity demanded after a price change
The change in consumption caused by the change in relative prices, with utility held constant
The shift from one good to a completely different market

questions.question: Why is the substitution effect always negative (opposite to the price change)?
questions.explanation: Holding utility fixed, a flatter budget line (cheaper X) can only be tangent to a convex curve further to the right. This holds for every good, normal or inferior. Only the income effect can work in the "wrong" direction.

options.text: With convex curves, a flatter budget line touches the same curve at more X
Because consumers always buy more when they feel richer
Because all goods are normal goods
Because the budget line always shifts outward after the price of a good falls

questions.question: Put the steps of decomposing a fall in Px (Hicksian method) in order.
questions.explanation: The hypothetical budget line has the new price ratio but just enough income to keep the consumer on the old curve. That isolates the pure effect of relative prices. The parallel shift from that line to the actual new line is the income effect.

options.text: Substitution effect = move along U₁ to that hypothetical tangency
Income effect = move from the hypothetical tangency to the new optimum
Rotate the budget line for the lower Px and find the new optimum on U₂
Find the original optimum on U₁ with the initial budget line
Draw a hypothetical line parallel to the new budget line but tangent to U₁

questions.question: The price of an imported normal good falls. Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: For a normal good both effects work in the same direction, so demand slopes down without doubt. The substitution effect holds utility (not nominal income) constant. For an inferior good the income effect would go against the substitution effect.

options.text: The substitution effect is measured holding nominal income constant
The substitution effect increases the quantity bought
The income effect also increases the quantity bought
The income effect reduces the quantity bought
The total effect unambiguously increases the quantity bought

questions.question: What separates a Giffen good from an ordinary inferior good?
questions.explanation: All Giffen goods are inferior, but in most inferior goods the substitution effect still dominates, so demand slopes down. Only when the opposing income effect is larger does a price rise increase quantity demanded.

options.text: For a Giffen good the income effect outweighs the substitution effect
A Giffen good is a luxury that people buy for status
There is no difference: every inferior good is a Giffen good
A Giffen good has positive income elasticity, an inferior good negative

questions.question: Why must every Giffen good be inferior?
questions.explanation: The substitution effect always pushes quantity opposite to price. For demand to slope upward, something must push the other way — and only the income effect of an inferior good does that. For a normal good both effects reinforce each other.

options.text: Only then does the income effect work against the substitution effect
Because a Giffen good's substitution effect is positive
Because inferior goods always have upward-sloping demand curves in practice
Because Giffen goods are bought only by people with low incomes

questions.question: Under what circumstances might Giffen behaviour actually be observed?
questions.explanation: The income effect is large only if the good takes a big share of the budget. When a staple like rice gets dearer, a very poor family can no longer afford meat and buys even more rice. Jensen and Miller (2008) found such behaviour among poor households in China. Status goods are a separate case (snob or Veblen effects).

options.text: A good has many close substitutes and takes only a tiny share of the budget
A staple food takes a large share of a poor household's budget
A firm buys inputs whose price is regulated
A rich household buys luxury goods to signal status

questions.question: How is market demand obtained from individual demand curves?
questions.explanation: For private goods each unit is consumed by one person, so at any price market quantity is the sum of individual quantities. Vertical summation is used for public goods, where everyone consumes the same units.

options.text: Take the average of the individual demand curves
Multiply the typical buyer's demand by the number of sellers
Add the quantities demanded by all buyers at each price (horizontal summation)
Add the prices each buyer would pay for each quantity (vertical summation)

questions.question: A large group of foreign buyers enters an open market. What happens to the market demand curve?
questions.explanation: Market demand is the horizontal sum of all buyers. Adding buyers adds their quantities at each price, so the curve shifts out. The equilibrium price then rises along the supply curve.

options.text: It does not change; only the market supply curve changes
It becomes vertical, because foreign demand is fixed
It shifts to the right: at every price the total quantity demanded is larger
It shifts to the left, because foreign buyers raise the price

questions.question: Why can a market demand curve have kinks?
questions.explanation: Above a buyer's maximum price, that buyer demands nothing. As price falls past each such choke price, a new buyer's quantities are added and the market curve becomes flatter at that point.

options.text: Because buyers have kinked indifference curves
Each buyer starts purchasing at a different price
Because sellers change prices in steps
Because horizontal summation is only an approximation

questions.question: What is consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: Each unit's value to the buyer is the height of the demand curve. Subtracting the price paid and adding across all units bought gives the triangle-shaped area between demand and price. The area above supply is producer surplus.

options.text: The revenue firms earn above their costs
The extra quantity consumers would buy if the price fell
The area between the supply curve and the market price, summed over all units
Willingness to pay minus the price actually paid, summed over units bought

questions.question: Higher shipping costs or a new tariff raise the price of an imported good. What happens to consumer surplus?
questions.explanation: Buyers lose the price increase on every unit they keep buying (a rectangle) and the net value of units they stop buying (a triangle). Part of the rectangle may become tariff revenue, but the triangle is lost to everyone.

options.text: It is unchanged, because the extra money goes to the government or shippers
It rises, because consumers value scarce goods more
It falls only by the extra tariff revenue
It falls: buyers pay more on units bought and lose units no longer bought

questions.question: Why is market demand for a messaging platform more price-elastic because of the bandwagon effect?
questions.explanation: With a positive network externality each buyer's demand depends on how many others buy. A lower price raises quantity directly, and the larger network then shifts each person's demand out — so the total response is larger than without the effect.

options.text: Users stop joining when many others are already on the platform
A price cut draws users in, which makes the platform worth more to others
A price cut reduces quality, which offsets the extra users
Network effects make demand perfectly inelastic once a platform dominates

questions.question: Why is market demand for exclusive luxury watches less elastic because of the snob effect?
questions.explanation: A negative network externality means more buyers make the good less desirable. A price cut still raises quantity, but the loss of exclusivity shifts individual demand back in, so the market response is smaller.

options.text: Snob effects only shift supply, not demand
Snobs always buy more when prices fall, making demand more elastic, not less
More owners make the watch less exclusive, offsetting part of the rise
Luxury watch buyers ignore price entirely

questions.question: Which products have demand shaped mainly by a POSITIVE network externality?
questions.explanation: Bandwagon goods become more valuable as more people use them: payments, multiplayer games and social networks all need other users. Limited editions rely on exclusivity (a snob effect). Salt has essentially no network effect.

options.text: A limited-edition designer handbag
A social network
An online multiplayer game
A mobile payment app
Table salt

questions.question: What is speculative demand?
questions.explanation: Speculators buy now to resell later or to avoid paying more later. That is why a rising price can increase current purchases — buyers expect further increases.

options.text: Demand for goods bought on credit
Demand driven by expected price increases rather than by use
Demand from consumers who buy only when prices are low, such as bargain hunters
Demand that depends on the price of a complement

questions.question: In a housing boom, rising prices are followed by MORE buying. How is this best explained?
questions.explanation: Utility-based demand still slopes down, but expectations are a shift factor. When price rises signal further rises, demand shifts out, pushing prices up again. This feedback loop can inflate bubbles in housing and commodities until expectations turn.

options.text: Buyers move along a normal demand curve to a higher quantity as prices climb
Rising prices make houses more useful to live in
Rising prices raise expected future prices, shifting demand right
Housing is a Giffen good, so its demand curve slopes upward

questions.question: What does a production function show?
questions.explanation: q = F(K, L) is a technical relationship: it says nothing about prices or costs. Cost minimisation comes later, when input prices are added. The last option describes a production possibilities frontier.

options.text: The combinations of two goods an economy can produce with all its resources
The total revenue a firm earns from each level of output it sells
The cheapest way to produce a given level of output at current input prices
The maximum output from each combination of inputs, given the technology

questions.question: What separates the short run from the long run in production theory?
questions.explanation: The short run is any period in which one or more inputs cannot be changed. The long run is long enough to vary all inputs. There is no fixed calendar length: for a coffee shop it may be weeks, for a power plant a decade.

options.text: Whether at least one input is fixed
Whether the period is shorter or longer than one year
Whether the firm is making a profit or a loss
Whether output prices are fixed or flexible during the period

questions.question: Building a new semiconductor fab takes about three years. For a chipmaker, what does this imply?
questions.explanation: An input is fixed when it cannot be changed within the planning horizon. As the horizon lengthens past the construction time, capacity becomes variable — that is how the short run turns into the long run.

options.text: Over a one-year horizon its fab capacity is a fixed input
Its capital is variable as soon as the board approves a new fab
Chipmakers have no short run, because they always plan years ahead
Capital is fixed only if the firm is unprofitable

questions.question: Why must the marginal product curve cut the average product curve at the maximum of AP?
questions.explanation: It is like grades: a new score above your average raises it, a score below lowers it. So while MP is above AP, AP rises; once MP falls below AP, AP falls. The turning point is where they are equal.

options.text: Because both curves are derived from the same isoquant and so must touch at its midpoint
If MP > AP the average rises, if MP < AP it falls, so AP peaks where MP = AP
Because total product is at its maximum where they cross
Because MP is always twice as large as AP

questions.question: On a total product curve, how can you read AP and MP graphically?
questions.explanation: AP = q/L is rise over run from the origin, so it is the slope of a ray. MP = Δq/ΔL is the slope of the tangent. AP is greatest where a ray from the origin is just tangent to the TP curve — exactly where AP = MP.

options.text: AP is the height of the curve; MP is its distance from the vertical axis
AP is the slope of the curve itself, while MP is the slope of a ray from the origin to the point
AP is the slope of a ray from the origin to the point; MP is the slope of the curve itself
Both are measured by the area under the total product curve

questions.question: Which statements about total, average and marginal product of labour are correct?
questions.explanation: TP stops rising when the extra worker adds nothing (MP = 0). MP peaks first, then falls through AP at AP's peak. AP is falling well before TP peaks, and MP is still positive in that range.

options.text: MP becomes negative as soon as AP starts falling
AP rises whenever MP is above AP
AP reaches its maximum where total product is at its maximum
MP reaches its maximum after AP does
Total product is at its maximum where MP = 0

questions.question: What does the law of diminishing marginal returns say?
questions.explanation: The law is about adding one input to fixed amounts of the others, such as more workers in the same factory. It is not about returns to scale, where all inputs grow. MP often rises at first, before diminishing returns set in.

options.text: With other inputs fixed, the marginal product of an input eventually falls
Doubling all inputs eventually yields less than double the output, whatever the technology
The marginal product of labour falls from the very first worker
Total output eventually falls as more labour is hired

questions.question: Diminishing marginal returns have set in, but MP is still positive. What happens to total output when one more worker is hired?
questions.explanation: Diminishing returns mean smaller increments, not negative ones. Output falls only if MP becomes negative — for example, when the factory floor is so crowded that workers get in each other's way.

options.text: It stays the same, because the fixed input is fully used
It rises by more than before, because the team is larger
It rises, but by less than the previous worker added
It falls, because each worker reduces the output of the others

questions.question: Malthus predicted mass hunger as population grew on fixed land. Why was he wrong for most of the world?
questions.explanation: Diminishing returns hold for a given technology. Better seeds, fertilisers and machinery shift the whole total product curve up, so output per worker can rise even with more labour on the same land. The same logic applies to new equipment in manufacturing.

options.text: Population stopped growing soon after his prediction
New technology kept shifting the production function up
Diminishing returns do not apply to agriculture
Farmers cut the amount of land they used, which raised productivity

questions.question: What is an isoquant?
questions.explanation: "Iso-quant" means "same quantity". The line of equal cost is the isocost. A family of isoquants (the isoquant map) describes the whole production function, just as an indifference map describes preferences.

options.text: A curve showing the combinations of goods that give equal utility
A curve showing all input combinations that cost the same amount
A curve showing all input combinations that give the same output
A curve showing how output changes when one input changes

questions.question: Why are isoquants normally convex to the origin?
questions.explanation: As the firm replaces capital with more and more labour, each extra worker has less capital to work with and adds less output. So it takes ever more labour to replace each unit of capital, and the isoquant flattens.

options.text: Because firms always use equal amounts of capital and labour
Because input prices rise as the firm buys more of an input, making extra units costlier
Because returns to scale are always increasing
Each input becomes less productive as more of it replaces the other, so MRTS diminishes

questions.question: What would an upward-sloping section of an isoquant mean?
questions.explanation: If more labour must be matched with more capital to keep output constant, the extra labour must be lowering output (negative MP). A firm could produce the same output with less of both inputs, so this "uneconomic region" is never chosen.

options.text: The firm enjoys increasing returns to scale in that range
Both inputs are perfect complements in that range
One input has a negative marginal product there
The firm has found its cost-minimising input mix

questions.question: Why does MRTS(L for K) equal MPL/MPK?
questions.explanation: Moving along an isoquant, the output gained from extra labour must exactly offset the output lost from less capital. Rearranging gives the slope of the isoquant as the ratio of marginal products.

options.text: Output is constant along an isoquant, so MPL·ΔL + MPK·ΔK = 0, which gives −ΔK/ΔL = MPL/MPK
Because MRTS is defined as total output divided by total labour
Because firms always pay each input its marginal product, so MRTS must equal the wage ratio
Because the isocost line has slope w/r

questions.question: Why does the MRTS diminish as a firm moves down an isoquant, using more labour and less capital?
questions.explanation: With more labour and less capital, labour's marginal product drops and capital's rises. Each extra worker can replace less and less capital, which is the same thing as a convex isoquant.

options.text: MPL rises and MPK falls, so the ratio rises
Both marginal products stay the same, but prices change
Output falls as the firm moves along the isoquant
MPL falls and MPK rises, so the ratio MPL/MPK falls

questions.question: A firm's production function is linear: q = aL + bK. What is true?
questions.explanation: With a linear function, one input can always replace the other at the same constant rate, so the elasticity of substitution is infinite. Example: oil- and gas-fired boilers in a dual-fuel plant.

options.text: Isoquants are L-shaped, so inputs are used in fixed proportions
Isoquants are straight lines, so the inputs are perfect substitutes
Isoquants are convex with an elasticity of substitution of exactly 1
Isoquants are vertical, so only labour matters

questions.question: What do fixed-proportions (Leontief) isoquants imply?
questions.explanation: Leontief isoquants are L-shaped: one worker per jackhammer, one pilot per plane. Adding only one input moves you along the flat or vertical arm with no extra output, so the elasticity of substitution is zero.

options.text: Inputs can always replace each other one-for-one, so the isoquants are straight lines
The firm can produce only one level of output
Output rises in proportion to any single input
Inputs cannot replace each other: extra labour without extra capital adds nothing

questions.question: What is the elasticity of input substitution for a Cobb-Douglas production function q = A·K^α·L^β?
questions.explanation: For Cobb-Douglas, a 1% change in the MRTS changes the K/L ratio by 1%. α + β measures returns to scale, not substitution. The linear case is infinite and Leontief is zero.

options.text: Infinite
Exactly 1
α + β
Zero

questions.question: Rank these production functions from the easiest to the hardest substitution between inputs.
questions.explanation: The elasticities of substitution are infinity, 1 and 0. The flatter and straighter the isoquants, the easier it is to swap one input for the other.

options.text: Fixed proportions (Leontief)
Linear (perfect substitutes)
Cobb-Douglas

questions.question: A supply shock makes one imported input scarce. Which firm suffers the largest drop in output?
questions.explanation: A Leontief firm cannot replace the missing input, so output falls in line with it. Firms with a high elasticity of substitution can switch to other inputs, which makes them more resilient to supply-chain shocks.

options.text: A fixed-proportions (Leontief) firm
A firm with a Cobb-Douglas technology
All suffer equally, because the shock affects all inputs
A firm with a linear production function

questions.question: What are increasing returns to scale?
questions.explanation: Returns to scale compare proportional changes in ALL inputs. If output rises by more than that proportion, returns are increasing; equal — constant; less — decreasing.

options.text: Average cost rises as output grows
Output rises as more labour is added to fixed capital
Doubling one input more than doubles output
Doubling all inputs more than doubles output

questions.question: How can q = K^0.6·L^0.6 have diminishing marginal returns to labour and increasing returns to scale at the same time?
questions.explanation: Adding labour alone to fixed capital gives a shrinking MP because 0.6 < 1. Scaling both inputs by 2 multiplies output by 2^1.2 ≈ 2.3. The two ideas answer different questions: one input versus all inputs.

options.text: Each exponent is below 1, so each input alone hits diminishing returns, but they sum to 1.2
The function has constant returns to scale, so both properties hold
It cannot: diminishing returns always mean decreasing returns to scale
Diminishing returns apply only in the long run and increasing returns only in the short run, so they never clash

questions.question: For a Cobb-Douglas function q = A·K^α·L^β, which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: Returns to scale depend on the sum of exponents; diminishing marginal product of one input depends on its own exponent being below 1. A function can have diminishing returns to each input and still have increasing returns to scale.

options.text: If α < 1, the marginal product of capital diminishes
If α + β = 1, there are constant returns to scale
If α + β > 1, there are increasing returns to scale
Diminishing returns to labour imply decreasing returns to scale
If α + β < 1, there are increasing returns to scale

questions.question: Which factors create economies of scale in chipmaking, car production and aerospace?
questions.explanation: Indivisible fixed costs, specialisation and bulk purchasing lower cost per unit as output grows. Extra layers of hierarchy are a source of diseconomies. Higher wages for scarce engineers are an external input-price effect, not a source of scale economies.

options.text: Rising wages for scarce engineers as the industry expands
Volume discounts on purchased components
Huge up-front costs (fabs, design, certification) spread over more units
Specialised workers and machines dedicated to narrow tasks
Longer chains of command as the firm grows

questions.question: Why do some large multinational firms eventually experience decreasing returns to scale?
questions.explanation: Doubling all inputs does not double the capacity to manage them. Information gets lost across layers, and local managers lose touch with the market. Diminishing returns are a short-run, one-input idea, not a cause of scale effects.

options.text: Machines wear out faster when more of them run at once, so output per machine keeps falling
Coordination gets harder: more management layers, slower decisions, weaker incentives
Diminishing returns to labour always appear in large firms
Larger firms must pay higher taxes on every unit

questions.question: How does economic cost differ from accounting cost?
questions.explanation: Accountants record explicit outlays and depreciation for financial statements. Economists ask what resources could earn in their best alternative use, so implicit costs such as forgone rent or the owner's forgone salary count too.

options.text: It excludes depreciation and interest payments
It counts only the cash payments the firm actually makes during the year
It is the same thing, measured at market prices
It includes opportunity costs, even when no money changes hands

questions.question: A firm uses an office building it owns outright. How do an accountant and an economist treat its cost?
questions.explanation: The firm pays no rent, so nothing appears in the books beyond depreciation. But using the building means giving up rental income — a real opportunity cost that should enter decisions such as whether to stay in business.

options.text: Both record the original purchase price as this year's cost
The economist records zero because no cash is paid, while the accountant charges market rent
The accountant records no rent; the economist counts the rent it could earn by leasing it out
Both record zero, because the building is already paid for

questions.question: An owner invests $1 million of her own money in her firm instead of in bonds paying 5%. What is the economic cost of that capital?
questions.explanation: Equity capital is not free: its opportunity cost is the return it could earn elsewhere. An accounting profit smaller than $50,000 means the firm is making an economic loss.

options.text: Only the bank fees on transferring the money
The $50,000 a year she gives up by not holding the bonds
Nothing, because she pays no interest to anyone
The full $1 million, charged in the first year

questions.question: What is a sunk cost?
questions.explanation: Money spent on specialised R&D or custom software is gone whatever the firm does next. Some fixed costs (like a lease that can be cancelled) are avoidable, so they are not sunk.

options.text: An expenditure that has been made and cannot be recovered
A cost that changes with the level of output
The cost of the next unit of output
A fixed cost that can be avoided by shutting down

questions.question: A firm has spent $50m on a project. Finishing it needs $20m more and will bring in $30m. What should it do?
questions.explanation: The $50m is sunk, so it is irrelevant to the decision. Going forward, finishing adds $30m of revenue for $20m of cost, a $10m gain compared with stopping now. Reasoning from total past spending is the sunk-cost fallacy.

options.text: Finish it: $30m extra beats $20m extra
Abandon it, because $30m does not cover the $70m total cost
Finish it only if it can recover the original $50m
Abandon it, because sunk money signals a bad project

questions.question: Which of these are sunk costs?
questions.explanation: A cost is sunk only if it has already been spent and cannot be recovered. A refundable fee and a resaleable truck can be recovered, and future rent can still be avoided.

options.text: A custom-built machine with no resale value
A delivery truck that can be sold at market price
A licence fee that will be refunded if the project is cancelled
Next year's rent on an office the firm has not yet leased
R&D already spent on a product that has now been abandoned

questions.question: Why does marginal cost not depend on fixed cost?
questions.explanation: Producing one more unit adds only to variable cost. That is why a change in fixed cost (for example a licence fee) does not change MC or the profit-maximising output, as long as the firm stays open.

options.text: Fixed cost is sunk, so firms forget about it
Fixed cost is already included in average cost, so counting it twice would be wrong
Fixed cost does not change with output, so ΔTC/Δq = ΔVC/Δq
Marginal cost is measured only in the long run

questions.question: Why does the MC curve pass through the minimum point of the ATC curve?
questions.explanation: Marginal cost pulls the average toward itself. The same logic explains why MC also cuts AVC at its minimum — it is the same rule that makes MP cut AP at its maximum.

options.text: MC below ATC pulls it down, MC above pulls it up
Because MC is the derivative of ATC
Because fixed cost is lowest at that level of output
Because the firm always produces at minimum ATC

questions.question: Which statements about short-run cost curves are correct?
questions.explanation: AFC = FC/q falls continuously, so ATC and AVC get closer as output grows. MC crosses AVC and ATC at their minimums, not at its own minimum — MC reaches its own minimum earlier.

options.text: Average fixed cost falls as output rises
ATC = AVC + AFC
MC is unaffected by a change in fixed cost
MC crosses AVC at the minimum point of MC
The gap between ATC and AVC narrows as output rises

questions.question: On the graph, where does MC cut the ATC curve?
questions.explanation: MC crosses AVC at its minimum (q₁, the shutdown point) and ATC at its minimum (q₂, the break-even point). The minimum of MC comes earlier, at a lower output.

options.text: At the minimum of MC itself
At the minimum of AVC, which is the shutdown point at q₁
At the minimum of ATC, the break-even point at q₂
MC never meets the ATC curve

questions.question: What is the slope of an isocost line TC = wL + rK, with labour on the horizontal axis?
questions.explanation: Solving for K gives K = TC/r − (w/r)·L. The slope is the market rate at which capital can be swapped for labour at constant cost. −MPL/MPK is the slope of an isoquant.

options.text: −MPL/MPK
−r/w
−TC/r
−w/r

questions.question: Which condition describes the cost-minimising input mix for a given output?
questions.explanation: The lowest isocost line that reaches the isoquant is tangent to it. At that point the extra output per dollar spent on labour equals the extra output per dollar on capital.

options.text: MRTS = w/r, or equivalently MPL/w = MPK/r
MPL = MPK, so each input adds the same output
MRTS = r/w
w·L = r·K, so spending is split equally between inputs

questions.question: A firm finds that MPL/w > MPK/r. How should it adjust?
questions.explanation: A dollar spent on labour adds more output than a dollar spent on capital. Moving money from capital to labour lowers cost for the same output, and as L rises MPL falls until the ratios are equal.

options.text: Use more labour and less capital
Raise wages to attract better workers
Cut both inputs in the same proportion
Use more capital and less labour

questions.question: What is a firm's long-run expansion path?
questions.explanation: For each isoquant, find the tangency with the lowest isocost line; linking these points gives the expansion path. From it you can read the long-run total cost of each output level.

options.text: The combinations of inputs that give the same output
The path of the firm's output over time as it grows and enters new markets
The cost-minimising input combinations for each level of output
The set of points where marginal cost equals price

questions.question: The wage doubles while the rental rate of capital stays the same. How does the firm's cost-minimising input mix change?
questions.explanation: The isocost becomes twice as steep, so the tangency moves to a point with less labour and more capital on each isoquant. The expansion path rotates toward the capital axis. How far depends on the elasticity of substitution.

options.text: The input mix stays the same, but output falls
It substitutes capital for labour, so the K/L ratio rises
It doubles both inputs to keep output constant
It uses more labour, because each worker is now more valuable

questions.question: How is the long-run average cost curve related to short-run average cost curves?
questions.explanation: In the long run the firm can pick any plant size, so for each output it chooses the plant with the lowest SAC. The envelope touches each SAC at one point, and it never lies above any of them.

options.text: LAC is their lower envelope: the lowest SAC for each output
LAC lies above all SAC curves because the long run is costlier
LAC is the horizontal sum of all SAC curves
LAC links the minimum points of all SAC curves

questions.question: With economies of scale, where does the LAC curve touch a short-run average cost curve?
questions.explanation: When LAC is falling, it is cheaper to produce a given output with a slightly larger plant run below capacity. Only at the bottom of LAC (constant returns) does the tangency fall on an SAC's minimum. With diseconomies, it falls to the right of it.

options.text: On the falling part of that SAC, to the left of its minimum
LAC never touches SAC curves when there are economies of scale
On the rising part of that SAC, to the right of its minimum
Exactly at the minimum of each SAC

questions.question: What are economies of scope?
questions.explanation: Scope economies come from shared inputs: one fleet of trucks, a shared brand, common R&D. They are distinct from scale economies (volume of one product) and learning effects (cumulative output).

options.text: One firm making two products costs less than two firms making one each
A firm's costs fall when it buys inputs from many suppliers
Average cost falls as a firm makes more and more of a single product line
Costs fall as workers gain experience

questions.question: How is the degree of economies of scope measured?
questions.explanation: The formula compares the cost of separate production with joint production. SC > 0 means economies of scope (joint is cheaper); SC < 0 means diseconomies. ΔC/C over Δq/q is the cost–output elasticity used for scale.

options.text: SC = (ΔC/C) ÷ (Δq/q)
SC = C(q₁, q₂) ÷ [C(q₁) + C(q₂)]
SC = 1 − MC/AC
SC = [C(q₁) + C(q₂) − C(q₁, q₂)] ÷ C(q₁, q₂)

questions.question: For a logistics firm carrying both parcels and freight, SC = 0.25. What does that mean?
questions.explanation: SC is the cost saving from joint production, measured as a share of the joint cost. Shared hubs, IT systems and trucks make the combined firm cheaper — a competitive edge over single-product rivals.

options.text: Each extra parcel costs 25% less than the last one
The firm enjoys 25% economies of scale
Producing both separately would cost 25% more than producing them together
Joint production costs 25% more than producing the two services separately

questions.question: How does the learning curve differ from economies of scale?
questions.explanation: Economies of scale move the firm along a given LAC curve when it produces more per period. Learning shifts the cost curves down as workers and managers gain experience, even at the same output rate.

options.text: Learning raises cost per unit, while scale lowers it
They are the same effect, just measured over different time horizons
Learning applies only to capital, scale only to labour
Learning depends on cumulative output; scale on output per period

questions.question: An aircraft maker has an 80% learning curve. What happens each time cumulative output doubles?
questions.explanation: If plane 1 takes 100,000 hours, plane 2 takes 80,000, plane 4 takes 64,000 and plane 8 about 51,200. The savings shrink in absolute terms as production matures, which is why new aircraft programmes start with high unit costs.

options.text: Total labour hours rise by 80%
Labour hours per plane fall to 80% of their previous level
Unit cost falls by 20% every year, whatever the output
Labour hours per plane fall by 80%

questions.question: Why might a firm price below its current cost when it is far up the learning curve?
questions.explanation: When cost depends on cumulative output, each unit sold today also reduces tomorrow's cost. Aggressive early pricing can therefore be profitable over the product's life. Pindyck uses this to explain pricing in chips and aircraft.

options.text: Because learning costs are sunk and can be ignored
Higher sales now speed up learning and lower future costs
Because learning curves raise demand for the product
To keep its cost curves from shifting down

questions.question: Which conditions define a perfectly competitive market?
questions.explanation: Price taking, product homogeneity and free entry/exit are the three conditions. Zero ECONOMIC profit is a long-run outcome, not a condition, and accounting profit is usually positive. Heavy advertising points to differentiated products.

options.text: Every firm earns zero accounting profit at all times
All firms sell an identical product
Each firm is too small to affect the market price
Firms can enter and exit freely
Firms compete mainly through advertising

questions.question: Why does a perfectly competitive firm face a horizontal demand curve?
questions.explanation: Raise your price slightly and you lose every customer to identical rivals; you can sell all you want at the market price. Market demand itself still slopes downward — only the individual firm's demand is flat.

options.text: It is tiny relative to the market, and rivals sell identical goods
Market demand for the product is perfectly elastic
Its marginal cost is constant, so it can supply any amount at one price
The government fixes the price in competitive markets

questions.question: Why does any firm maximise profit where MR = MC?
questions.explanation: Profit π(q) = R(q) − C(q) peaks where dπ/dq = MR − MC = 0. This holds for all firms — competitive, monopolies and oligopolists. It maximises profit, not revenue.

options.text: Because total revenue is at its maximum at the output where MR equals MC
Below that point extra units add profit; above it they cut profit
Because average cost is lowest at that point
Because price equals average cost at that point

questions.question: Why does MR = MC become P = MC for a competitive firm?
questions.explanation: Selling one more unit does not lower the price on other units, so each unit adds exactly P to revenue. For a firm with a downward-sloping demand curve, MR < P.

options.text: Price equals marginal cost because demand is downward sloping
A price taker gets the market price for every extra unit, so MR = P
Competitive firms are required by law to price at marginal cost
Competitive firms ignore marginal revenue and set price by cost

questions.question: The P line crosses the MC curve twice — once where MC is falling and once where MC is rising. Which output maximises profit?
questions.explanation: Where MC is falling, producing one more unit costs less than P, so expanding raises profit — that point is a profit minimum. The second-order condition requires MC to cut P from below.

options.text: The output where MC is falling
The output where MC is rising
Neither, because the firm should shut down
Either, because both satisfy P = MC

questions.question: What is the short-run shutdown rule for a competitive firm?
