questions.explanation: Below AVCmin, revenue does not even cover variable costs, so every unit adds to the loss. Above it, producing covers VC and part of FC, which beats shutting down.

options.text: Shut down if price is below minimum average total cost
Shut down if price is below marginal cost at current output
Shut down whenever the firm makes an economic loss
Shut down if price is below minimum average variable cost

questions.question: The price is below ATC but above AVC. What should a competitive firm do in the short run?
questions.explanation: Shutting down loses the whole fixed cost. Producing loses less: total revenue covers variable cost, and what is left helps pay fixed cost. In the long run, if prices stay this low, the firm will exit.

options.text: Raise its price to cover average total cost
Produce at the output where ATC is lowest, to keep the loss per unit small
Shut down immediately, because it is making a loss
Keep producing where P = MC to cover all variable cost

questions.question: Why are fixed costs irrelevant to the short-run decision to produce?
questions.explanation: Shutting down in the short run does not remove fixed costs such as rent under a lease. Only costs that change with the decision — variable costs — matter.

options.text: Because they are always small compared with variable costs
They are paid whether or not the firm produces
Because accountants exclude them from the income statement
Because they become zero once the firm shuts down

questions.question: The market price is $10. Using the graph (AVCmin = $6, ATCmin = $15), what should this firm do?
questions.explanation: $10 is above the shutdown price of $6, so producing covers all variable cost and some fixed cost. The best output is where P = MC, on the rising MC curve between the shutdown and break-even points. The loss per unit is ATC − P.

options.text: Produce at q₂, where average total cost is lowest
Produce where AVC = $10, because the price covers AVC
Shut down, because the price is below ATCmin
Produce where MC = $10, between q₁ and q₂, accepting a loss

questions.question: Using the graph, the market price falls to $5. What should the firm do in the short run?
questions.explanation: Below the minimum of AVC, every unit loses more than its variable cost. Shutting down limits the loss to the fixed cost.

options.text: Keep producing where MC = $5 to minimise the loss
Produce at q₂, the break-even point
Produce at q₁, the shutdown point
Shut down: $5 is below AVCmin

questions.question: Why is a competitive firm's short-run supply curve its MC curve above AVCmin?
questions.explanation: For each possible price, the profit-maximising quantity is read off the MC curve. Below AVCmin the firm produces nothing, so that part of MC is not on the supply curve.

options.text: Because a competitive firm always produces at minimum MC
Because supply is the horizontal sum of fixed and variable costs
Because the supply curve must pass through ATCmin
For each price above the shutdown point, the firm produces where P = MC

questions.question: The price of a variable input (such as fuel) rises. What happens to a competitive firm's supply curve?
questions.explanation: A higher variable input price raises the cost of each extra unit. At any given market price, the firm now produces less — a leftward shift of supply. A change in fixed cost would not shift supply.

options.text: MC shifts down, so supply shifts right
Supply shifts left
Only fixed cost rises, so supply is unchanged
The firm moves along its supply curve to a lower output

questions.question: With constant input prices, how is the short-run market supply curve derived?
questions.explanation: At each price, add up the quantities that all firms would supply. Firms with lower shutdown points start supplying at lower prices, so the market curve can have steps or kinks.

options.text: By averaging the firms' ATC curves
By vertically summing each firm's marginal cost
By horizontally summing each firm's supply (MC above AVCmin)
By drawing a line through each firm's break-even point

questions.question: Why is industry supply steeper than the horizontal sum of firms' MC curves when input prices rise with industry output?
questions.explanation: The simple sum assumes each firm's MC is fixed. If the whole industry expands at once and bids up the price of a scarce input, each firm's MC shifts up, so the industry supplies less at each price.

options.text: Because demand becomes more elastic as output rises
Because some firms exit the market as output expands
Because each firm's fixed cost rises with industry output, raising every firm's shutdown price
As all firms expand together, input prices rise, which shifts every firm's MC curve up

questions.question: What is producer surplus for a firm?
questions.explanation: Producer surplus is the area above the supply (MC) curve and below the price. Profit subtracts all costs, including fixed costs, so the two differ.

options.text: Total revenue minus total cost
The fixed cost the firm recovers in the short run
The sum over all units of price minus marginal cost
Price minus average total cost on the last unit

questions.question: How do producer surplus and profit relate in the short run?
questions.explanation: The area under MC adds up variable cost only, so PS = TR − VC. Profit = TR − VC − FC, so PS exceeds profit by the fixed cost. In the long run (no fixed costs), PS and profit coincide.

options.text: PS = profit + fixed cost = TR − VC
PS = profit, because both use total revenue
PS = TR − TC + VC
PS = profit − fixed cost

questions.question: A firm has revenue of $100, variable cost of $60 and fixed cost of $30. What are its producer surplus and profit?
questions.explanation: PS = TR − VC = 100 − 60 = 40. Profit subtracts fixed cost as well: 40 − 30 = 10. A positive PS even with a loss is why firms keep producing in the short run.

options.text: PS = $40, profit = $40
PS = $10, profit = $40
PS = $40, profit = $10
PS = $70, profit = $10

questions.question: Firms in a competitive industry earn positive economic profits. What happens in the long run?
questions.explanation: Free entry is the key. Profit attracts new firms, which shifts market supply out until the price equals the minimum of LAC. Losses work in reverse, through exit.

options.text: Existing firms raise prices further to keep profits high
New firms enter, supply shifts right and price falls until economic profit is zero
The government taxes the profits away
Firms leave, because rivals start a price war that drives price below average variable cost

questions.question: Why do owners keep running firms that earn zero economic profit?
questions.explanation: Economic cost already includes the owner's opportunity costs. Zero economic profit means the firm earns exactly what its resources could earn elsewhere — accounting profit is positive.

options.text: They expect the government to subsidise them
Because exit is forbidden in competitive markets
Zero economic profit means a normal return on their capital and time
Because zero economic profit means zero accounting profit as well

questions.question: Demand for a product rises in a constant-cost competitive industry. Put the adjustment in order.
questions.explanation: Short-run profit is the signal; entry is the response. In a constant-cost industry, the long-run price ends where it started, but more firms are producing a larger total output.

options.text: Price returns to LACmin and economic profit is zero again
New firms enter the industry
Market supply shifts right
Existing firms expand along their MC curves and earn economic profit
The market price rises above LACmin

questions.question: In a constant-cost industry, what does the long-run supply curve look like?
questions.explanation: If expanding the industry does not change input prices, new firms produce at the same LACmin, so any quantity can be supplied at that price.

options.text: Downward sloping, because firms learn over time
Vertical, because the number of firms is fixed
Upward sloping, because input prices rise
Horizontal at the minimum of LAC

questions.question: Why is the long-run supply curve in an increasing-cost industry upward sloping?
questions.explanation: Oil, mining and farming need scarce land, deposits or skills. When the industry expands, these inputs get dearer (an external diseconomy), so the long-run price at which firms break even rises with output.

options.text: Expansion bids up the prices of scarce inputs, raising every firm's costs
Demand becomes less elastic as the industry grows
Each firm faces diminishing returns to labour in the long run as it hires more
New firms are always less efficient than existing ones

questions.question: What could make a competitive industry's long-run supply curve downward sloping?
questions.explanation: In a decreasing-cost industry, expansion produces external economies: suppliers achieve scale economies, specialised services appear, or the labour pool improves. Each firm's cost curves shift down as the industry grows.

options.text: Each firm enjoys increasing returns to scale, so the largest firm ends up serving the market
Industry growth lowers input prices, for example through scale economies at suppliers
Demand falls as more firms enter
Firms collude to cut prices as the industry grows

questions.question: In welfare economics, when is a competitive market outcome called efficient?
questions.explanation: At the competitive equilibrium every unit worth more to a buyer than it costs to produce is traded, and no other unit is. Any intervention that changes quantity lowers total surplus.

options.text: When it maximises the sum of consumer and producer surplus
When the government's revenue from the market is as large as it can be
When every consumer pays the same price
When producers earn the highest possible profit

questions.question: What is a deadweight loss?
questions.explanation: Transfers move surplus from one group to another; a deadweight loss is surplus that disappears because mutually beneficial trades no longer happen.

options.text: The fixed cost a firm pays even when it shuts down
Total surplus that nobody gets
A transfer of surplus from consumers to producers
The tax revenue the government collects

questions.question: On the graph, which areas make up the deadweight loss of the price ceiling?
questions.explanation: B is the surplus consumers lose on units no longer produced, and C is the surplus producers lose on those units. A is a transfer from producers to the consumers who still buy, so it is not a net loss.

options.text: A + B
B + C
A + C
A only

questions.question: On the graph, what does area A represent?
questions.explanation: Consumers who still get the good now pay Pmax instead of P₀, so the rectangle A moves from sellers to buyers. Unlike B + C, it stays inside the economy.

options.text: The government's revenue from the price control
Producer surplus lost on units that are no longer sold
Surplus lost by consumers who can no longer buy
Surplus transferred from producers to consumers who still buy

questions.question: Which statements about the price ceiling on the graph are correct?
questions.explanation: Consumers gain the rectangle A but lose the triangle B. If demand is steep, B can exceed A, so even consumers lose. Producers lose both A and C; the deadweight loss is B + C.

options.text: The change in producer surplus is −A − C
The change in consumer surplus is A − B
Producers gain area A
The deadweight loss equals A + B
If demand is very inelastic, consumers as a group can lose (B > A)

questions.question: When is the deadweight loss of a price ceiling largest?
questions.explanation: Elastic supply means output collapses when the price is held down, so many valuable trades are lost. Inelastic (steep) demand makes each lost unit very valuable to buyers. With perfectly inelastic supply, quantity does not change, so the ceiling is a pure transfer.

options.text: When supply is perfectly inelastic
When demand is perfectly elastic and supply is inelastic
When supply is elastic and demand is inelastic
When the ceiling is set just below the equilibrium price

questions.question: A minimum wage is set above the market-clearing wage. What happens in the labour market?
questions.explanation: At the higher wage, firms demand less labour while more people want to work. Workers who keep their jobs gain; those priced out lose, and the jobs that are no longer created are a deadweight loss.

options.text: Employment rises because work pays better
Employment falls and there is excess supply of labour
Firms hire more workers to spread the higher wage cost over more output
The wage returns to equilibrium as firms bid it down

questions.question: A price floor is set above equilibrium, but the government does not buy the surplus. Why might producers end up WORSE off?
questions.explanation: Producers gain on the units they sell at the higher price, but buyers take less. If firms expand output in the hope of selling at the floor, they pay for production that ends up unsold — this can wipe out their gain.

options.text: Because the floor lowers the price they receive on every unit they sell
Unsold output can cost them more than they gain on units sold
Producers always gain from a price floor
Because consumers buy more at the higher price, and producers cannot keep up with demand

questions.question: Which effects of a binding minimum wage should you expect?
questions.explanation: A wage floor raises quantity supplied and cuts quantity demanded, so the gap — unemployment — widens. The gain to employed workers is a transfer from employers; the jobs lost are a deadweight loss.

options.text: Unemployment falls
Fewer workers are employed
More people want to work at the higher wage
Firms hire more workers to raise productivity
Workers who keep their jobs earn more

questions.question: Under a price support, the state buys all surplus output at the support price Ps. Why is this so costly to society?
questions.explanation: Consumers pay more and buy less; the state buys (Q₂ − Q₁) at Ps. Producers gain, but the total cost to consumers and taxpayers far exceeds that gain, especially when the surplus has little value.

options.text: The support lowers the market price that consumers pay
The state earns a profit by reselling the surplus abroad at world prices
Taxpayers pay for the surplus, which is often stored or destroyed, on top of the consumer loss
Farmers produce less, so food becomes scarce

questions.question: Why is a direct cash payment to farmers cheaper for society than a price support that gives them the same gain?
questions.explanation: Pindyck shows that giving farmers a sum equal to their gain from the support costs much less than the support itself, which makes consumers pay more and leaves the state buying unwanted output.

options.text: Because cash payments are smaller than the farmers' gain from the price support
A cash transfer leaves quantities unchanged, so nothing is wasted
Because consumers pay for the cash transfer through higher food prices
Because cash transfers raise output and lower food prices for consumers

questions.question: A city caps the number of taxi medallions below the competitive number of taxis. What follows?
questions.explanation: Restricting supply raises the price above marginal cost. The extra margin flows to whoever holds the scarce licence, which is why medallions sold for over $1 million in New York before ride-hailing apps cut their value.

options.text: Riders are better off because the taxis are less crowded
Fares fall because each taxi carries more passengers
Fares rise, licence holders earn rents, and lost trips are a deadweight loss
Drivers' incomes fall, because each driver must share the market with more taxis

questions.question: A production quota (or acreage limit) cuts supply below the competitive level. Who gains and who loses?
questions.explanation: A quota works like a monopoly restriction. Prices rise, consumers lose surplus and producers gain on the units they still sell. The output that is no longer produced, although valued above its cost, is the deadweight loss.

options.text: Consumers gain because quotas lower prices
Producers always lose, because they sell fewer units at the same price as before
Both groups gain, because the quota corrects a market failure
Consumers lose, producers may gain, and society bears a deadweight loss

questions.question: On the graph, which area is the government's tariff revenue?
questions.explanation: Revenue is the tariff per unit (P* − Pw) times the quantity still imported (Q′d − Q′s), which is the rectangle D. A is the gain to domestic producers.

options.text: D
A
A + B + C + D
B + C

questions.question: On the graph, which areas are the deadweight loss of the tariff?
questions.explanation: B is the production distortion: domestic firms make units that could be imported more cheaply. C is the consumption distortion: buyers give up units they value above the world price. A and D are transfers.

options.text: A + D
D only
B + C
A + B

questions.question: Which statements about the tariff on the graph are correct?
questions.explanation: Consumers lose the whole trapezoid between the two price lines. A goes to producers and D to the state, so the net loss is B + C. D is lost only if the restriction is a quota whose rents are captured by foreigners.

options.text: Domestic consumers lose A + B + C + D
Area B is the extra cost of producing at home what could be imported more cheaply
Under a tariff, area D is lost to the importing country
Area C is the value of purchases consumers give up
Domestic producers gain A

questions.question: An import quota restricts imports to the same volume as a tariff would. When is its welfare cost the same?
questions.explanation: Both raise the domestic price to the same level. Under a tariff, D is government revenue. Under a quota, D is a "quota rent" earned by whoever holds the licences — if domestic hands keep it, the net loss is still B + C.

options.text: Only when domestic demand is perfectly elastic
Never — a quota always costs more than a tariff
When the domestic government auctions the import licences
When foreign exporters receive the import licences for free

questions.question: Why can a "voluntary" export restraint (like Japan's car export quotas to the US in the 1980s) hurt the importing country more than a tariff?
questions.explanation: Exporters sell fewer cars at the higher domestic price and keep the extra margin. The importing country loses B + C + D instead of B + C.

options.text: Because a quota lowers domestic prices more than a tariff
Because quotas lead to more imports than tariffs
The foreign exporters capture the quota rent (area D), so it leaves the country
Because foreign firms must cut their prices, which hurts domestic producers

questions.question: Who bears most of the burden of a per-unit tax?
questions.explanation: The side that cannot easily walk away ends up absorbing the tax. Cigarette smokers (inelastic demand) bear most of tobacco taxes; workers with inelastic supply bear most of payroll taxes.

options.text: The side of the market whose demand or supply is less elastic
Always the sellers, because they hand the money to the government
Always the buyers, because prices rise
The side of the market that is more elastic

questions.question: What does the formula Es/(Es − Ed) measure?
questions.explanation: With Ed negative, the denominator is positive. If demand is perfectly inelastic (Ed = 0), buyers bear the whole tax; if supply is perfectly inelastic (Es = 0), sellers bear it all. Sellers' share is −Ed/(Es − Ed).

options.text: The share of a per-unit tax passed on to buyers
The change in quantity caused by the tax
The share of the tax borne by sellers
The deadweight loss of the tax as a share of revenue

questions.question: On the graph the tax is Pb − Ps = 3. Who bears more of it, and why?
questions.explanation: The buyers' price rises from 4 to 6 and the sellers' price falls from 4 to 3. At the original equilibrium Ed = −0.5 and Es = 1, so buyers bear 1/(1 + 0.5) = 2/3 of the tax.

options.text: Buyers (2 of the 3): demand is less elastic than supply here
They split it equally, because the tax is a fixed amount per unit
Sellers (2 of the 3): sellers pay the tax to the government
Buyers bear all of it, because the buyers' price rises

questions.question: On the graph, which areas make up the government's tax revenue?
questions.explanation: Revenue = tax × quantity sold = (Pb − Ps)·Q₁. A is the part paid by buyers, D the part paid by sellers. B + C is the deadweight loss on units that are no longer traded.

options.text: D only
A + D
B + C
A + B

questions.question: Does it matter whether a sales tax is legally levied on sellers or on buyers?
questions.explanation: Legal (statutory) incidence is about who writes the cheque. Economic incidence depends only on elasticities. A tax on sellers shifts supply up by t; a tax on buyers shifts demand down by t — the result is the same.

options.text: No: either way the wedge between Pb and Ps is the same
Only in the long run, when firms can pass the tax on in their prices
Yes: a tax on buyers creates no deadweight loss
Yes: the side that legally pays the tax bears all of its burden

questions.question: Why does a per-unit production subsidy create a deadweight loss?
questions.explanation: With a subsidy s, buyers' price falls and sellers' price rises until Ps − Pb = s. The extra units cost more to produce than buyers are willing to pay. The cost to taxpayers is larger than the combined gain in consumer and producer surplus.

options.text: Because it lowers output below the competitive level
Extra units cost more to make than buyers value them
It does not: the subsidy is a pure transfer from taxpayers to firms
Because consumers pay more for the good

questions.question: How is the benefit of a per-unit subsidy split between buyers and sellers?
questions.explanation: A subsidy is a negative tax. The less elastic side of the market gets the larger share, whichever side the money is paid to.

options.text: It is split equally between buyers and sellers
Buyers always get the whole subsidy, through lower prices
Sellers always keep the whole subsidy
By the same elasticity rule as a tax: buyers get Es/(Es − Ed) of it

questions.question: Where does MR = P·(1 + 1/Ed) come from?
questions.explanation: Selling one more unit brings in P but lowers the price on all units sold, by Q·ΔP/ΔQ. Writing that term as P·(Q/P)(ΔP/ΔQ) = P/Ed gives the formula, valid for any demand curve.

options.text: MR = P·Q divided by the elasticity of demand
MR = P + Q·(ΔP/ΔQ), and Q·(ΔP/ΔQ) = P/Ed
MR equals price times the percentage change in quantity
It is an approximation that only holds for linear demand

questions.question: Why does a profit-maximising monopolist never produce on the inelastic part of the demand curve?
questions.explanation: With |Ed| < 1, MR = P(1 + 1/Ed) is negative. Producing less raises revenue and saves cost, so profit rises. The monopolist moves up the demand curve until MR = MC > 0, which is only possible where demand is elastic.

options.text: Because demand is always elastic for a monopolist's product
There MR < 0, so cutting output would raise revenue and lower cost
Because the government forbids it
Because consumers refuse to buy when demand is inelastic

questions.question: On a straight-line demand curve, where is marginal revenue equal to zero?
questions.explanation: With linear demand P = a − bQ, MR = a − 2bQ falls twice as fast, hitting zero at half the maximum quantity. That is where |Ed| = 1 and total revenue peaks.

options.text: At the midpoint, where demand is unit elastic
At the point where the curve meets the quantity axis
Wherever price equals marginal cost
At the point where the curve meets the price axis

questions.question: On the graph, what output and price does the monopolist choose?
questions.explanation: The monopolist picks the quantity where MR = MC, then charges the highest price buyers will pay for that quantity — read up to the demand curve, not off the MC curve.

options.text: Qm, where MR = MC, and price Pm
Qc, where demand meets MC, and price Pc
Qm, where MR = MC, and price equal to MC at Qm
The output where MR = 0, to maximise revenue

questions.question: What does the Lerner index measure?
questions.explanation: L ranges from 0 (perfect competition, P = MC) toward 1. A high Lerner index does not guarantee high profit — average cost may also be high.

options.text: The firm's share of total industry sales, measured in revenue
(P − MC)/P, the markup of price over marginal cost
The ratio of price to average cost
The firm's profit as a share of revenue

questions.question: A monopolist faces Ed = −4 at its chosen output. How high is its price relative to marginal cost?
questions.explanation: L = −1/Ed = 0.25, so P = MC/(1 − 0.25) = 1.33·MC. The rule of thumb P = MC/(1 + 1/Ed) shows the markup shrinks as demand gets more elastic.

options.text: About 33% above MC (L = 0.25)
About 25% above MC (L = 0.33)
Equal to MC, because demand is elastic
Four times MC

questions.question: Cheap imports of close substitutes become available. What happens to a domestic monopolist's markup?
questions.explanation: The Lerner index depends on the elasticity of the firm's own demand. Import competition gives buyers alternatives, so demand becomes more elastic and the profit-maximising markup falls — even if the firm remains the only domestic producer.

options.text: It disappears entirely, because the firm becomes a price taker
It rises, because the monopolist must cover higher costs
It shrinks, because its own demand becomes more elastic
It stays the same, because the monopolist still has no domestic rival

questions.question: According to Pindyck & Rubinfeld, which factors determine a firm's monopoly power?
questions.explanation: A firm's own demand is at least as elastic as market demand. More rivals and more aggressive competition make it more elastic. Fixed costs and past profits do not change the markup a firm can charge.

options.text: How the firms interact with each other
The firm's accounting profit last year
The size of the firm's fixed costs
The number of firms in the market
The elasticity of market demand

questions.question: How do patents and economies of scale sustain monopoly power?
questions.explanation: Market power lasts only if entry is blocked. Patents and licences block it legally. Large economies of scale mean a small entrant has a much higher average cost than the incumbent.

options.text: They block entry, legally or through a cost advantage
They raise demand for the monopolist's product
They make market demand perfectly inelastic
They let the monopolist set price below marginal cost to drive rivals out

questions.question: On the graph, which areas make up the deadweight loss of monopoly?
questions.explanation: Between Qm and Qc, each unit is valued by buyers above its marginal cost but is not produced. B is the consumer surplus lost on those units, C the producer surplus lost on them.

options.text: B + C
C only
A
A + B

questions.question: Compared with perfect competition, which statements about the monopoly on the graph are correct?
questions.explanation: Consumers pay more on the units they still buy (A) and lose units they valued (B). The monopolist gains A but loses C on units no longer sold. Only B + C is a net loss.

options.text: A is part of the deadweight loss
Consumers lose A + B
A is a transfer from consumers to the monopolist
Consumers gain C
The producer's surplus changes by A − C

questions.question: Why might the true social cost of monopoly exceed the deadweight loss triangle?
questions.explanation: Rent-seeking — lobbying, litigation, excess capacity built to deter entry — uses up real resources. In the extreme, firms may spend the whole monopoly profit trying to get it, so the social cost includes much of A as well as B + C.

options.text: Because the deadweight loss triangle ignores the losses suffered by the monopolist's own suppliers
Firms may spend much of the monopoly profit on lobbying to get or keep it
Because monopolists always produce above the competitive level
Because consumer surplus under monopoly is always zero

questions.question: A regulator caps a monopolist's price at the competitive level Pc, where demand meets MC. What happens?
questions.explanation: Below the cap, the monopolist cannot raise its price by cutting output, so each extra unit adds Pc to revenue. It expands until MC = Pc. A cap that is set too low would push output down and create a shortage.

options.text: Nothing changes, because the monopolist sets its own price
Output rises to the competitive level, and the deadweight loss disappears
Output falls, because the monopolist earns less per unit
A shortage appears, exactly as with a price ceiling imposed on a competitive market

questions.question: How does a price ceiling on a monopolist differ from one on a competitive market?
questions.explanation: In a competitive market the price was already at MC, so a ceiling below it cuts supply. A monopolist restricts output to keep the price high, and a well-set cap removes that incentive.

options.text: In both cases output rises toward the efficient level
In both cases output falls by the same amount
On a monopolist it can raise output; in a competitive market it always lowers output
On a monopolist it always causes shortages; in a competitive market it never does

questions.question: What is a natural monopoly?
questions.explanation: The key is cost subadditivity: one firm producing everything costs less than splitting output, usually because LAC keeps falling over the relevant range (power grids, water mains, rail tracks).

options.text: One firm can serve the whole market more cheaply than several
A monopoly that controls a natural resource such as oil or water
Any monopoly that the government has not created
A firm that is the first to enter a new market

questions.question: Why does marginal-cost pricing make a natural monopoly lose money?
questions.explanation: When average cost falls, each extra unit costs less than the average, so MC < AC. Pricing at MC gives the efficient quantity but loses (AC − MC) on every unit, which would require a subsidy.

options.text: Because marginal cost is always zero for utilities
With falling average cost, MC lies below AC, so P = MC does not cover AC
Because the regulator also taxes the firm's profits
Because demand is inelastic, so revenue falls when price is low

questions.question: What does average-cost pricing achieve for a regulated natural monopoly?
questions.explanation: Setting P = AC where AC meets demand covers all costs, so the firm needs no subsidy. Because P > MC at that point, a small deadweight loss remains — a compromise between efficiency and solvency.

options.text: The same output and price as an unregulated monopoly, just with lower costs
Losses that must be covered by taxpayers
The efficient output with zero deadweight loss
The firm breaks even, but output is still below the efficient level

questions.question: Why does marginal expenditure lie above average expenditure for a monopsonist?
questions.explanation: Facing an upward-sloping supply curve, the buyer pays a higher price for the extra unit and for every unit already bought. So the cost of the extra unit exceeds the price (the AE curve).

options.text: To buy one more unit it must raise the price paid on all units
Because sellers charge the monopsonist a premium
Because the monopsonist has higher fixed costs than other buyers
Because average expenditure is falling as more is bought

questions.question: On the graph, how much labour does the monopsonist hire and what wage does it pay?
questions.explanation: The buyer adds labour until the extra value (MV) equals the extra expenditure (ME). It then pays only what the supply curve says is needed to attract Lm workers — the lower wage wm.

options.text: Lm, where ME = MV, at the wage given by the ME curve
Lc, at the wage given by the ME curve
Lm, where ME = MV, at wage wm read off the supply curve
Lc, where supply meets MV, at wage wc

questions.question: On the graph, which areas make up the deadweight loss of monopsony?
questions.explanation: The workers between Lm and Lc would produce more value (MV) than they need to be paid (supply). B is the buyer's lost surplus and C the sellers' lost surplus on those units. A is a transfer from workers to the monopsonist.

options.text: A
A + C
B only
B + C

questions.question: Why is monopsony power often found in regional labour markets?
questions.explanation: A mine, hospital or factory that is the main employer in a town faces an upward-sloping labour supply. It can pay below the value of what workers produce, because they would have to move or commute to work elsewhere.

options.text: Employers must pay a premium to attract workers to remote areas
Labour supply to the firm is perfectly elastic in small towns
One large employer dominates, so workers have few alternatives nearby
Workers form unions that set wages above the market level

questions.question: Using the monopsony graph, rank these values from highest to lowest.
questions.explanation: At Lm, MV = ME = 10, well above the competitive wage of 8, while the monopsonist pays only 6. The gap between MV and the wage paid measures monopsony power.

options.text: Monopsony wage wm
Competitive wage wc
Marginal value of the last worker hired under monopsony

questions.question: Why does charging one uniform price leave a monopolist's potential profit unrealised?
questions.explanation: The area above the price under demand is consumer surplus the firm does not collect. The deadweight loss triangle is profitable trade that does not happen. Price discrimination tries to capture both.

options.text: Because a single price maximises consumer surplus, not profit
Because a single price is always below marginal cost
Because buyers who pay the single price resell the good to others at a higher price
It leaves both consumer surplus and deadweight loss uncaptured

questions.question: What is first-degree (perfect) price discrimination?
questions.explanation: Each unit is sold at the most that buyer is willing to pay. The other options describe second-degree pricing, third-degree pricing and a two-part tariff.

options.text: Charging a fixed fee plus a price per unit
Charging lower prices for larger quantities
Charging different prices to different groups, such as students
Charging each customer their own reservation price

questions.question: Under perfect first-degree price discrimination, what happens to output and surplus?
questions.explanation: The demand curve becomes the firm's MR curve, because selling an extra unit no longer lowers the price of other units. The firm sells until the reservation price equals MC — the efficient quantity — but consumers keep no surplus.

options.text: Output rises above the competitive level and a deadweight loss appears
Output falls below the monopoly level and consumer surplus rises
Output stays at the monopoly level, but price is lower
Output becomes efficient, but the firm takes all the surplus

questions.question: What does a firm need in order to practise first-degree price discrimination?
questions.explanation: The firm must know or estimate each reservation price and prevent arbitrage. With many rivals it would have no power to set prices. If all buyers were identical, there would be nothing to discriminate on.

options.text: Customers with identical demand curves
Knowledge of each customer's willingness to pay
Market power over price
Many competing sellers of the same product
A way to stop customers reselling the product

questions.question: What is second-degree price discrimination?
questions.explanation: Declining block rates for electricity, bulk discounts and data plans are examples. Larger buyers pay less per unit, which lets the firm sell more and capture some surplus from both small and large buyers.

options.text: Charging different prices in different countries
Charging each customer exactly their own reservation price for every unit
Different unit prices for different quantities bought
Charging higher prices at times of peak demand

questions.question: How do quantity discounts let a utility capture surplus without knowing each customer's willingness to pay?
questions.explanation: This is self-selection: the firm designs a menu and lets buyers sort themselves. Heavy users choose the bulk tariff and light users the basic one, so the firm extracts more surplus than with a single price.

options.text: The utility surveys each customer before setting prices
The utility charges each customer the same total amount
Customers pick the block or plan that suits them, revealing their type
The law obliges customers to report their income

questions.question: What conditions maximise profit under third-degree price discrimination between two markets?
questions.explanation: The firm chooses total output where combined MR = MC, then allocates it so the last unit sold in each market adds the same revenue. Prices then differ across markets.

options.text: MR₁ + MR₂ = MC
P₁ = P₂ and MR = MC
MR₁ = MR₂ = MC
P₁ = P₂ = MC

questions.question: Why must marginal revenue be equal in both markets?
questions.explanation: Any gap in MR is an unexploited gain: shifting sales toward the market with higher MR raises revenue while total output and cost stay the same.

options.text: Because competition authorities require it
Otherwise shifting sales between markets would raise revenue
Because the firm must charge the same price in both markets
Because costs are always lower in the market with the higher marginal revenue

questions.question: Under third-degree price discrimination, where will the firm charge the higher price?
questions.explanation: From MR = P(1 + 1/E) in each market: P₁/P₂ = (1 + 1/E₂)/(1 + 1/E₁). Less elastic buyers (business travellers, rich-country patients) get the higher price.

options.text: In the market with more elastic demand
In the market with more customers
Where demand is less elastic
In the market where marginal cost is lower

questions.question: A drug maker faces Ed = −2 in the US and Ed = −4 in Europe, with the same MC. How does the US price compare?
questions.explanation: P_US/P_EU = (1 − 1/4)/(1 − 1/2) = 0.75/0.5 = 1.5. Even with identical costs, the market with less elastic demand pays more.

options.text: 1.5 times the EU price
It is the same, because MC is the same
It is twice the European price
It is half the European price

questions.question: Which are examples of THIRD-degree price discrimination?
questions.explanation: Third-degree pricing splits customers into identifiable groups with different elasticities. Volume discounts are second-degree pricing, a cheaper suite is bundling, and peak pricing is driven by marginal cost (peak-load pricing).

options.text: Student and senior discounts on cinema tickets
A software suite sold for less than its parts
Higher electricity prices at times of peak demand
Lower prices for the same medicine in poorer countries
Lower electricity rates per kWh for very large users

questions.question: How does intertemporal price discrimination work for new electronics or hardcover books?
questions.explanation: Fans with inelastic demand pay a premium to buy first. As time passes, the firm lowers prices to reach buyers with more elastic demand — the hardcover-then-paperback pattern.

options.text: Prices are higher at peak hours because capacity is limited
Every buyer is charged their own reservation price at launch
The firm charges more for larger quantities purchased
High launch prices, lower prices later

questions.question: Why do electricity grids charge more at peak hours?
questions.explanation: Peak-load pricing sets price close to MC in each period. It is efficient: high peak prices reflect high peak costs and shift usage to off-peak hours. Extracting surplus is not the driving force.

options.text: Because demand is more elastic at peak times
To extract consumer surplus from households that cannot switch
Peak marginal cost is higher, as costlier plants must run
Because regulators require a uniform daily price

questions.question: What is the key difference between intertemporal price discrimination and peak-load pricing?
questions.explanation: In intertemporal discrimination the cost is the same over time, but the buyers differ. In peak-load pricing the same buyers may face higher prices, because serving them at the peak costs more.

options.text: There is no difference: both charge more at some times
Different buyers versus different marginal costs
The first is efficient; the second creates deadweight loss
The first applies only to services, the second only to goods

questions.question: A firm with identical customers uses a two-part tariff. What should it set?
questions.explanation: Pricing usage at MC maximises the surplus each customer gets from using the product. The firm then takes all of that surplus through the entry fee, so it captures the whole area under demand above MC.

options.text: Usage price at the monopoly level and entry fee of zero
Usage price of zero and entry fee equal to total cost
Usage price P = MC and entry fee T = each customer's consumer surplus
Entry fee equal to fixed cost and usage price above MC

questions.question: How does a two-part tariff change when customers have different demands?
questions.explanation: A fee equal to the biggest customer's surplus would drive smaller customers away. The firm lowers T, raises P above MC to earn more from heavy users, and balances the two to maximise profit.

options.text: It does not change, because every customer pays the same fee
The usage price is set above MC and the entry fee is lowered so that smaller users still join
The usage price is set at MC, and the entry fee equals the surplus of the largest user
The firm drops the entry fee and charges the monopoly price

questions.question: Which pricing schemes are two-part tariffs?
questions.explanation: Each has an access charge and a usage charge (even if one is hidden, as with printer ink). A single uniform price has no entry component.

options.text: A cheap printer sold with pricey ink cartridges
A monthly phone fee plus a charge per gigabyte
An amusement park with an entry ticket plus a price per ride
A single price per bottle, whatever the quantity bought
A gym membership plus a fee for each class

questions.question: What is the difference between pure and mixed bundling?
questions.explanation: Mixed bundling offers a menu — the bundle at a discount plus each good on its own — which can reach buyers who value only one of the goods highly.

options.text: Pure: goods are sold only as a package. Mixed: goods are sold both as a package and separately
Pure: the bundle is cheaper. Mixed: the bundle costs the sum of the separate prices
Pure: two goods in one package. Mixed: three or more goods
Pure: identical goods sold together. Mixed: different goods sold together

questions.question: When is bundling more profitable than selling goods separately?
questions.explanation: If one customer values the word processor highly and the spreadsheet little, and another the reverse, their total valuations of the bundle are similar. The firm can charge a bundle price near both totals, capturing more surplus than with separate prices.

options.text: When the goods are perfect complements
When customers' reservation prices for the goods are negatively correlated
When marginal costs are very high
When the reservation prices of the goods are positively correlated across customers

questions.question: Why might mixed bundling beat pure bundling for a software or media company?
questions.explanation: With significant marginal cost, forcing a product on someone who values it below cost wastes money. Mixed bundling lets such buyers take one item separately while keeping the bundle for buyers who value both.

options.text: Mixed bundling always gives every buyer the bundle
Pure bundling only works when marginal cost is high, which is rare for software
Pure bundling is illegal in most countries
Some buyers value one item below its marginal cost

questions.question: How does tying (for example, a printer that only accepts the maker's cartridges) let a firm price discriminate?
questions.explanation: Tying works as a metering device. The firm sells the machine cheaply and earns its margin on the supplies, so its revenue rises with each customer's usage intensity — a proxy for willingness to pay. IBM and Xerox used this logic with punch cards and paper.

options.text: It makes printer demand perfectly elastic
It stops customers from buying the printer
Heavy users buy more cartridges and so pay more in total
It lowers the cost of producing cartridges, which are then sold at marginal cost

questions.question: Besides metering, why else might a firm tie products?
questions.explanation: McDonald's makes franchisees buy approved supplies to protect its brand. Tying can also extend market power into the tied product, which is why competition authorities examine it closely.

options.text: To raise the cost of its own products
To reduce its market power in the main product and avoid antitrust scrutiny
To protect its brand by controlling the quality of supplies
Because tied products have lower marginal cost

questions.question: Which features define monopolistic competition?
questions.explanation: Each firm has a little market power from its brand or variety (a downward-sloping demand curve), but free entry eliminates long-run profit. Identical products mean perfect competition; high barriers point to oligopoly or monopoly.

options.text: Many firms
Differentiated but substitutable products
Free entry and exit
Identical products sold at one market price
High barriers that keep new firms out

questions.question: Restaurants in a district earn economic profits. What happens in the long run under monopolistic competition?
questions.explanation: Entry takes customers from incumbents, so each firm's demand curve shifts in (and becomes more elastic). Profit disappears once demand just touches LAC at the profit-maximising output, so P = AC.

options.text: Prices rise as more restaurants open, increasing profits further
Existing firms merge until a single firm remains
Profits persist, because each restaurant's product is unique
New entrants shift each firm's demand left until it is tangent to LAC

questions.question: Why does long-run equilibrium in monopolistic competition occur below minimum efficient scale?
questions.explanation: A downward-sloping demand curve can only be tangent to the U-shaped LAC to the left of its minimum. Each firm produces less than the output that would minimise average cost — this is excess capacity.

options.text: Regulations limit the size of each firm
Demand slopes down, so its tangency with LAC is on the falling part of LAC
Firms deliberately build plants that are too small
Because marginal cost is above average cost at that output, so expanding would raise AC

questions.question: Is the excess capacity of monopolistic competition simply a waste?
questions.explanation: With fewer, larger firms average cost would be lower, but there would be less choice. If demand is very elastic (products are close substitutes) the inefficiency is small. Pindyck concludes it is usually not a serious problem.

options.text: No, because monopolistically competitive firms produce at minimum average cost
Yes, and it should always be removed by regulation
Yes, because these markets also have high barriers to entry
Not necessarily: it is the cost of product variety, which consumers value

questions.question: What does each firm assume about its rival in the Cournot model?
questions.explanation: Cournot firms choose quantities simultaneously, each treating the other's quantity as given. A fixed rival price is the Bertrand model; reacting after the leader is the Stackelberg follower.

options.text: That the rival will choose output after seeing its own choice
That the rival will match any price change
That the rival's price is fixed
That the rival's output is fixed

questions.question: What is a firm's reaction function in the Cournot model?
questions.explanation: The reaction curve Q₁*(Q₂) gives firm 1's best response to every possible Q₂. With linear demand it slopes down: the more the rival produces, the smaller the residual demand left for you.

options.text: The rate at which it learns from its rival's past mistakes
The output both firms would choose if they colluded and split the monopoly profit
The price it will charge for each price its rival sets
Its profit-maximising output for each output the rival might produce

questions.question: On the graph, where is the Cournot equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Only where both curves meet is each firm producing its best response to the other's output, so neither wants to change. That is the Cournot–Nash equilibrium.

options.text: Where the collusion curve meets firm 1's reaction curve
At 15 units each, on the line of competitive outcomes
At 7.5 units each, on the collusion curve
Where the two reaction curves cross, at 10 units each

questions.question: Using the graph's example, rank market outcomes by total industry output, from highest to lowest.
questions.explanation: The more aggressively firms compete for output, the higher total output and the lower the price. Stackelberg exceeds Cournot because the leader commits to a large output.

options.text: Cournot (20 units)
Stackelberg (22.5 units)
Collusion / monopoly (15 units)
Perfect competition (30 units)

questions.question: How do the Cournot price and output compare with competition and monopoly?
questions.explanation: Each Cournot firm ignores that its extra output lowers its rival's profit, so it produces more than a cartel would. But each still restricts output somewhat, so the price stays above MC.

options.text: They are identical to the monopoly outcome
Between the two: more output and a lower price than monopoly, less than competition
Output is higher than under competition, but the price is higher than a monopolist would charge
They are identical to the competitive outcome

questions.question: Why is the Cournot equilibrium a Nash equilibrium?
questions.explanation: At the crossing point neither firm can raise its profit by changing output on its own. That is the definition of a Nash equilibrium — not joint profit maximisation, which would be collusion.

options.text: Both firms maximise their joint profit
Each firm earns zero economic profit
Each firm's output is a best response to the other's
Each firm has a dominant strategy that does not depend on the rival's output

questions.question: In the Bertrand model with identical products, why does the price fall to marginal cost even with only two firms?
questions.explanation: If the rival charges P > MC, you capture all buyers by charging slightly less. Both firms reason the same way, so the only stable outcome is P = MC — the Bertrand paradox.

options.text: Because each firm's demand curve is perfectly inelastic below marginal cost
Because the two firms agree to price at marginal cost
Any price above MC can be slightly undercut to win the whole market
Because the government regulates prices at MC

questions.question: Which conditions can resolve the Bertrand paradox, keeping prices above marginal cost?
questions.explanation: The paradox relies on one firm taking every customer with a tiny price cut. Limits on capacity or brand loyalty break that logic, and repetition lets firms punish undercutting. More identical rivals only strengthen the push to MC.

options.text: Entry of more firms with identical products
Perfectly identical products and unlimited capacity
Repeated interaction that supports tacit collusion
Product differentiation, so not every buyer switches to the cheaper firm
Capacity constraints, so a price cutter cannot serve the whole market

questions.question: In the Stackelberg model, why does the leader produce more and earn more than in the Cournot equilibrium?
questions.explanation: The leader chooses output knowing the follower's reaction function. Once its large output is set, the follower's best response is to produce less. With identical costs the leader earns more than in Cournot and the follower less.

options.text: Because the leader has lower marginal costs
Because the leader is protected by a patent
Because the follower must match the leader's price, which is set above the Cournot level
By committing first, it forces the follower to accept a smaller share

questions.question: On the graph, the Stackelberg point is at Q₁ = 15, Q₂ = 7.5. What does this show?
questions.explanation: The leader picks the point on firm 2's reaction curve that maximises its own profit. In Pindyck's example the leader's output is double the follower's, and total output (22.5) exceeds Cournot (20).

options.text: Both firms produce the collusive output
The follower produces more, because it can see the leader's choice before deciding its own output
The leader produces twice as much as the follower, which stays on its reaction curve
The leader moves off the follower's reaction curve to punish it

questions.question: Why is the kinked demand curve elastic above the current price and inelastic below it?
questions.explanation: If you raise your price alone, you lose many customers to rivals (elastic). If you cut it, rivals follow and you gain few customers (inelastic). The kink in demand creates a vertical gap in MR.

options.text: Costs are higher above the kink than below it
Consumers are loyal at high prices but switch at low prices
Rivals match cuts but not rises
Regulators allow price cuts but not price rises

questions.question: On the graph, marginal cost rises from MC to MC′. What happens to price and output?
questions.explanation: MR jumps down at Q*. As long as MC passes through that vertical gap, MR = MC still holds at Q*, so the profit-maximising price does not change. This is Sweezy's explanation of price rigidity in oligopoly.

options.text: Output rises because MC′ is steeper
The firm moves to the inelastic part of demand and lowers its price
Nothing: both MC curves pass through the gap in MR, so P* and Q* stay the same
Price rises and output falls, as in any monopoly

questions.question: What is a key weakness of the kinked demand curve model?
questions.explanation: The model explains why a price might stay put, but it takes P* as given. It is a description of rigidity rather than a theory of price determination.

options.text: It predicts that prices change constantly
It assumes only one firm is in the market, so it cannot describe oligopoly
It does not explain how the kink price was set
It cannot be drawn on a graph

questions.question: How does a dominant firm with a competitive fringe set price?
questions.explanation: The residual demand curve D_D = market demand − fringe supply. The dominant firm sets its MR (from D_D) equal to its MC, then charges the price from D_D. The fringe takes that price and supplies where P = their MC.

options.text: It sets price equal to the fringe's marginal cost
It produces where market demand meets its own marginal cost and lets the fringe follow
It lets the fringe set the price and supplies the rest
It sets MR = MC on residual demand (market demand minus fringe supply)

questions.question: What happens to the dominant firm's pricing power as more fringe producers enter?
questions.explanation: More fringe supply at every price leaves less residual demand, which also becomes more elastic. Over time the dominant firm's markup and market share erode — a pattern seen in steel and soft drinks.

options.text: Nothing, because the fringe is too small to matter
Its residual demand shrinks and grows more elastic, so its price and share fall
Its pricing power rises, because the fringe follows its price
Its residual demand grows, because more firms validate its price and follow its lead

questions.question: Which conditions does a cartel need to raise prices successfully?
questions.explanation: Pindyck stresses two conditions: a stable organisation whose members agree and do not cheat, and real potential for monopoly power. If buyers or non-members can easily respond to a higher price, the cartel cannot raise it much.

options.text: There must be many small competitors outside the cartel
Members must have identical costs and products, or they cannot agree on a price
Market demand must be highly elastic
Discipline among members, plus inelastic demand and outside supply

questions.question: Why was OPEC far more successful than CIPEC, the copper exporters' cartel?
questions.explanation: The cartel's residual demand is market demand minus competitive supply. For oil in the 1970s, both were inelastic, so OPEC could raise prices a lot. Copper buyers and non-member producers (including recyclers) reacted strongly, so CIPEC had little power.

options.text: CIPEC members had much higher production costs than OPEC members, so they could not cut prices
Oil demand and non-OPEC supply were far less elastic than for copper
Copper is a luxury good, oil a necessity
OPEC controlled all of the world's oil supply

questions.question: Why does every cartel member face a temptation to cheat?
questions.explanation: The cartel restricts output so P > MC for each member. Selling a bit more in secret at a slightly lower price is profitable for the cheater — but if all members do it, the price collapses.

options.text: Because each member's marginal cost is above the cartel price
At the cartel price, extra sales earn more than they cost
Because cartel agreements are always illegal
Because the cartel sets output where demand is inelastic

questions.question: What is a dominant strategy?
questions.explanation: A dominant strategy does not depend on guessing the rival's choice. It need not give the highest payoff in the game — in a prisoners' dilemma both players have one and still end up badly.

options.text: The best choice whatever the rival does
A strategy that is best only if the rival cooperates
A strategy that gives the highest possible payoff in the game
The strategy chosen by the larger firm in an oligopoly

questions.question: What is a Nash equilibrium?
questions.explanation: In a Nash equilibrium no player can gain by changing strategy alone. It does not require dominant strategies, and it need not be efficient.

options.text: A cooperative agreement enforced by a contract
An outcome that maximises the sum of all players' payoffs
An outcome in which every player has a dominant strategy
Each player best-responds to the others

questions.question: Why is every equilibrium in dominant strategies a Nash equilibrium, but not the other way round?
questions.explanation: If your strategy is best against everything, it is certainly best against the rival's equilibrium choice. A Nash strategy only has to be best against what the rival actually does, so it may not be dominant.

options.text: Because Nash equilibria are always unique
Because dominant strategies exist only in sequential games
A dominant strategy is a best response to every choice
Because Nash equilibria always involve cooperation

questions.question: Payoffs (A, B): both advertise (10, 5); A advertises, B does not (15, 0); A does not, B advertises (6, 8); neither advertises (10, 2). What is the equilibrium?
questions.explanation: For A: 10 > 6 if B advertises, 15 > 10 if B does not, so A always advertises. For B: 5 > 0 and 8 > 2, so B always advertises. (Advertise, Advertise) is an equilibrium in dominant strategies — and hence also a Nash equilibrium.

options.text: Only A advertises — it gives A its highest payoff
Neither advertises — it gives the highest total payoff
There is no equilibrium in this game
Both advertise — it is each firm's dominant strategy

questions.question: In the same game, A's payoff when neither firm advertises rises to 20. What changes?
questions.explanation: A's best choice now depends on B: advertise if B advertises (10 > 6), don't if B doesn't (20 > 15). B still always advertises, so A best-responds by advertising. The outcome is a Nash equilibrium that is not in dominant strategies for both.

options.text: Both firms now prefer not to advertise, since that gives A its best payoff
B loses its dominant strategy
A loses its dominant strategy but still advertises
The game now has no Nash equilibrium

questions.question: Which statements about Nash equilibrium are correct?
questions.explanation: Coordination games (such as the product-choice game) have several Nash equilibria. The prisoners' dilemma shows a Nash outcome can be worse for everyone. Many games have no dominant strategies at all.

options.text: In a Nash equilibrium the players must cooperate
A Nash equilibrium can exist when no player has a dominant strategy
A Nash equilibrium may leave every player worse off than another outcome
Every game has an equilibrium in dominant strategies
A game can have more than one Nash equilibrium

questions.question: Two countries choose between free trade and protection. Each gains by protecting whatever the other does, but both are better off with mutual free trade. What is the noncooperative outcome?
questions.explanation: Protection is each country's dominant strategy, so (protect, protect) is the Nash equilibrium — even though (free trade, free trade) would make both better off. This is why trade liberalisation usually needs negotiated, enforceable agreements.

options.text: There is no equilibrium, because payoffs are symmetric
Both protect: a prisoners' dilemma
Both choose free trade, because it maximises joint welfare
One protects and the other chooses free trade

questions.question: Which mechanisms help countries escape the trade-policy prisoners' dilemma?
questions.explanation: Cooperation needs enforcement or the shadow of the future. The WTO's dispute rules and the prospect of retaliation make free trade sustainable. An unenforceable promise changes no payoffs, and pre-emptive tariffs push countries toward the bad equilibrium.

options.text: Binding agreements with dispute settlement, as in the WTO
Repeated interaction, in which retaliation is expected
A promise of free trade that cannot be enforced
Each country raising tariffs first to gain bargaining power
Keeping trade policies secret from partners

questions.question: What is the tit-for-tat strategy?
questions.explanation: Tit-for-tat rewards cooperation and punishes cheating immediately, but forgives as soon as the rival returns to cooperation. In Axelrod's tournaments it did very well because it is nice, retaliatory, forgiving and clear.

options.text: Always cheat, because cheating is the dominant strategy
Cheat in the first round, then cooperate for the rest of the game
Cooperate forever, whatever the rival does
Cooperate first, then copy whatever the rival did last round

questions.question: Why can cooperation be sustained in an infinitely repeated prisoners' dilemma?
questions.explanation: If players value the future enough (a low discount rate), the punishment that follows cheating outweighs the short-term gain. Cooperation then becomes a best response to strategies like tit-for-tat.

options.text: Because cheating becomes illegal in repeated games
Because the payoffs grow over time
Because players forget past rounds in repeated games and start fresh each time
Future punishment costs more than cheating gains once

questions.question: Why does cooperation break down if the game is repeated a known, finite number of times?
questions.explanation: In the final round cheating is dominant. Knowing that, there is no reason to cooperate in the second-to-last round, and so on back to the start. In practice, uncertainty about the end date and limited rationality often keep cooperation alive.

options.text: In the last round cheating is dominant, and this unravels backward
Because cooperation is a dominant strategy in finite games
Because tit-for-tat is illegal in finite games
Because players run out of money before the game ends and cannot punish anyone

questions.question: Which conditions make tacit collusion easier to sustain in a repeated game?
questions.explanation: Cooperation lasts when cheating is spotted quickly and punished, and when the future matters. Many firms, hidden prices and unstable demand make cheating harder to detect and more tempting.

options.text: High discount rates and a short time horizon
Many firms with secret prices and volatile demand
Few firms, easy detection of cheating and patient players
Products that are very different from each other's

questions.question: How are sequential games usually represented?
questions.explanation: The extensive form shows the order of moves, what each player knows, and payoffs at the end of each branch. Simultaneous games are usually shown as a payoff matrix.

options.text: As a single 2×2 payoff matrix in which both players move at once
As a game tree (extensive form) showing who moves when
As a reaction curve diagram
As a supply and demand diagram

questions.question: Put the steps of solving a sequential game by backward induction in order.
questions.explanation: Working backward makes each earlier player anticipate how later players will actually respond. The resulting strategies form a subgame perfect equilibrium.

options.text: Find the last mover's best choice at each node
Replace those nodes with the payoffs they lead to
Move back to the earlier mover and choose the best branch
Start at the final decision nodes

questions.question: What is a subgame perfect equilibrium?
questions.explanation: Some Nash equilibria rely on threats that would never be carried out. Subgame perfection removes them by requiring optimal play at every point of the tree.

options.text: A Nash equilibrium that is also a Nash equilibrium in every subgame
An equilibrium in which every player has a dominant strategy
Any Nash equilibrium of the matrix form
The outcome that maximises joint payoffs

questions.question: Two cereal makers can launch a sweet or a crunchy product, and only one product is very profitable. Why does moving first matter?
questions.explanation: Once the leader commits, the follower chooses the best remaining option. This first-mover advantage explains why firms rush to launch products and build capacity.

options.text: The leader takes the better product; the follower takes the other
Order does not matter in sequential games
Moving first always loses, because the second mover can copy the product and undercut it
The first mover must take the less profitable product

questions.question: When is a threat credible?
questions.explanation: If carrying out a threat would cost the threatener more than giving in, rivals will assume it is empty. Threats become credible when payoffs (or commitments) make following through the best response.

options.text: When carrying it out would be in the threatener's interest
When the threatened action would hurt the rival a lot more than the threatener
Whenever it is announced publicly
When the threatener is the larger firm

questions.question: How did DuPont use investment to deter entry in titanium dioxide?
questions.explanation: Sunk, irreversible capacity changes DuPont's own payoffs: once built, it is rational to use it. Potential entrants foresee low prices after entry, so they stay out.

options.text: It threatened to sue any firm that entered
It built capacity ahead of demand, committing to high output
It lowered its R&D spending to cut costs
It signed long-term contracts with its rivals to share the market by region

questions.question: In a two-stage entry game, when is investing in extra capacity to deter entry profitable for the incumbent?
questions.explanation: Deterrence pays only if the cost of the commitment is below the gain from keeping the market to yourself. If capacity is very costly or the market can easily support two firms, accommodating entry is the profit-maximising choice.

options.text: When the cost of the extra capacity is less than the profit it protects
Always, because entry must be prevented at any cost
Never, because capacity is a sunk cost
Only when the entrant has lower costs than the incumbent and would win a price war

questions.question: An incumbent threatens a price war if a rival enters, but after entry accommodating would be more profitable. What follows?
questions.explanation: The entrant uses backward induction: once it has entered, the incumbent's best reply is to accommodate. Only a commitment such as sunk capacity — making warfare the best response — makes the threat credible.

options.text: The rival stays out, because the threat was announced
The incumbent must start a price war to keep its reputation
Both firms collude to share monopoly profit
The threat is empty, so the rival enters

questions.question: In the Brander–Spencer model of Boeing vs Airbus, how does a European subsidy change the outcome?
questions.explanation: Without a subsidy, either firm alone is profitable, but both lose if both produce. A subsidy that makes Airbus profitable even when Boeing produces commits Airbus to produce, so Boeing stays out and Europe captures the market.

options.text: It lowers Boeing's costs too, because the two firms share suppliers, so both produce
It has no effect, because subsidies are just transfers
It forces both firms to stop producing the new plane
It commits Airbus to produce, so Boeing's best reply is to stay out

questions.question: What is a key caveat to using strategic trade policy like Brander–Spencer?
questions.explanation: If the other side also subsidises, both governments pay and neither firm leaves — a subsidy war. Misjudging payoffs can also mean paying for a project that loses money.

options.text: Governments may misjudge payoffs, and rivals may retaliate
It works only in perfectly competitive markets
It only works when both governments subsidise their firms by the same amount
Subsidies always raise world welfare

questions.question: How do English and Dutch auctions differ?
questions.explanation: In an English (ascending) auction bidders drop out as the price rises. In a Dutch (descending) auction, used for flowers, the price falls until the first bidder accepts it. A Dutch auction is strategically equivalent to a first-price sealed-bid auction.

options.text: English: bids are sealed. Dutch: bids are spoken aloud
There is no difference: both are sealed-bid formats
English: the price rises until one bidder remains. Dutch: the price falls until someone bids
English: the highest bidder pays the second price. Dutch: the winner pays their own bid

questions.question: In a second-price (Vickrey) sealed-bid auction, what is each bidder's best strategy?
questions.explanation: The price you pay is set by someone else's bid, so your bid only decides whether you win. Bidding your true value means you win exactly when the price is below your value — truth-telling is a dominant strategy.

options.text: Bid above your valuation to make sure you win
Bid exactly the expected second-highest bid
Bid well below your valuation
Bid your true valuation

questions.question: What is the winner's curse?
questions.explanation: When the item is worth roughly the same to everyone (an oil tract), each bidder has a noisy estimate. The highest bid usually comes from the most optimistic estimate, so the winner often overpays.

options.text: The winner is usually the bidder who overestimated the value most
The seller earns less than the item's value
In private-value auctions, the winner always pays less than the item is worth to them
The second-highest bidder must pay a penalty

questions.question: How can a rational bidder avoid the winner's curse in a common-value auction?
questions.explanation: Winning is itself bad news about your estimate. Smart bidders shade their bids to allow for this, and they shade more when many rivals bid or estimates are noisy.

options.text: Bid exactly your estimate of the value
Always bid the minimum allowed
Shade your bid below your estimate of the value
Bid above your estimate to signal confidence and scare off other bidders

questions.question: Which items are sold in common-value auctions?
questions.explanation: In common-value auctions the item is worth about the same to everyone, but nobody knows exactly how much. Items bought for personal enjoyment have private values that differ across bidders.

options.text: A signed shirt for a fan's private collection
A jar of coins whose total is unknown
Offshore oil drilling rights
A stand of timber to be cut and sold
A painting bought to hang in the buyer's home

questions.question: Why is the demand for labour a derived demand?
questions.explanation: Labour is not wanted for its own sake. When demand for cars falls, demand for autoworkers falls too. That is why input demand depends on both productivity and the output price.

options.text: Labour demand depends only on the wage rate
Workers decide how much labour to supply
Governments determine the number of jobs
Firms want workers for the output they produce

questions.question: What is the marginal revenue product of labour?
questions.explanation: An extra worker adds MP_L units of output, each bringing in MR of revenue. MRP is the firm's benefit from hiring; the wage is the cost.

options.text: The wage paid to the last worker hired
MP_L × MR: the extra revenue from one more worker
MP_L × w: the extra cost of one more worker
Total revenue divided by the number of workers

questions.question: A firm has monopoly power in its output market. How does its MRP compare with the value of marginal product (VMP = MP × P)?
questions.explanation: Selling the extra output requires a lower price on all units, so MR < P. The firm hires fewer workers than a competitive firm would, which is another way monopoly restricts output.

options.text: They cannot be compared
MRP < VMP, because MR is below price
MRP > VMP, because the monopolist charges more
MRP = VMP, because the firm is a price taker in the labour market

questions.question: Why does a profit-maximising firm hire labour until MRP_L = w?
questions.explanation: It is the MR = MC rule applied to inputs: the marginal benefit of a worker (MRP) is compared with the marginal cost (the wage, in a competitive labour market).

options.text: Below that point, a worker adds more revenue than cost; above it, less
Because the firm's total revenue is at its maximum when MRP equals the wage
Because the wage is set by the firm at the MRP
Because the law requires wages to equal productivity

questions.question: The output price is constant. Why does a firm's labour demand curve still slope down?
questions.explanation: With MRP = MP × P and P fixed, MRP falls only because MP falls. The firm hires more workers only if the wage drops to the lower MRP of the extra worker.

options.text: Because wages rise as the firm hires more, even in a competitive labour market
Because workers are less motivated in large firms
Diminishing marginal product makes each extra worker's MRP smaller
Because the output price falls as more workers are hired

questions.question: The wage falls in an industry and all firms hire more. Why is industry labour demand steeper than the horizontal sum of firms' MRP curves?
questions.explanation: Each firm's MRP curve assumes a fixed output price. When the whole industry expands, the extra output lowers the price, so each firm's MRP is smaller than expected and the industry hires fewer workers than the simple sum suggests.

options.text: Because diminishing returns disappear when the whole industry hires at once
Because some firms leave the industry when wages fall
Because workers refuse to work at lower wages
The output price falls when all firms expand together

questions.question: In the labour–leisure model, what does a higher wage do through the substitution effect?
questions.explanation: The wage is the price of an hour of leisure. A higher wage makes leisure more expensive relative to the goods that work buys, so the substitution effect always increases hours worked.

options.text: The worker feels richer and takes more leisure
The worker's total income falls
Leisure becomes cheaper, so the worker works less
Leisure becomes costlier, so the worker supplies more hours

questions.question: What does the income effect of a higher wage do to hours worked, assuming leisure is a normal good?
questions.explanation: With higher income for each hour, the worker can afford more of everything — including leisure. This pulls in the opposite direction to the substitution effect.

options.text: It has no effect on hours worked
It reduces leisure, because leisure is an inferior good
It increases hours, because work becomes more attractive
It reduces hours, because the richer worker buys more leisure

questions.question: When does the labour supply curve bend backward?
questions.explanation: At low wages the substitution effect usually dominates, so hours rise with the wage. At high wages the income effect may win, so further rises lead people to work less. Inferior leisure would make the curve slope up even more.

options.text: When the substitution effect outweighs the income effect
When the income effect of a wage rise outweighs the substitution effect
When wages fall below the poverty line and workers need extra hours to survive
When leisure becomes an inferior good

questions.question: Which statements about the labour–leisure choice are correct?
questions.explanation: The substitution effect always raises hours when the wage rises; only the income effect can reduce them. Backward bending is usually expected at high, not low, wages.

options.text: Leisure is normally treated as a normal good
At very low wages, the income effect usually dominates
The wage is the opportunity cost of an hour of leisure
A backward-bending curve means the income effect dominates at high wages
The substitution effect reduces hours worked when the wage rises

questions.question: What is economic rent in a factor market?
questions.explanation: Economic rent is the excess over the input's opportunity cost (its transfer earnings). It is like producer surplus for an input owner.

options.text: The rent a firm pays each month to a landlord for the land or buildings it uses
The total wage bill of a firm
Payment above the minimum needed to keep the input in its current use
The interest paid on borrowed capital

questions.question: A footballer earns $5 million a year; his best alternative job pays $100,000. How is his pay split?
questions.explanation: Transfer earnings are what is needed to keep him in this occupation — his opportunity cost. Everything above that is rent, which arises from his scarce talent.

options.text: All of it is rent, because footballers are unique
$5 million transfer earnings and no economic rent
$4.9 million transfer earnings and $100,000 rent
$100,000 transfer earnings and $4.9 million economic rent

questions.question: Why is all payment to a factor in perfectly inelastic supply pure economic rent?
questions.explanation: Prime city-centre land exists whatever it earns. Its price is determined entirely by demand, and none of the payment is needed to call it into supply.

options.text: Because the owner pays no taxes on it
Because demand for it is also perfectly inelastic
Because its price is set by the government
Its quantity would be the same even at a price of zero
