questions.question: Compared with a competitive labour market, what does the monopsonist on the graph do?
questions.explanation: Because ME lies above the supply curve, each extra worker costs more than the wage. The firm stops at Lm, where ME = MV, and pays only the supply price of Lm workers, wm.

options.text: Hires more workers and pays a higher wage
Hires fewer workers (Lm < Lc) and pays a lower wage (wm < wc)
Hires fewer workers but pays a higher wage
Hires the same number of workers at a lower wage

questions.question: Why might a minimum wage raise employment in a monopsony labour market?
questions.explanation: With a wage floor, hiring one more worker no longer raises the wage for everyone, so ME equals the floor up to the supply curve. Set between wm and wc, it moves employment toward the competitive level — unlike in a competitive market.

options.text: Because minimum wages always increase employment
Because the monopsonist must then hire everyone who wants to work at that wage
At a floor between wm and wc, hiring more no longer raises the wage
Because a minimum wage lowers marginal value

questions.question: A union faces a competitive employer's labour demand curve. Rank these union objectives by the wage they lead to, from highest to lowest.
questions.explanation: Rent maximisation acts like a monopolist: choose employment where the "marginal revenue" of labour equals the supply curve, giving the highest wage and fewest jobs. Wage-bill maximisation picks the unit-elastic point. Maximising employment means accepting the competitive wage.

options.text: Maximise the total wage bill
Maximise the number of members employed
Maximise economic rent of employed members

questions.question: A union wants to maximise its members' total wage bill. Where does it set employment?
questions.explanation: The wage bill w·L is the "revenue" from selling labour. It peaks where its marginal revenue is zero — the unit-elastic point on the labour demand curve.

options.text: Where labour demand meets labour supply
At the highest wage employers will pay
Where the marginal revenue from labour is zero
Where marginal revenue from labour equals the supply curve

questions.question: What does a union that maximises its employed members' economic rent do?
questions.explanation: Rent is the wage above members' reservation wages (the supply curve). Maximising it is exactly the monopolist's problem with supply as the marginal cost curve, so the union picks the highest wage and fewest jobs.

options.text: Sets the wage equal to the members' reservation wage to keep everyone employed
Picks employment where labour demand meets labour supply
Picks employment where MR from labour is zero
Picks employment where MR from labour equals labour supply

questions.question: In a bilateral monopoly, why can't theory predict a unique wage or price?
questions.explanation: A monopsonist wants a low price, a monopolist a high one. Where they settle depends on patience, information, threats and outside options. Pindyck notes that the two powers tend to offset each other, often pulling the outcome closer to the competitive one.

options.text: It depends on bargaining power between two price setters
Because both sides always choose the competitive price
Because the government always sets the price
Because supply and demand curves do not exist when there is only one buyer and one seller

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a stock and a flow?
questions.explanation: A stock is measured at a moment ("we own 40 machines"); a flow is measured per period ("we bought 5 machines this year"). Investment adds to the capital stock; depreciation subtracts from it.

options.text: Stock: monthly wages; flow: the number of machines installed in the plant
Stock: this year's revenue; flow: the firm's factory
Stock: the firm's machinery; flow: this year's investment
Stock: annual depreciation; flow: the building

questions.question: Which of these are flow variables?
questions.explanation: Flows have a time dimension ("per year", "per quarter"). The truck fleet, the year-end inventory and the cash balance are stocks measured at a single date.

options.text: The firm's fleet of delivery trucks
The inventory in the warehouse on 31 December
Depreciation of equipment during the year
Investment spending in 2026
The firm's cash balance at the end of the quarter

questions.question: What is the present discounted value (PDV) of a future payment?
questions.explanation: PDV = FV/(1 + R)ᵗ: how much money you would need to invest today at rate R to have FV in t years.

options.text: Its future value multiplied by the interest rate for the period
Its value today, after discounting at the interest rate
Its value at the date it is paid, adjusted for inflation
The sum of all future payments with no adjustment

questions.question: Why is a dollar received in the future worth less than a dollar today, even with zero inflation?
questions.explanation: With a positive real interest rate, $1 today grows to $(1 + R) next year. So $1 next year is worth only $1/(1 + R) today. That reflects the productivity of capital and people's preference for consuming sooner.

options.text: Because people value future consumption more than consumption today
Because inflation always erodes the value of future dollars
Today's dollar can be invested to earn interest
Because future dollars are taxed at a higher rate

questions.question: Which formula gives the present value of payments FV₁, FV₂, … FVₙ at discount rate R?
questions.explanation: Each payment is discounted by (1 + R) raised to the number of years until it arrives, then the results are added. Multiplying by (1 + R)ᵗ gives future value instead.

options.text: PDV = Σ FVₜ/(1 + R·t)
PDV = Σ FVₜ·(1 + R)ᵗ
PDV = (Σ FVₜ)/R
PDV = Σ FVₜ/(1 + R)ᵗ

questions.question: The interest rate rises. What happens to the present value of a payment 20 years away compared with one due next year?
questions.explanation: The discount factor 1/(1 + R)ᵗ shrinks faster for large t. That is why long-lived projects and long bonds are so sensitive to interest rates.

options.text: Only the payment due next year falls in value
Both rise, because the payments now earn more interest
Both fall by the same percentage, whatever the timing of the payment
Both fall, but the distant payment falls by much more

questions.question: What is the present value of a perpetuity paying C every year forever, at interest rate R?
questions.explanation: The infinite sum C/(1 + R) + C/(1 + R)² + … simplifies to C/R. A perpetuity of $100 a year at 5% is worth $2,000 today.

options.text: C/R
C·R

questions.question: Why do bond prices fall when market interest rates rise?
questions.explanation: A bond's price is the PDV of its coupons plus its face value. With fixed payments, a higher discount rate means a lower PDV. New bonds offer higher yields, so old ones must get cheaper to compete.

options.text: The bond's fixed payments are discounted at a higher rate
Because investors expect the issuer to default whenever interest rates go up
Because the face value of the bond falls
Because the issuer must pay higher coupons on existing bonds

questions.question: What is a bond's effective yield?
questions.explanation: The effective yield (yield to maturity) is the return you earn if you buy at today's price and hold to maturity. Coupon ÷ face value is only the coupon rate.

options.text: The central bank's policy rate
Its internal rate of return at today's price
The coupon rate minus inflation
The coupon payment divided by the face value of the bond

questions.question: Interest rates rise by one percentage point. Which bond's price falls the most?
questions.explanation: Distant payments are hit hardest by a higher discount rate, so long maturities mean larger price swings. A perpetuity at 5% loses about 17% of its value when rates rise to 6% (C/0.05 → C/0.06).

options.text: All bond prices fall by the same amount
A one-year bond, because it matures soonest
A bond with a very high coupon and short maturity, since it pays out the most
A long-term bond, such as a 30-year bond or a perpetuity

questions.question: What does the NPV rule say?
questions.explanation: NPV = −C + Σ πₜ/(1 + R)ᵗ. A positive NPV means the project earns more than the opportunity cost of capital, R.

options.text: Invest if accounting profit is positive in the first year
Invest if the project pays back its cost within three years
Invest if the PDV of future cash flows exceeds the cost
Invest if total future cash flows exceed the cost

questions.question: Why should a firm invest if and only if NPV > 0?
questions.explanation: The discount rate R is what the money could earn in its next-best use. A positive NPV means the project adds value beyond that; a negative NPV means the firm would do better investing elsewhere.

options.text: Because a positive NPV guarantees the project will have no risk
Because shareholders prefer projects with long payback periods
NPV > 0 means the project beats the return available elsewhere
Because NPV ignores the opportunity cost of capital

questions.question: A firm must choose between two mutually exclusive projects with different upfront costs. Which should it pick?
questions.explanation: With no capital limit, the project that adds the most value — the highest NPV — is best, whatever its size. Ratios and payback periods can favour small projects that add less value.

options.text: The one with the higher NPV
The one that pays back its initial cost the fastest
The one with the lower upfront cost
The one with the higher ratio of revenue to cost

questions.question: What does the Fisher equation state, approximately?
questions.explanation: i ≈ r + π. If lenders want a 3% real return and expect 2% inflation, they charge about 5% nominal.

options.text: Nominal interest rate = real interest rate + expected inflation
Real interest rate = nominal interest rate + expected inflation
Inflation = nominal interest rate + real interest rate
Nominal interest rate = real interest rate × expected inflation

questions.question: A firm discounts NOMINAL cash flows (which include inflation) using a REAL interest rate. What is the result?
questions.explanation: The cash flows grow with inflation, but the discount rate does not account for it, so future flows look too valuable. Discounting real flows at a nominal rate makes the opposite mistake and understates NPV. Keep the two consistent.

options.text: It understates the cost of the project
No error, because inflation cancels out of the calculation
It overstates the NPV
It understates the NPV

questions.question: What is diversifiable risk?
questions.explanation: A failed drug trial or a factory fire hits one company. In a broad portfolio these events largely cancel out. Market-wide risk (recessions, rate shocks) cannot be diversified away.

options.text: Firm-specific risk that a portfolio can remove
Risk that cannot be reduced by any means
Risk that affects the whole economy at the same time
The risk that interest rates will rise for all borrowers

questions.question: Why do investors earn a risk premium only for nondiversifiable risk?
questions.explanation: Nobody will pay you for bearing a risk you can get rid of for free by holding a portfolio. Only risk that remains after diversification commands a higher expected return.

options.text: Because governments insure investors against company-specific risk
Because diversifiable risk is always smaller than market risk
Because nondiversifiable risk is easier to measure
Diversifiable risk can be removed cheaply

questions.question: What does an asset's beta measure in the CAPM?
questions.explanation: β = 1 means the asset moves with the market; β = 2 means it swings twice as much. The CAPM sets the risk premium as β times the market risk premium: r = r_f + β(r_m − r_f).

options.text: How much of its risk can be diversified away
Its sensitivity to market-wide movements
The asset's average return over the last year
The interest rate on risk-free government bonds

questions.question: The risk-free rate is 3%, the expected market return is 9% and a stock's beta is 1.5. What return does the CAPM require?
questions.explanation: r = 3% + 1.5 × (9% − 3%) = 3% + 9% = 12%. That is the discount rate to use for a project with the same systematic risk as this stock.

questions.question: How should a student apply the NPV rule to a specialised master's degree?
questions.explanation: Education is an investment in human capital. Costs come first (tuition and the salary you give up while studying); benefits come later as a wage premium over a working life, so they must be discounted.

options.text: Compare the starting salary after graduation with the total tuition fees
Ignore the wages you give up, since they are not paid out
Enrol if graduates earn more than non-graduates on average
Compare the PDV of extra lifetime earnings with tuition plus forgone wages

questions.question: Which items belong in the NPV calculation for a full-time graduate degree?
questions.explanation: Only costs and benefits caused by the decision count. Living costs you would pay anyway are not extra costs, and your earlier degree is sunk.

options.text: Salary given up while studying
The cost of the undergraduate degree you already have
Food and rent you would pay whether you studied or not
The higher salary expected after graduating
Tuition and fees

questions.question: What does Hotelling's rule say about an exhaustible resource in a competitive market?
questions.explanation: A barrel left in the ground is an asset. Its net value must grow at the interest rate, or producers would shift extraction to whichever period pays more.

options.text: The market price rises at the rate of inflation
The net price (P − MC) rises at the rate of interest
The market price stays constant until the resource runs out
Extraction stays the same each year until reserves are gone

questions.question: Why must the net price of oil rise at the rate of interest?
questions.explanation: If P − MC grew faster than R, keeping oil in the ground would beat selling it and investing the money, so producers would wait, raising today's price. If it grew slower, they would extract now. Equilibrium requires indifference.

options.text: Because demand for oil grows at the rate of interest every year
Because the government sets oil prices to grow with interest rates
Because extraction costs always rise at the rate of interest
Otherwise producers would shift extraction to an earlier or later period

questions.question: What is user cost in the extraction of an exhaustible resource?
questions.explanation: Extracting today means the unit is not available tomorrow. Under competition, user cost equals P − MC, and producers set price equal to marginal extraction cost plus user cost.

options.text: The tax paid by consumers on each unit they use
The opportunity cost of extracting a unit now rather than later
The cost of cleaning up pollution after extraction
The cost of the drilling and pumping equipment used to extract the resource

questions.question: Why have real oil prices not climbed steadily as Hotelling's rule might suggest?
questions.explanation: Pindyck notes that for most resources user cost is a small part of price, because known reserves are large. New discoveries, better technology and shifts in market power (OPEC) matter far more for prices.

options.text: User cost is small, and new reserves and technology cut costs
Because Hotelling's rule applies only to metals
Because oil is not an exhaustible resource
Because interest rates have been negative ever since the 1970s

questions.question: How does general equilibrium analysis differ from partial equilibrium analysis?
questions.explanation: Partial equilibrium looks at one market and treats others as given. General equilibrium determines prices and quantities in several markets at once, tracing how a change in one feeds into others and back.

options.text: It ignores prices and focuses on quantities alone
It applies only to monopolies and oligopolies
It tracks feedback between markets
It studies one market while holding all other markets fixed

questions.question: A tariff on imported ethanol raises its domestic price. Which chain of effects does a general-equilibrium view add?
questions.explanation: Substitutes (domestic ethanol, gasoline) and inputs (corn) are affected, and through corn, livestock feed and food prices. These changes can feed back into the ethanol market, so the full effect differs from the single-market estimate.

options.text: Ethanol imports rise because domestic ethanol is now dearer
Corn and food prices rise, feeding back to ethanol
Only the government budget changes
No other markets change, because only ethanol is taxed

questions.question: Why can a partial-equilibrium estimate of a policy's effect be misleading?
questions.explanation: In Pindyck's example of a tax on one good, rising demand for a substitute raises its price, which shifts demand back to the taxed good. The final price change can be larger or smaller than the one-market analysis predicts.

options.text: Because partial equilibrium ignores the demand curve
Because partial equilibrium always overstates price changes
Because general equilibrium effects are too small to matter
Feedback from related markets changes the result

questions.question: What do the dimensions of an Edgeworth box represent in an exchange economy?
questions.explanation: The width is the total amount of one good, the height the total of the other. Each point in the box splits these totals between consumer A (measured from one corner) and consumer B (from the opposite corner).

options.text: The prices of the two goods
The incomes of the two consumers
The amounts of labour and capital in the economy
The total amounts of the two goods available

questions.question: At an allocation, consumer A's MRS of food for clothing differs from consumer B's. Why is it Pareto inefficient?
questions.explanation: Unequal MRS means the indifference curves cross, leaving a lens of allocations that both prefer. Trading inside that lens makes at least one better off and nobody worse off.

options.text: Because the total amounts of the goods are not fully used
Because inefficiency means both consumers have equal utility
A trade could make both better off
Because one consumer has more of both goods

questions.question: What is the contract curve?
questions.explanation: On the contract curve MRS_A = MRS_B, so no further mutually beneficial trade exists. Every point on it is Pareto efficient, but the points differ in how the gains are split.

options.text: Allocations where their indifference curves are tangent
The line along which the two consumers' incomes are exactly equal
The initial endowment of the two consumers
The budget line both consumers face

questions.question: A would give up 3 units of clothing for 1 more food; B would give up only 1 unit of clothing for 1 food. Which trade benefits both?
questions.explanation: A values food more highly (MRS 3) than B does (MRS 1). Any price between 1 and 3 units of clothing leaves both better off. They keep trading until their MRSs are equal, on the contract curve.

options.text: A buys food from B, paying between 1 and 3 clothing per food
No trade can make both better off
A buys food from B, paying more than 3 clothing per food
B buys food from A, paying between 1 and 3 clothing per food

questions.question: What does the First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics state?
questions.explanation: If markets are competitive and there are no externalities, public goods or information problems, the equilibrium allocation lies on the contract curve.

options.text: Every Pareto efficient allocation is fair
Governments must redistribute income to achieve efficiency
A competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient
Monopoly outcomes are Pareto efficient

questions.question: Why does a competitive price system lead an exchange economy to the contract curve?
questions.explanation: Everyone faces the same prices, and each consumer's optimum equates their MRS with the price ratio. So MRS_A = Px/Py = MRS_B — the efficiency condition — without anyone needing to know others' preferences.

options.text: Each consumer sets MRS = Px/Py, so all MRSs end up equal
Because consumers trade until each has equal amounts of both goods
Because prices are set by the richest consumer
Because the government assigns goods where MRSs are equal

questions.question: Why is the First Welfare Theorem important for decentralised market economies?
questions.explanation: This is the formal version of Adam Smith's invisible hand. Its assumptions also show when markets fail: market power, externalities, public goods and incomplete information.

options.text: It shows that central planners can always outperform markets when information is good
It proves that markets always produce fair outcomes
It proves that externalities do not affect efficiency
Markets coordinate without a planner

questions.question: What does the Second Welfare Theorem add?
questions.explanation: Society can separate equity from efficiency in principle: redistribute endowments, then let competitive markets work. In practice, lump-sum transfers are hard to design, so real redistribution tends to cost some efficiency.

options.text: Markets cannot achieve efficient outcomes without regulation
Only the competitive equilibrium allocation reached from the initial endowment can be efficient
Redistribution always reduces efficiency
Any efficient allocation is reachable after lump-sum transfers

questions.question: What does the utility possibilities frontier show?
questions.explanation: Mapping each efficient allocation from the Edgeworth box into utility space gives the UPF. Points inside it are inefficient; points beyond it are unattainable.

options.text: All possible bundles of goods the economy can produce
The utility each consumer gets from the initial endowment
Utility levels along the contract curve
The trade-off between work and leisure for each consumer

questions.question: Why is an allocation on the UPF not necessarily better for society than an inefficient allocation inside it?
questions.explanation: Moving from an interior point to the frontier in the right direction can help both people. But a frontier point where one person has almost everything may be judged worse than a fairer interior point. That judgement requires a social welfare function.

options.text: Because points on the UPF give both consumers less utility
Because inefficient points always have more total output than efficient ones
Because the UPF only applies to production
Efficiency says nothing about distribution; an efficient point may be very unequal

questions.question: Which statements about equity and efficiency are correct?
questions.explanation: The UPF captures efficiency only. Fairness needs a value judgement (utilitarian, Rawlsian, egalitarian, market-oriented). Distorting taxes create a trade-off: more equity can cost some efficiency.

options.text: Every point on the UPF is equally fair
From a point inside the UPF, both consumers can be made better off
Redistribution through taxes can weaken incentives and push the economy inside the UPF
Competitive markets guarantee an equitable distribution
On the UPF, helping one consumer means hurting the other

questions.question: What is the condition for technical efficiency in production between two industries?
questions.explanation: If MRTS differs, moving labour and capital between industries can raise output of one good without cutting the other. Efficient allocations lie on the production contract curve where isoquants are tangent.

options.text: Both industries use the same amounts of labour and capital
MRTS of labour for capital is the same in both industries
Each industry's marginal product of labour equals the wage
Both industries produce the same amount of output

questions.question: How is the production possibilities frontier derived from the production Edgeworth box?
questions.explanation: Each efficient input allocation gives a pair of outputs (X, Y). Plotting those pairs gives the PPF, the boundary of what the economy can produce with its resources.

options.text: By plotting consumers' utility levels for each output the economy produces
By adding the isoquants of the two industries
By plotting the outputs at each point on the production contract curve
By drawing the budget lines of the two industries

questions.question: Why is the PPF usually bowed out (concave to the origin)?
questions.explanation: As resources move from Y to X, the inputs that are least suited to X are moved last, so each extra unit of X requires giving up more Y. The marginal rate of transformation rises along the curve.

options.text: Because consumers prefer balanced bundles of goods
Inputs suit the industries unequally, so producing more X costs ever more Y
Because the economy's resources grow as output rises
Because there are increasing returns to scale in both industries at all output levels

questions.question: What is the marginal rate of transformation (MRT)?
questions.explanation: The MRT is a production concept, the counterpart of the consumer's MRS. Output efficiency requires the two to be equal.

options.text: The amount of Y given up to produce one more X — the slope of the PPF
The rate at which labour can replace capital
The rate at which consumers are willing to swap Y for X along an indifference curve
The ratio of the prices of the two goods

questions.question: Why is MRT = MCx/MCy?
questions.explanation: If an extra X costs $10 and an extra Y costs $5, the resources for one X could have made two Y. So the economy gives up MCx/MCy units of Y per extra X.

options.text: Because competitive firms set prices equal to average cost in the long run
Because the PPF is a straight line
One more X uses resources that could make MCx/MCy units of Y
Because MRT equals MRS in every economy

questions.question: The economy produces where MRS = 3 and MRT = 2. What should change?
questions.explanation: Consumers would give up 3 Y for one more X, but producing one more X costs only 2 Y. Shifting production toward X raises satisfaction until MRS = MRT.

options.text: Produce more Y and less X
Produce more X and less Y
Cut total output to lower costs
Nothing, because both are positive

questions.question: How do competitive markets achieve MRS = MRT?
questions.explanation: Prices link both sides: utility maximisation equates MRS with relative prices, and profit maximisation equates prices with marginal costs. Both sides then face the same trade-off.

options.text: Firms set MRS equal to MRT when choosing their inputs, as consumers do with goods
The government sets output so that MRS equals MRT
Consumers set MRS = Px/Py, and firms set P = MC, so Px/Py = MCx/MCy = MRT
Consumers choose MRT, and firms choose MRS

questions.question: How can international trade let a country consume a bundle outside its own PPF?
questions.explanation: The country produces where its MRT equals the world price ratio, then trades along the world price line to a consumption point beyond the PPF. The gains come from exchanging at better terms than domestic production allows.

options.text: It raises its production beyond the PPF by importing labour
Trade shifts the PPF of every country outward immediately
It cannot: consumption is always limited by the PPF
It specialises by comparative advantage and trades at world prices

questions.question: A partner has an absolute advantage in every good. Why can both countries still gain from trade?
questions.explanation: Each country specialises in the good it gives up least to produce. Even a country that is less productive in everything has a comparative advantage somewhere, so total output and both countries' consumption can rise.

options.text: They cannot: only the more productive country gains
Because the less productive country can charge higher prices
Gains depend on differences in opportunity costs, not in absolute productivity
Because absolute advantage disappears once the two countries begin to trade with each other

questions.question: Which are the main reasons competitive markets can fail to be efficient?
questions.explanation: Each breaks a condition of the First Welfare Theorem: market power drives P above MC, poor information distorts choices, externalities leave costs or benefits out of prices, and public goods cannot be charged for. High prices alone are not a market failure.

options.text: Prices that are too high for some consumers
Public goods
Incomplete or asymmetric information
Market power
Externalities

questions.question: How does asymmetric information cause market failure in the used-car market?
questions.explanation: Akerlof's "lemons" problem: buyers offer an average price, so owners of good cars withdraw, lowering average quality and price further. Mutually beneficial trades in good cars never happen.

options.text: Sellers know too little about their own cars, so they underprice them
Information is free, so there are too many sellers
Buyers cannot judge quality, so good cars are driven out
Buyers always overpay, so too many cars are traded

questions.question: What is a negative externality?
questions.explanation: Pollution from a factory harms nearby residents who are not part of the transaction. Because the firm does not pay for that harm, its private cost understates the cost to society.

options.text: A cost borne by third parties, outside the price
A fall in demand caused by higher prices
A tax imposed on producers by the government
A cost that the producer pays but the consumer does not

questions.question: What is the marginal social cost of a polluting good?
questions.explanation: Society bears both the producer's own cost of the extra unit (MC) and the damage it imposes on others (marginal external cost).

options.text: MSC = MEC only
MSC = MC + MEC
MSC = MC − MEC
MSC = MC × MEC

questions.question: On the graph, how much does the unregulated market produce, compared with the efficient output?
questions.explanation: Firms produce where demand meets their private MC (Q₁). The efficient output is where demand meets MSC (Q*), which is lower because each unit also does external damage.

options.text: Q₁, less than the efficient output Q*
Q*, the efficient level
Less than Q*, because pollution reduces demand
Q₁, more than the efficient output Q*

questions.question: On the graph, why is the shaded triangle between Q* and Q₁ a deadweight loss?
questions.explanation: Between Q* and Q₁ the MSC curve lies above demand: each unit does more harm, including the external cost, than it is worth to buyers. Summing that gap over the extra units gives the triangle.

options.text: Units there cost society more (MSC) than buyers value them (D)
Because buyers pay too little for the good
Because the government collects no tax on those units
Because firms earn economic losses on those units, so they should not produce them

questions.question: On the graph, what per-unit fee would lead firms to produce the efficient output Q*?
questions.explanation: With the fee, the firm's cost becomes MC + fee. Setting the fee equal to the marginal external damage at the efficient output makes private and social cost meet at Q*.

options.text: A fee equal to the price P₁
A fee equal to MEC at Q* — the gap between MSC and MC there
A fee equal to MEC at the market output Q₁, where damage is largest
A fee equal to the whole deadweight loss triangle

questions.question: Why do emissions fees give stronger incentives to innovate than emissions standards?
questions.explanation: Under a standard, once a firm meets the limit it gains nothing from cutting more. Under a fee, every extra ton cut saves the fee, so cheaper abatement technology keeps paying off.

options.text: Each ton still emitted costs the fee
Because standards prohibit new technology
Because fees are refunded to firms that innovate
Because fees are always lower than the cost of meeting standards

questions.question: With uncertain abatement costs, when does Pindyck say a standard is preferable to a fee?
questions.explanation: If damage rises sharply with emissions, a mistake in quantity is very costly, so fixing the quantity (a standard) is safer. If abatement costs rise sharply, a mistake in the fee is less costly than forcing a wrong quantity.

options.text: Never — fees are always preferable to standards
Whenever firms have complete information about their costs
When the marginal social cost of emissions is steep and abatement cost is fairly flat
When the marginal social cost of emissions is flat and abatement cost is steep

questions.question: How does a cap-and-trade system work?
questions.explanation: The cap fixes total emissions; trading sets the permit price. The EU Emissions Trading System is the best-known example.

options.text: Firms pay a fee only if they exceed a voluntary target
The state sets a fixed tax on every ton of emissions
Each firm must cut emissions by the same percentage, with no trading allowed
The state caps total emissions with permits, and firms trade the permits

questions.question: Why does trading permits achieve the emissions target at the lowest total cost?
questions.explanation: A firm with abatement cost below the permit price cuts more and sells permits; one with higher costs buys permits. In equilibrium every firm's marginal abatement cost equals the permit price — the cost-minimising condition.

options.text: Because every firm cuts emissions by the same amount
Because permits are always given away for free
Marginal abatement costs end up equal across firms
Because the state chooses which firms must abate, using detailed cost data

questions.question: Does the initial allocation of permits affect efficiency?
questions.explanation: Whatever the initial allocation, trading moves permits to the firms that value them most. The allocation decides who gains the permit value, which matters for fairness and politics, not for the cost-minimising pattern of abatement.

options.text: Yes: firms that receive more permits always pollute more than others
Yes: only auctioned permits lead to efficient abatement
No, because permits cannot be traded once allocated
No: it changes who pays whom, not where abatement happens

questions.question: Firm A can cut emissions for $20 a ton, firm B only for $50 a ton. What does permit trading lead to?
questions.explanation: B saves money by buying a permit for less than $50 instead of abating, and A earns more than its $20 cost by abating and selling. Trade continues until their marginal abatement costs are equal.

options.text: B cuts more and sells permits to A
A cuts more and sells permits to B at a price between $20 and $50
Both cut the same amount, because the cap is shared equally
No trade, because both firms face the same permit price

questions.question: What does the Coase theorem state?
questions.explanation: If the parties can negotiate freely, they will reach the outcome that maximises their joint surplus. The assignment of the right affects who pays whom, not the efficient result.

options.text: Property rights should be assigned to the party that suffers the externality
With clear property rights and no transaction costs, bargaining is efficient
Externalities can only be corrected by government taxes
The polluter must always compensate the victim

questions.question: A factory and a fishery downstream bargain over pollution. Why does it not matter for efficiency who holds the property right?
questions.explanation: If the fishery has the right, the factory pays it to accept pollution only if that is worth more than the damage. If the factory has the right, the fishery pays it to cut pollution if that is worth more than the abatement cost. The same efficient level results.

options.text: Either way, they agree on the outcome with the largest joint gain
Because pollution has no cost when property rights are clear
Because the court always decides the outcome
Because the factory always wins the bargaining

questions.question: Which obstacles limit the Coase theorem in practice?
questions.explanation: Coase bargaining works best with few parties, clear rights and good information. Large-scale pollution affects millions of people, making negotiation impractical — which is why governments often use fees, standards or permits instead.

options.text: Free riders who hope others will pay for the deal
Strategic bargaining and hidden information
Clearly defined property rights
Only two parties being affected
High costs of negotiating among many parties

questions.question: What is a positive externality?
questions.explanation: Vaccination protects others as well as the person vaccinated. A firm's R&D creates knowledge that others copy. Since the decision-maker ignores these spillover benefits, they undertake too little of the activity.

options.text: A higher profit earned by the producer from selling a popular product
A subsidy paid by the government
A benefit to third parties that the producer is not paid for
A rise in demand caused by lower prices

questions.question: Why do private markets underinvest in R&D or green technology?
questions.explanation: The market equates MC with private marginal benefit. Because MSB lies above D, the efficient quantity — where MSB = MC — is higher than the market's.

options.text: Because the marginal cost of R&D is always zero
Because governments forbid private R&D
Because consumers do not value new technologies until they are proven
They ignore the benefit spilling over to others

questions.question: Which policy corrects a positive externality?
questions.explanation: The subsidy raises the private return to equal the social return, so private decision-makers choose the efficient quantity. Patents, public research funding and vaccination subsidies are examples.

options.text: A subsidy equal to MEB at the efficient output
A price ceiling set below the market price to make the good affordable
A ban on the activity
A tax equal to the marginal external benefit

questions.question: What is a common property resource?
questions.explanation: Ocean fisheries and busy shipping routes are rival (my catch reduces yours) but non-excludable (no one can easily be kept out). Non-rival, non-excludable goods are public goods.

options.text: A resource owned by a single firm and rented to others
A good that is non-rival and non-excludable
A rival resource that nobody can be kept from using
A resource whose use is controlled by a market price

questions.question: Why does free access to a fishery lead to overfishing?
questions.explanation: Each user fishes until private cost equals the benefit, ignoring that each extra catch depletes the stock for others. Too much fishing occurs compared with the social optimum, where marginal social cost equals marginal benefit.

options.text: Because the fishery is owned by one large firm
Because fish prices are set too high by the government
Each fisher ignores the cost their catch imposes on the others
Because fishers prefer to catch fewer fish than is efficient

questions.question: How can the tragedy of the commons be prevented?
questions.explanation: Giving someone the right to control access — an owner, a regulator or holders of individual transferable quotas — makes users account for the cost of depletion. Iceland and New Zealand used tradable quotas to restore fish stocks.

options.text: By lowering the price of fish so that fishers earn less from each catch
By private ownership, licences or tradable catch quotas
By removing all limits on access
By subsidising extra boats to raise competition

questions.question: Which two properties define a pure public good?
questions.explanation: Non-rival: one person's use does not reduce what others get. Non-excludable: nobody can be kept from enjoying it. Rival + non-excludable is common property; non-rival + excludable is a club good (pay-TV).

options.text: Rival and excludable
Non-rival and excludable
Non-rival and non-excludable
Rival and non-excludable

questions.question: Which are close to pure public goods?
questions.explanation: Defence, navigation aids and basic science benefit everyone at once and are hard to charge for. A toll road can exclude non-payers; ocean fish are rival (a common-property resource).

options.text: National defence
Basic scientific knowledge
Fish in the open ocean
A toll motorway
A lighthouse that guides passing ships

questions.question: Why do private markets provide too little of a public good?
questions.explanation: If you benefit whether or not you pay, you have little reason to pay. Private revenue falls far short of the social value, so too little is produced — which is why governments usually finance public goods through taxes.

options.text: Non-payers can't be excluded
Because the marginal cost of public goods is infinite
Because firms are forbidden to produce public goods
Because public goods have no value to consumers

questions.question: What is a free rider?
questions.explanation: Free riding is rational for each individual but leads to underprovision. Voluntary schemes such as public radio rely on some people paying even though they could free-ride.

options.text: A consumer who buys goods only when they are on sale
Someone who benefits without paying
Someone who pays a lower price for using public transport
A firm that enters a market without paying entry costs

questions.question: Why are individual demand curves summed VERTICALLY to find the efficient level of a public good?
questions.explanation: For a private good, people consume different quantities at one price, so we add quantities (horizontally). For a public good, everyone gets the same quantity, so society's marginal benefit at each quantity is the sum of individual marginal benefits.

options.text: Everyone consumes the same quantity, so their marginal benefits add up
Because vertical summation gives the market price of the good
Because each unit can only be consumed by one person
Because public goods are always provided by the state

questions.question: What is the efficient level of a public good?
questions.explanation: An extra unit is worth producing if everyone's combined benefit from it exceeds its cost. Comparing any one person's benefit with the cost would understate the value and lead to underprovision.

options.text: Where the market price equals average cost
Where each person's marginal benefit equals marginal cost
Where the sum of marginal benefits equals marginal cost
Where the government's budget is balanced

Point elasticity uses one point; arc elasticity uses midpoints so the direction does not matter
On a straight line the slope is constant but P/Q changes, so elasticity changes along the line

examQuestions.title: Income and cross-price elasticity (EV example)
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the economic significance of income elasticity and cross-price elasticity of demand. If the cross-price elasticity between imported electric vehicles and domestic gasoline cars is +0.8, and the income elasticity of demand for luxury electric vehicles is +2.2, what do these values signify for multinational automotive manufacturers in international commerce?
keyPoints: Income elasticity: < 0 inferior, 0–1 necessity, > 1 luxury
Cross-price elasticity: > 0 substitutes, < 0 complements, 0 unrelated
+0.8 between imported EVs and gasoline cars: substitutes — rivals' price moves shift your sales
+2.2 for luxury EVs: sales grow faster than income and swing with the business cycle; target rich, fast-growing markets

examQuestions.title: Short-run vs long-run demand elasticity: gasoline vs aircraft
examQuestions.originalTitle: Why do short-run and long-run price elasticities of demand differ dramatically across durable versus nondurable goods? Compare the demand for gasoline with the demand for commercial passenger aircraft, explaining which exhibits greater elasticity in the long run and why.
keyPoints: Nondurables (gasoline): demand is more elastic in the long run — people change cars, homes, habits
Durables (cars, aircraft): demand is more elastic in the short run — buyers can postpone replacement
In the long run the stock of durables must be maintained, so purchases recover
Gasoline has greater long-run elasticity; aircraft orders swing sharply in the short run
examQuestions.draw: Two demand curves for each good: steep SR and flat LR for gasoline; the reverse for aircraft

examQuestions.title: Long-run supply elasticity and secondary supply (scrap)
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain why the long-run price elasticity of supply is typically much larger than the short-run elasticity for primary industrial commodities (such as aluminum or agricultural crops). How does the presence of secondary supply (recycling of metal scrap) affect the overall price elasticity of market supply?
keyPoints: Short run: capacity (mines, smelters, land) is fixed, so supply is inelastic
Long run: new capacity comes on stream, so supply is much more elastic
Secondary supply (scrap) is more elastic in the short run than in the long run: high prices pull scrap out, but the stock runs down
Recycling raises the short-run elasticity of total supply (Pindyck's copper table)
examQuestions.draw: Steep short-run supply and flatter long-run supply through the same point

examQuestions.title: Copper demand shift (calculation task)
examQuestions.originalTitle: Suppose the world demand for copper is given by QD = 32 - 0.20P and competitive supply is QS = 18 + 0.12P (quantities in million metric tons, price in dollars per pound). If a global industrial expansion increases total world demand by 20% at each price, calculate and explain the resulting change in the equilibrium market-clearing price and quantity.
keyPoints: Method: set QD = QS for the original equilibrium, then scale demand by 1.2 and solve again
"20% more at every price" multiplies the whole demand function: both intercept and slope
Price rises much more than quantity because supply is relatively inelastic
examQuestions.draw: Supply line with demand shifting right; label old and new equilibrium

examQuestions.title: Price ceiling on an essential import
examQuestions.originalTitle: Analyze the economic consequences of imposing a price ceiling below the market-clearing level on an essential intermediate import. Identify who benefits, who is harmed, and explain why rationing mechanisms (such as queues, coupons, or black markets) inevitably emerge.
keyPoints: Below equilibrium, importers bring in less while buyers want more: a shortage
Gainers: buyers who still get the good at the low price
Losers: rationed-out buyers, importers and foreign suppliers; deadweight loss B + C
Price no longer rations, so queues, coupons, favouritism or black markets do
examQuestions.draw: Ceiling below P₀; mark Q₁ (supplied), Q₂ (demanded), areas A, B, C

examQuestions.title: Preference assumptions; indifference curves cannot cross
examQuestions.originalTitle: Outline the four fundamental assumptions regarding consumer preferences (completeness, transitivity, more is better than less / non-satiation, and convexity). Explain why two distinct indifference curves can never intersect, illustrating your answer graphically.
keyPoints: Completeness, transitivity, more is better, diminishing MRS (convexity)
Utility is ordinal: it only ranks bundles
If two curves crossed, transitivity would make two bundles equally good even though one has more of both goods — contradicting "more is better"
examQuestions.draw: Two crossing indifference curves with points A, B, D to show the contradiction

examQuestions.title: Marginal rate of substitution
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define the marginal rate of substitution (MRS) of good X for good Y. Explain why the MRS is diminishing along a strictly convex indifference curve. How does the MRS relate to the marginal utilities of the two goods (MU_X and MU_Y)?
keyPoints: MRS of X for Y: the most Y a consumer gives up for one more X and stays equally well off
It is the absolute slope of the indifference curve
Diminishing MRS: the more X you have, the less Y you give up for more X — convex curves
examQuestions.draw: Convex indifference curve with two slope triangles getting flatter to the right

examQuestions.title: Special preferences: substitutes, complements, bads, neutral goods
examQuestions.originalTitle: Draw and interpret the indifference curves and calculate the MRS for: (a) perfect substitutes; (b) perfect complements (Leontief preferences); (c) economic 'bads' (such as industrial pollution); and (d) neutral goods. How does optimal choice differ across these cases?
keyPoints: Perfect substitutes: straight lines, constant MRS; optimum usually a corner
Perfect complements (Leontief): L-shapes; optimum at the kink; no substitution effect
A bad (pollution): upward-sloping curves; consumer chooses zero of it if possible
Neutral good X: horizontal lines (MRS = 0); all income goes to Y
formulas: Substitutes U = aX + bY: MRS = a/b
Complements U = min(aX, bY): MRS undefined at the kink
examQuestions.draw: Four small panels with the four shapes and the optimum on each

examQuestions.title: Budget constraint and how it shifts
examQuestions.originalTitle: Formulate the consumer's algebraic budget constraint (I = P_X * X + P_Y * Y). What determines the slope of the budget line? Explain graphically and algebraically how the budget line shifts in response to: (a) a proportional 20% inflation rate across all prices with constant nominal income; and (b) a 10% import tariff applied strictly to imported good X.
keyPoints: Budget line: I = Px·X + Py·Y; intercepts I/Px and I/Py
Slope = −Px/Py, the market rate of exchange
20% inflation in all prices, nominal income fixed: parallel inward shift (slope unchanged)
10% tariff on X only: rotates inward around the Y-intercept, slope −1.1·Px/Py
examQuestions.draw: Original line; a parallel inward line; a line pivoted around the Y-intercept

examQuestions.title: Utility maximisation: MRS = Px/Py
examQuestions.originalTitle: State the algebraic condition for interior utility maximization subject to a budget constraint (MRS = P_X / P_Y). Explain why an allocation where MRS > P_X / P_Y cannot be optimal for a rational consumer. What adjustments in consumption will the individual undertake to restore equilibrium?
keyPoints: At an interior optimum the budget line is tangent to the highest reachable indifference curve
Equal marginal principle: the last dollar on each good gives the same utility
MRS > Px/Py: the consumer values X above its price, so buys more X and less Y until MRS falls
examQuestions.draw: Budget line tangent to U₂ at A; points B, C on U₁ with arrows toward A

examQuestions.title: Corner solutions
examQuestions.originalTitle: What is a corner solution? Under what conditions does a corner solution arise in commercial consumer choices? If a multinational consumer regards domestic and foreign airlines as perfect substitutes but faces differing ticket prices, demonstrate how a corner solution determines their purchase decision.
keyPoints: A corner solution: the consumer buys none of one good
It arises when MRS ≠ Px/Py even at the edge of the budget line (e.g. perfect substitutes)
Airlines as perfect substitutes (MRS = 1): all flights go to the cheaper airline; any mix only if prices are equal
formulas: Corner at X = 0 when MRS < Px/Py for every bundle
examQuestions.draw: Straight-line indifference curves meeting the budget line at an axis

examQuestions.title: Revealed preference and WARP
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the principle of revealed preference. If an international consumer purchases consumption bundle A over bundle B when bundle B is affordable, under what circumstances would the purchase of bundle B in a subsequent period violate the Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP)?
keyPoints: If A is chosen when B is affordable, A is revealed preferred to B
Revealed preference builds preferences from observed choices
WARP: if A is revealed preferred to B, B must never be chosen when A is also affordable
Choosing B later is consistent only if A has become unaffordable
examQuestions.draw: Two budget lines: A chosen on the first, B on the second; shade the revealed-preferred region

examQuestions.title: Laspeyres vs Paasche and CPI bias
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain why the Laspeyres price index typically overstates changes in the true cost of living, whereas the Paasche index tends to understate them. How does the concept of consumer substitution between goods explain the upward bias in official consumer price indexes (CPI)?
keyPoints: Laspeyres uses base-period quantities: it overstates the cost-of-living increase
Paasche uses current-period quantities: it understates it
Bias comes from substitution toward goods that became relatively cheaper
Other CPI biases: quality changes and new goods added late; chain-weighting reduces the bias

examQuestions.title: Price-consumption curve and individual demand
examQuestions.originalTitle: Demonstrate graphically how an individual demand curve is derived from changes in the price of a good using the price-consumption curve (PCC). Under what preference conditions will the price-consumption curve be downward sloping, horizontal, or upward sloping?
keyPoints: Vary Px with income and Py fixed; link the tangencies to form the PCC
Plot each Px against the X chosen: the individual demand curve
With Y as "all other goods": downward PCC = elastic, horizontal = unit elastic, upward = inelastic demand
examQuestions.draw: Upper panel: budget lines pivoting with three tangencies; lower panel: the derived demand curve

examQuestions.title: Income-consumption curve and Engel curves
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain how the income-consumption curve (ICC) traces the consumer's optimal choices as nominal purchasing power expands. Using ICC diagrams, derive the Engel curves for: (a) a normal necessity; (b) a luxury good; and (c) an inferior good. What is the sign of the income elasticity of demand in each case?
keyPoints: Shift the budget line out in parallel; link the tangencies to form the ICC
Engel curve: quantity of X at each income level
Necessity 0 < E_I < 1 (budget share falls), luxury E_I > 1 (share rises), inferior E_I < 0 (Engel curve bends back)
examQuestions.draw: ICC panel above, three Engel curves below: necessity, luxury, inferior

examQuestions.title: Hicksian decomposition: substitution and income effects
examQuestions.originalTitle: Using the Hicksian decomposition method, explain how a price drop for an imported good breaks down into a substitution effect and an income effect. Illustrate this graphically for a normal good. Why must the substitution effect always be negative (inverse to price)?
keyPoints: Draw a hypothetical budget line with the new slope, tangent to the original indifference curve
Substitution effect: move along U₁ to that tangency — always opposite to the price change
Income effect: move from the hypothetical line to the new optimum; same direction for a normal good
Convex indifference curves guarantee the negative substitution effect
examQuestions.draw: Original and pivoted budget lines, the dashed hypothetical line, points A → B (SE) → C (IE)

examQuestions.title: Inferior vs Giffen goods
examQuestions.originalTitle: Distinguish clearly between an inferior good and a Giffen good. Under what rare economic circumstances will a good exhibit an upward-sloping demand curve? Explain why every Giffen good must be an inferior good, but not every inferior good is a Giffen good.
keyPoints: Inferior: demand falls as income rises (negative income effect)
Giffen: inferior AND the income effect outweighs the substitution effect, so demand slopes up
Every Giffen good is inferior; most inferior goods are not Giffen
Plausible only for staples taking a large budget share of very poor households (Jensen & Miller, rice in China)
examQuestions.draw: Decomposition where the income effect arrow is longer and points opposite to the substitution effect

examQuestions.title: Horizontal summation and market demand
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the procedure of horizontal summation used to derive aggregate market demand from individual demand curves. What happens to the market demand curve when a new group of foreign buyers enters an open international market? Why might the aggregate demand curve feature kinks?
keyPoints: Market demand: add quantities demanded by all buyers at each price
New foreign buyers shift market demand to the right
Kinks appear where a new buyer's choke price is reached and their demand is added
examQuestions.draw: Two individual demands and their horizontal sum with a kink

examQuestions.title: Consumer surplus; tariffs and transport costs
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define consumer surplus and explain how it can be measured using an individual or market demand curve. How do changes in commercial transport costs or international tariffs affect aggregate consumer surplus?
keyPoints: Consumer surplus: willingness to pay minus the price paid, summed over units
Graphically: area under demand and above price
A tariff or higher transport cost raises price: CS falls by a trapezoid (rectangle on units still bought + triangle on units given up)
formulas: CS ≈ ½·(Pmax − P)·Q for linear demand
examQuestions.draw: Demand with CS triangle; a higher price line showing the lost trapezoid

examQuestions.title: Network externalities: bandwagon and snob effects
examQuestions.originalTitle: Distinguish between a positive network externality (the bandwagon effect) and a negative network externality (the snob effect). Explain why the market demand curve for a high-tech communication platform is more price-elastic than it would be without network externalities, whereas the demand for exclusive luxury watches is more inelastic.
keyPoints: Bandwagon (positive): more users make the good more valuable; a price cut draws users, which shifts demand out again — more elastic
Snob (negative): more owners reduce exclusivity; a price cut's effect is partly offset — less elastic
Examples: messaging and payment platforms (bandwagon); luxury watches and limited editions (snob)
examQuestions.draw: Demand curves for 20k, 40k, 60k users; market demand flatter (bandwagon) or steeper (snob)

examQuestions.title: Speculative demand
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define speculative demand. How does an expectation of future price appreciation alter current consumer demand? Contrast standard downward-sloping utility-driven demand with demand driven by speculative feedback in real estate and commodity markets.
keyPoints: Demand driven by expected future price rises, not by the good's direct use
Rising prices can raise expected prices, shifting demand right: a feedback loop
The law of demand still holds for utility-based demand; expectations are a shift factor
Examples: housing booms, commodity hoarding — bubbles end when expectations turn
examQuestions.draw: Demand shifting right repeatedly as price rises

examQuestions.title: Production function; short run vs long run
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define a production function and clearly delineate the economic difference between the short run and the long run. Under what operational constraints can a capital asset be treated as fixed, and how does the length of planning horizon transform fixed inputs into variable inputs?
keyPoints: Production function: maximum output from each input combination with given technology
Short run: at least one input fixed (usually capital); long run: all inputs variable
An asset is fixed when it cannot be changed within the planning horizon (fab construction takes years)
As the horizon lengthens, fixed inputs become variable

examQuestions.title: TP, AP and MP; why MP cuts AP at its maximum
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define total product (TP), average product (AP_L), and marginal product (MP_L). Explain mathematically and intuitively why the marginal product curve must intersect the average product curve at the exact maximum point of the average product curve.
keyPoints: AP = q/L; MP = Δq/ΔL
MP above AP pulls AP up; MP below AP pulls it down, so MP = AP at AP's maximum
Graph: AP = slope of a ray from the origin to TP; MP = slope of TP
TP is at its maximum where MP = 0
examQuestions.draw: TP curve above; AP and MP below, with MP crossing AP at AP's peak

examQuestions.title: Diminishing marginal returns
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns. Why does diminishing returns to a single factor not imply that total output decreases? How do continuous technological improvements in capital equipment offset or delay the onset of diminishing marginal returns to labor in commercial agriculture and manufacturing?
keyPoints: With other inputs fixed, the marginal product of an input eventually falls
Output still rises as long as MP > 0 — it just rises more slowly
Better technology shifts TP upward and delays diminishing returns (Malthus was wrong)
Applies to one input at a time, not to scaling all inputs
examQuestions.draw: TP curve shifting up from O₁ to O₂ to O₃ with technological progress

examQuestions.title: Isoquants and isoquant maps
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define an isoquant and an isoquant map. What economic assumptions ensure that isoquants are smooth, downward sloping, and convex to the origin? What would an upward-sloping portion of an isoquant imply about input utilization?
keyPoints: Isoquant: all input combinations giving the same output
Downward sloping (both MPs positive), convex (diminishing MRTS), never crossing
An upward-sloping section means one input has a negative MP — an uneconomic region
examQuestions.draw: Isoquant map with q₁ < q₂ < q₃; a bent-back section outside the ridge lines

examQuestions.title: MRTS = MPL/MPK
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define the Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution of labor for capital (MRTS_LK). Prove that along any isoquant, MRTS_LK = MP_L / MP_K. Why does the MRTS diminish as a firm substitutes labor for capital while holding output constant?
keyPoints: MRTS: how much capital can be replaced by one more unit of labour at constant output
Output constant along the isoquant gives the ratio of marginal products
MRTS diminishes: more labour lowers MPL and raises MPK
examQuestions.draw: Convex isoquant with flatter slope triangles moving right

examQuestions.title: Linear, Leontief and Cobb-Douglas technologies
examQuestions.originalTitle: Contrast the substitution possibilities of a linear production function (perfect substitutes), a fixed-proportions production function (Leontief), and a Cobb-Douglas production function (Q = A * K^alpha * L^beta). How does the elasticity of input substitution affect a firm's operational resilience when facing international supply shocks?
keyPoints: Linear (perfect substitutes): straight isoquants, elasticity of substitution σ = ∞
Fixed proportions (Leontief): L-shaped isoquants, σ = 0
Cobb-Douglas: smooth convex isoquants, σ = 1
High σ makes a firm resilient to shocks in one input; Leontief firms cannot switch
formulas: q = aL + bK;  q = min(aL, bK);  q = A·K^α·L^β
examQuestions.draw: Three isoquant panels side by side

examQuestions.title: Returns to scale vs diminishing returns
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define increasing, constant, and decreasing returns to scale. How can a production function simultaneously exhibit diminishing marginal returns to an individual input (holding the other input constant) and increasing returns to scale when all inputs are scaled proportionately?
keyPoints: Increasing, constant, decreasing RTS: output rises by more, the same or less than the proportional rise in all inputs
Diminishing returns concern one input; returns to scale concern all inputs together
Example q = K^0.6·L^0.6: each MP diminishes (0.6 < 1), but 0.6 + 0.6 = 1.2 > 1 gives IRS
examQuestions.draw: Isoquants for q = 10, 20, 30 getting closer together along a ray (IRS)

examQuestions.title: Economies and diseconomies of scale in global industries
examQuestions.originalTitle: In capital-intensive global industries (such as commercial semiconductor fabrication, automobile manufacturing, and aerospace), what technological and organizational factors generate significant economies of scale? Why do some multinational enterprises eventually experience decreasing returns to scale as corporate hierarchy expands?
keyPoints: Sources: huge indivisible fixed costs (fabs, design, certification), specialisation, volume purchasing
Chips, cars, aerospace: few producers worldwide, because minimum efficient scale is huge
Diseconomies: layers of hierarchy, slow decisions, weak incentives, information loss
Scale economies concern all inputs; external input-price effects are a separate idea
examQuestions.draw: U-shaped LAC with economies, minimum efficient scale and diseconomies marked

examQuestions.title: Accounting, economic and opportunity cost
examQuestions.originalTitle: Distinguish rigorously between accounting cost, economic cost, and opportunity cost. Why is the cost of utilizing a company-owned building or self-provided equity capital considered zero by financial accountants but treated as a positive cost by economists?
keyPoints: Accounting cost: explicit outlays and depreciation
Economic cost = opportunity cost: includes implicit costs
A firm's own building: no rent in the books, but forgone rental income is an economic cost
Owner's equity: forgone return elsewhere is a cost, so accounting profit can hide an economic loss
formulas: Economic profit = revenue − explicit costs − implicit costs

examQuestions.title: Sunk costs
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define a sunk cost. Why should sunk expenditures (such as unrecoverable specialized software or R&D for an abandoned commercial project) be completely ignored when deciding whether to continue operating or terminate an investment project?
keyPoints: Sunk cost: already spent and unrecoverable
Ignore sunk costs: only future costs and benefits matter for the decision
Example: spent $50m, need $20m more to earn $30m — finish it
Not sunk: assets with resale value, avoidable future costs

examQuestions.title: Short-run cost curves
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the geometric and mathematical relationships between Total Cost (TC), Fixed Cost (FC), Variable Cost (VC), Marginal Cost (MC), Average Total Cost (ATC), and Average Variable Cost (AVC). Why does the MC curve intersect both AVC and ATC at their minimum points?
keyPoints: TC = FC + VC; ATC = AFC + AVC
MC = ΔVC/Δq, so fixed cost does not affect MC
MC cuts AVC and ATC at their minimum points; AFC falls continuously
examQuestions.draw: U-shaped MC, ATC and AVC with MC crossing both at their minimums

examQuestions.title: Isocost lines and cost minimisation
examQuestions.originalTitle: Formulate the equation of an isocost line (TC = wL + rK). What determines its slope? Demonstrate graphically and algebraically that a firm minimizes the total cost of producing a given output level when MRTS_LK = w / r, or equivalently, when MP_L / w = MP_K / r.
keyPoints: Isocost: C = wL + rK, slope −w/r
Lowest cost for a given output: isocost tangent to the isoquant
If MPL/w > MPK/r, use more labour and less capital
examQuestions.draw: Isoquant with three isocost lines; tangency at the cheapest one

examQuestions.title: Expansion path after a wage increase
examQuestions.originalTitle: What is a firm's long-run expansion path? If an international trade disruption or regulatory reform permanently doubles the wage rate of labor (w) while keeping the rental cost of capital (r) constant, how will the firm's cost-minimizing expansion path and capital-labor ratio adjust?
keyPoints: Expansion path: cost-minimising input mixes for each output level
If w doubles with r fixed, isocosts get steeper: the firm substitutes capital for labour
K/L rises; the expansion path rotates toward the capital axis
How far it rotates depends on the elasticity of substitution
examQuestions.draw: Isoquants with old and new tangencies; old and new expansion paths from the origin

examQuestions.title: LAC as the envelope of SAC curves
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain how the Long-Run Average Cost (LAC) curve is constructed as the lower envelope of a sequence of Short-Run Average Cost (SAC) curves. Under what circumstances will the point of minimum long-run average cost not coincide with the minimum point of a short-run average cost curve?
keyPoints: For each output, the long-run choice is the plant with the lowest SAC
LAC touches each SAC once and never lies above any SAC
With economies of scale the tangency is left of the SAC minimum; with diseconomies to its right
Only at the bottom of LAC does tangency fall on an SAC's minimum
examQuestions.draw: Several SAC curves with LAC as their lower envelope

examQuestions.title: Economies of scope
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define economies of scope and compare them with economies of scale. How is the degree of economies of scope measured algebraically? Provide an example from international freight logistics or multi-product consumer electronics where economies of scope provide a decisive competitive advantage.
keyPoints: Joint production of two products costs less than producing them separately
Different from scale (volume of one product) and from learning
Sources: shared networks, hubs, IT, brands, R&D (logistics, consumer electronics)
SC > 0 means economies of scope; SC < 0 diseconomies
formulas: SC = [C(q₁) + C(q₂) − C(q₁, q₂)] / C(q₁, q₂)

examQuestions.title: Learning curve
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the concept of the learning curve. How does learning-by-doing differ from traditional economies of scale? If a multinational aircraft manufacturer experiences an 80% learning curve, what does this imply for labor hours required per unit as cumulative production doubles?
keyPoints: Cost per unit falls as cumulative output rises (workers, managers and engineers learn)
Learning shifts cost curves down over time; scale moves along LAC with the output rate
80% curve: each doubling of cumulative output cuts labour hours per unit to 80%
Rationale for aggressive early pricing (aircraft, chips)
examQuestions.draw: Labour hours per unit falling with cumulative output; LAC₁ shifting down to LAC₂

examQuestions.title: Perfect competition: conditions and horizontal firm demand
examQuestions.originalTitle: State and evaluate the three central conditions that characterize a perfectly competitive market: price taking, product homogeneity, and free entry and exit. Why must an individual competitive firm view its individual demand curve as infinitely elastic at the prevailing market price?
keyPoints: Price taking, homogeneous product, free entry and exit
The firm's output is tiny, and buyers can switch to identical goods
So firm demand is perfectly elastic at the market price, while market demand slopes down
examQuestions.draw: Two panels: market S and D setting P; the firm's horizontal d = MR = P

examQuestions.title: MR = MC and P = MC
examQuestions.originalTitle: Prove that any firm maximizes profit where Marginal Revenue equals Marginal Cost (MR = MC). Why does this general condition simplify to Price equals Marginal Cost (P = MC) specifically for a price-taking firm?
keyPoints: Profit π(q) = R(q) − C(q) peaks where dπ/dq = MR − MC = 0
If MR > MC, expand; if MR < MC, contract
For a price taker MR = P, so P = MC; MC must be rising (second-order condition)
examQuestions.draw: Firm diagram: P line crossing rising MC at q*

examQuestions.title: Short-run losses and the shutdown rule
examQuestions.originalTitle: Under what market conditions should a competitive firm continue producing at an economic loss in the short run? State the exact shutdown rule in terms of price and Average Variable Cost (P < AVC_min), explaining why fixed costs are irrelevant to this operational decision.
keyPoints: Produce at a loss if P ≥ AVCmin: revenue covers variable cost and part of fixed cost
Shut down if P < AVCmin
Fixed costs are paid either way, so they do not affect the decision
Long-run exit if P < ATC persists
formulas: Shut down if P < AVCmin  (equivalently R < VC)
examQuestions.draw: Cost curves with prices above ATCmin, between AVCmin and ATCmin, and below AVCmin

examQuestions.title: The firm's short-run supply curve
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain why the short-run supply curve of a perfectly competitive firm is identical to the portion of its marginal cost curve that lies above the minimum of average variable cost. How does an increase in the price of a variable factor shift this supply curve?
keyPoints: For each price, the firm produces where P = MC
Below AVCmin it produces nothing
So supply = MC curve above AVCmin
A higher variable input price shifts MC up and supply left; fixed costs do not shift it
examQuestions.draw: The bold part of MC above the shutdown point

examQuestions.title: Short-run market supply
examQuestions.originalTitle: How is the short-run market supply curve derived from individual competitive firms? Why is the short-run industry supply curve not always the exact horizontal sum of individual marginal cost curves if factor prices rise as total industry output expands?
keyPoints: With constant input prices: horizontal sum of firms' supply curves
If input prices rise as the whole industry expands, each MC shifts up
So industry supply is steeper than the simple horizontal sum
examQuestions.draw: Three firms' MC curves and their horizontal sum

examQuestions.title: Producer surplus vs profit
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define producer surplus and distinguish it carefully from economic profit. Show that in the short run, Producer Surplus = Profit + Fixed Costs = Total Revenue - Variable Costs. How is producer surplus represented graphically on a firm-level and market-level diagram?
keyPoints: Producer surplus: sum over units of (P − MC); area above supply, below price
PS = profit + FC = TR − VC
In the long run (no fixed costs) PS and profit coincide
Market PS: area above market supply and below price
formulas: PS = R − VC;  π = R − VC − FC
examQuestions.draw: Firm panel and market panel with PS shaded

examQuestions.title: Long-run competitive equilibrium
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the dynamic market adjustment mechanism of entry and exit that guarantees zero economic profit in long-run competitive equilibrium (P = MC = LAC_min). Why do entrepreneurs and international investors continue operating businesses when economic profit is zero?
keyPoints: Profits attract entry, losses cause exit, shifting market supply
Long run: zero economic profit, P = MC = LACmin
Zero economic profit = normal return; accounting profit is positive
Owners stay because they earn their opportunity cost
examQuestions.draw: Market supply shifting right to S′ and the firm at the bottom of LAC

examQuestions.title: Long-run industry supply: constant, increasing, decreasing cost
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain why the long-run industry supply curve can be horizontal, upward-sloping, or downward-sloping. What role do external factor price adjustments (pecuniary diseconomies or economies) play in determining whether an industry is constant-cost or increasing-cost?
keyPoints: Constant-cost: input prices unchanged as the industry grows — horizontal supply at LACmin
Increasing-cost: scarce inputs get dearer — upward-sloping supply
Decreasing-cost: suppliers' scale economies cut input prices — downward-sloping supply
External (pecuniary) economies and diseconomies decide which case applies
examQuestions.draw: Demand shifting right with three different long-run supply curves

examQuestions.title: Efficiency and the deadweight loss of a price ceiling
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define economic efficiency and deadweight loss. Using consumer and producer surplus areas, demonstrate graphically the deadweight loss resulting from a government-mandated price ceiling on a competitive market. Under what elasticity conditions is the deadweight loss minimized or maximized?
keyPoints: Efficiency: competitive equilibrium maximises CS + PS
Under a ceiling: ΔCS = A − B, ΔPS = −A − C, deadweight loss = B + C
DWL is largest with elastic supply and inelastic demand; zero with perfectly inelastic supply
With very inelastic demand, consumers as a group can lose (B > A)
examQuestions.draw: Ceiling diagram with areas A, B, C

examQuestions.title: Price floors and minimum wages
examQuestions.originalTitle: Analyze the welfare impact of an effective minimum price (such as an agricultural price floor or a minimum wage). Show graphically the changes in consumer surplus, producer surplus, and the deadweight loss resulting from excess supply when output cannot be purchased.
keyPoints: A floor above equilibrium creates excess supply (unemployment for a minimum wage)
Workers who keep jobs gain; employers and priced-out workers lose
Deadweight loss on trades that no longer happen
If producers make more than they can sell, the cost of unsold output can wipe out their gain
examQuestions.draw: Floor above P₀ with Qd, Qs and the excess supply; triangles B, C

examQuestions.title: Price supports vs direct subsidies
examQuestions.originalTitle: Compare a government price support program (where the state purchases surplus production at price P_s) with a direct income subsidy to producers. Prove that government price supports impose a substantially larger total cost on society and taxpayers than direct cash transfers.
keyPoints: Support: the state buys the surplus (Q₂ − Q₁) at Ps
Consumers lose, producers gain, taxpayers pay for unwanted output
Total cost to consumers and taxpayers far exceeds producers' gain
A direct cash transfer of the same gain is much cheaper and creates no waste
examQuestions.draw: Support price above P₀; consumer loss A + B, producer gain A + B + D, state purchases

examQuestions.title: Production quotas and licences (taxi medallions)
examQuestions.originalTitle: Analyze the welfare effects of a government production quota or license limitation (e.g., taxi medallions or crop acreage restrictions). Show how supply restriction transfers surplus from consumers to incumbent producers and calculate the resulting net deadweight loss.
keyPoints: A cap on quantity raises price above MC
Consumers lose; incumbents with licences gain the rents
Lost trades are a deadweight loss
Tradable licences capture the rent in their price (New York medallions)
examQuestions.draw: Vertical supply cap at Q₁ below Q₀; areas A (transfer), B + C (DWL)

examQuestions.title: Import tariff in a small importing country
examQuestions.originalTitle: Using a partial equilibrium diagram of an importing nation, evaluate the welfare effects of an import tariff. Identify: (a) domestic consumer surplus loss; (b) domestic producer surplus gain; (c) government tariff revenue; and (d) the two deadweight loss triangles (production and consumption distortions).
keyPoints: Tariff raises the domestic price from Pw to Pw + t
Consumers lose A + B + C + D; producers gain A; state revenue D
Deadweight loss B (production distortion) + C (consumption distortion)
examQuestions.draw: World price line, tariff line, areas A, B, D, C

examQuestions.title: Quota vs tariff; quota rents
examQuestions.originalTitle: Contrast an import tariff with an import quota that restricts foreign imports to the exact same volume. Under what circumstances does an import quota produce the exact same net welfare loss as a tariff, and when does it generate an even larger loss for the domestic economy due to foreign quota rent extraction?
