keyPoints: A quota with the same import volume raises the price by the same amount
If the state auctions licences (or domestic firms hold them), the loss is still B + C
If foreign exporters get the quota rent (VERs), the country also loses D
Example: Japan's car export restraints to the US in the 1980s
examQuestions.draw: Same diagram as the tariff, with D labelled "quota rent"

examQuestions.title: Tax incidence and pass-through
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain how the economic burden (incidence) of a specific per-unit sales tax is divided between buyers and sellers. Derive the pass-through fraction (Es / (Es - Ed)). Why does statutory legal liability (whether the tax is levied on producers or consumers) have zero impact on economic incidence?
keyPoints: A tax opens a wedge Pb − Ps = t
The less elastic side bears more of the burden
Statutory incidence does not matter: taxing buyers or sellers gives the same result
Revenue A + D, deadweight loss B + C
examQuestions.draw: Tax wedge diagram with Pb, Ps, Q₁ and areas A, D, B, C

examQuestions.title: Per-unit subsidy
examQuestions.originalTitle: Analyze the welfare effects of a per-unit government subsidy provided to domestic exporters or producers. Show graphically why a subsidy causes production to expand beyond the efficient competitive quantity, creating a deadweight loss where marginal cost exceeds consumer valuation.
keyPoints: A subsidy s creates a wedge Ps − Pb = s
Output expands past the efficient level: extra units cost more than buyers value them
Taxpayers' cost exceeds the gain in CS + PS: a deadweight loss
Benefit split by the same elasticity rule as a tax
examQuestions.draw: Supply and demand with Ps above and Pb below P₀, quantity Q₁ > Q₀, DWL triangle

examQuestions.title: MR, price and elasticity; why monopoly avoids inelastic demand
examQuestions.originalTitle: Derive the relationship between marginal revenue, price, and price elasticity of demand (MR = P * [1 + 1/Ed]). Prove that a profit-maximizing monopolist will never choose an output level that falls on the inelastic portion of its market demand curve.
keyPoints: Selling one more unit brings in P but lowers the price on all units
MR is positive only where demand is elastic (|Ed| > 1)
On the inelastic part MR < 0: cutting output raises revenue and lowers cost
examQuestions.draw: Linear demand with MR twice as steep, MR = 0 at the midpoint

examQuestions.title: Lerner index and the markup rule
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define the Lerner Index of Monopoly Power (L = [P - MC] / P). Show that for a profit-maximizing monopolist, L = -1 / Ed. How does the availability of international substitute goods constrain a domestic monopolist's markup?
keyPoints: Lerner index measures monopoly power: 0 under competition
Profit maximisation gives the inverse-elasticity rule
Import substitutes make the firm's demand more elastic and shrink its markup

examQuestions.title: Sources of monopoly power and barriers to entry
examQuestions.originalTitle: Identify and analyze the three key structural determinants of monopoly power: the elasticity of market demand, the number of firms in the industry, and the interaction among firms. How do legal barriers (patents, exclusive concessions) and economies of scale sustain monopoly power?
keyPoints: Elasticity of market demand
Number of firms in the market
Interaction among firms
Barriers: patents, copyrights, licences, scale economies, control of key inputs

examQuestions.title: Deadweight loss of monopoly and rent-seeking
examQuestions.originalTitle: Demonstrate graphically the deadweight loss (welfare loss) of monopoly relative to a competitive market. Explain why the full social cost of monopoly may substantially exceed the standard deadweight loss triangle when firms engage in rent-seeking expenditures to secure exclusive market privileges.
keyPoints: Monopoly output Qm < Qc, price Pm > Pc
Consumers lose A + B, producer gains A − C, deadweight loss B + C
Rent-seeking (lobbying to win or keep monopoly) can waste much of A as well
examQuestions.draw: Demand, MR, MC with Pm, Qm, Pc, Qc and areas A, B, C

examQuestions.title: Price ceiling on a monopolist
examQuestions.originalTitle: Show graphically how imposing a maximum price ceiling (P_reg) on a monopolist can simultaneously lower price, eliminate monopoly deadweight loss, and increase total output toward the competitive benchmark. Contrast this with the effect of a price ceiling in a competitive industry.
keyPoints: Below the cap, MR equals the cap price up to the demand curve
A cap at the competitive price raises output to Qc and removes the deadweight loss
A cap set too low cuts output and creates a shortage
In a competitive industry a ceiling always reduces output
examQuestions.draw: Monopoly diagram with a horizontal cap line and the new kinked MR

examQuestions.title: Natural monopoly and regulation
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define a natural monopoly in terms of subadditive costs and declining long-run average cost (LAC). Explain the regulatory dilemma: why does marginal cost pricing (P = MC) cause the firm to incur chronic financial losses, and how does average-cost pricing (P = AC) solve this solvency problem?
keyPoints: Subadditive costs: one firm can serve the market more cheaply than several
Typically LAC keeps falling over the relevant range (grids, water, rail)
P = MC is efficient but below AC: the firm loses money
P = AC lets it break even but leaves a small deadweight loss
examQuestions.draw: Falling AC with MC below it; mark Pm, P = AC and P = MC outcomes

examQuestions.title: Monopsony: average vs marginal expenditure
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define monopsony and contrast average expenditure (AE) with marginal expenditure (ME). Why does the marginal expenditure curve lie strictly above the average expenditure curve for an input buyer facing an upward-sloping supply curve?
keyPoints: Monopsony: a single (or dominant) buyer
AE is the supply curve the buyer faces
To buy one more unit it must pay more on all units, so ME > AE
examQuestions.draw: Upward-sloping AE and a steeper ME above it

examQuestions.title: Monopsony equilibrium and deadweight loss
examQuestions.originalTitle: Demonstrate graphically how a profit-maximizing monopsonist chooses input quantity and price where Marginal Value equals Marginal Expenditure (MV = ME). Identify the deadweight loss of monopsony power and explain why monopsonistic exploitation occurs in regional labor markets.
keyPoints: Buy where MV = ME, then pay the AE (supply) price
Less is bought at a lower price than under competition
Buyer gains A − B, sellers lose A + C, deadweight loss B + C
Regional labour markets with one big employer
examQuestions.draw: MV, AE, ME with Qm, Pm and areas A, B, C

examQuestions.title: Why a single price leaves profit on the table
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the strategic dilemma of a single-price monopolist: why does charging a uniform price leave potential profits unrealized in the form of consumer surplus and deadweight loss? How do price discrimination schemes capture this surplus?
keyPoints: Some buyers would pay more than the single price (uncaptured consumer surplus)
Some would buy at prices above MC but below the single price (deadweight loss)
Price discrimination aims to capture both
examQuestions.draw: Monopoly diagram highlighting CS above Pm and the DWL triangle

examQuestions.title: First-degree price discrimination
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define first-degree price discrimination. What are the informational and arbitrage-prevention prerequisites for its implementation? Show that under perfect price discrimination, output expands to the competitive level, deadweight loss is zero, and consumer surplus is entirely converted into producer profit.
keyPoints: Charge each buyer their reservation price
Needs knowledge of willingness to pay and no resale
Demand becomes the MR curve, so output rises to where D = MC
No deadweight loss, but all consumer surplus goes to the firm
examQuestions.draw: Demand and MC with the whole area between them shaded as profit

examQuestions.title: Second-degree price discrimination
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain how second-degree price discrimination (declining block pricing or quantity discounts) operates. How does self-selection enable commercial utilities and telecommunications providers to capture consumer surplus without prior individual knowledge of consumer willingness to pay?
keyPoints: Different unit prices for different quantities (block pricing, quantity discounts)
Self-selection: buyers choose their block or plan, revealing their type
Utilities and telecoms extract surplus without knowing individual demand
examQuestions.draw: Stepped price schedule P₁, P₂, P₃ over blocks of quantity

examQuestions.title: Third-degree price discrimination
examQuestions.originalTitle: Derive the optimality conditions for a multinational corporation practicing third-degree price discrimination across two geographically separated international markets (MR1 = MR2 = MC). Prove that the firm will charge a higher price in the market with the lower price elasticity of demand.
keyPoints: Separate groups (countries, students) with different elasticities
Allocate output so that MR is equal across markets and equal to MC
Higher price where demand is less elastic
examQuestions.draw: Two market panels plus combined MR_T crossing MC

examQuestions.title: Intertemporal discrimination vs peak-load pricing
examQuestions.originalTitle: Distinguish between intertemporal price discrimination (e.g., high initial pricing for newly released electronics or hardcover books) and peak-load pricing (e.g., electricity grids or seasonal airline flights). Why is peak-load pricing driven by marginal cost capacity constraints rather than consumer surplus extraction?
keyPoints: Intertemporal: high launch price for eager buyers, lower later (electronics, hardcover then paperback)
Peak-load: higher prices at peak times because MC is higher when capacity is stretched
Peak-load pricing is efficient (P ≈ MC in each period), not surplus extraction
formulas: Peak-load: MR = MC in each period
examQuestions.draw: Two demand curves (peak, off-peak) with the same rising MC

examQuestions.title: Two-part tariff
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain how a two-part tariff operates (fixed entry fee T plus per-unit usage fee P). If a firm serves identical consumers, prove that profit maximization requires setting P = MC and setting the entry fee T equal to total consumer surplus. How does this strategy change when consumers have heterogeneous demands?
keyPoints: Price = entry fee T + usage price P per unit
Identical consumers: P = MC, T = each consumer's consumer surplus
Different consumers: P > MC and a lower T, trading off entry fees against usage margins
Examples: amusement parks, gyms, razors and blades, phone plans

examQuestions.title: Pure and mixed bundling
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define pure bundling and mixed bundling. Under what conditions regarding the correlation of consumer reservation prices does bundling yield higher profits than selling goods separately? Provide an example from international enterprise software or media licensing.
keyPoints: Pure: only the package is sold; mixed: package and items separately
Bundling pays when reservation prices are negatively correlated
Mixed bundling beats pure when MC is significant and some buyers value one item below cost
Examples: software suites, media and streaming licences
examQuestions.draw: Reservation-price scatter (r₁, r₂) with a negative correlation and the bundle price line

examQuestions.title: Tying as metering
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the economic rationale for tying agreements (e.g., requiring purchasers of a specialized machine to exclusively purchase proprietary supplies). How does tying function as a metering device that enables a firm to price discriminate based on consumer usage intensity?
keyPoints: Buyers of the main product must buy the firm's supplies
Usage intensity reveals willingness to pay, so heavy users pay more
Examples: printers and cartridges, Xerox paper, IBM punch cards
Also used to protect quality (franchising) — watched by competition authorities

examQuestions.title: Monopolistic competition and long-run tangency
examQuestions.originalTitle: Outline the defining characteristics of monopolistic competition. Demonstrate graphically how short-run economic profits attract new entrants, shifting each incumbent firm's demand curve inward until a long-run equilibrium of zero economic profit is achieved (tangency of demand to LAC).
keyPoints: Many firms, differentiated products, free entry
Short-run profits attract entry; each firm's demand shifts in
Long run: demand tangent to LAC — zero profit, P > MC
formulas: Long run: MR = MC and P = LAC
examQuestions.draw: Short-run panel with profit; long-run panel with tangency

examQuestions.title: Excess capacity theorem
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the Excess Capacity Theorem in monopolistic competition. Why does long-run equilibrium occur at an output level below the minimum efficient scale of the average cost curve? Discuss whether this excess capacity represents an economic waste or a socially desirable premium for product variety.
keyPoints: Tangency is on the falling part of LAC, so output is below minimum efficient scale
Costs are higher than the minimum, and P > MC
Trade-off: the inefficiency is the price of variety consumers value
Small if products are close substitutes (very elastic demand)
examQuestions.draw: LAC with the tangency point left of its minimum

examQuestions.title: Cournot duopoly
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the assumptions of the Cournot duopoly model with homogeneous products. Define a firm's reaction function. Show graphically and algebraically how the Cournot-Nash equilibrium is determined, and compare the equilibrium price and industry output with competitive and monopoly benchmarks.
keyPoints: Firms choose quantities simultaneously, each taking the other's output as given
Reaction function: best output for each rival output
Nash equilibrium where reaction curves cross
Output between monopoly and competition; price between too
formulas: Example P = 30 − Q, MC = 0: Q₁ = 15 − Q₂/2;  Q₁ = Q₂ = 10, P = 10
examQuestions.draw: Reaction curves crossing at 10, 10 with collusion and competition lines

examQuestions.title: Bertrand price competition
examQuestions.originalTitle: State the assumptions of the Bertrand price-competition model for identical goods. Explain why the equilibrium price drops immediately to marginal cost (P = MC) even with only two competing firms (the Bertrand Paradox). What market conditions (capacity constraints, product differentiation) resolve this paradox?
keyPoints: Firms choose prices simultaneously; identical products
Any price above MC can be undercut to win the whole market
So P = MC even with two firms (Bertrand paradox)
Resolved by capacity constraints, differentiation or repeated interaction

examQuestions.title: Stackelberg leadership
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the Stackelberg model of quantity leadership. Why does the leader firm enjoy a decisive strategic advantage over the follower firm? Show that the Stackelberg leader produces more output and earns higher profits than in the Cournot equilibrium, while the follower earns less.
keyPoints: The leader commits to output first; the follower responds on its reaction curve
The leader picks the point on the follower's reaction curve that maximises its own profit
First-mover advantage: leader produces more and earns more than in Cournot; follower less
examQuestions.draw: Stackelberg point on firm 2's reaction curve

examQuestions.title: Kinked demand curve (Sweezy)
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the logic of Paul Sweezy's kinked demand curve model. Why is the demand curve highly elastic for price increases but inelastic for price cuts? Demonstrate how the resulting vertical discontinuity in the marginal revenue curve generates price rigidity in oligopolistic markets.
keyPoints: Rivals match price cuts but not price rises
Demand is elastic above the kink and inelastic below it
MR has a vertical gap at Q*
MC can move within the gap without changing P* or Q*: price rigidity
Weakness: it does not explain how P* is set
examQuestions.draw: Kinked demand, broken MR and two MC curves through the gap

examQuestions.title: Dominant firm and competitive fringe
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain how a dominant firm in an oligopoly sets market price while accommodating a competitive fringe of small firms. How is the residual demand curve for the dominant firm constructed, and how does entry by fringe producers erode the dominant firm's pricing power over time?
keyPoints: Residual demand = market demand − fringe supply
The dominant firm sets MR_D = MC_D and charges P from residual demand
The fringe takes that price and supplies where P = MC
Fringe entry shrinks residual demand and erodes the dominant firm's power

examQuestions.title: Cartels: OPEC vs CIPEC
examQuestions.originalTitle: Analyze the conditions required for a successful international cartel. Using the comparative cases of OPEC (oil) and CIPEC (copper) from Pindyck, explain why non-cartel supply elasticity, market demand elasticity, and the internal incentive to cheat determine the long-term viability of a cartel.
keyPoints: Need a stable organisation (agreement, no cheating) and potential monopoly power
Power depends on inelastic market demand and inelastic non-member supply
OPEC: inelastic oil demand and non-OPEC supply — large price increases
CIPEC: elastic copper demand, scrap and outside supply — little power
Each member is tempted to cheat because P > its MC at the cartel output

examQuestions.title: Dominant strategies and Nash equilibrium
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define a dominant strategy and a Nash equilibrium. Explain why every equilibrium in dominant strategies is a Nash equilibrium, but not every Nash equilibrium is an equilibrium in dominant strategies. Provide an illustrative 2x2 payoff matrix.
keyPoints: Dominant strategy: best whatever the rival does
Nash equilibrium: each player's choice is a best response to the others'
Every dominant-strategy equilibrium is Nash, not vice versa
Example matrix: advertising game where both advertise
examQuestions.draw: 2×2 payoff matrix: (Adv, Adv) 10,5; (Adv, Don't) 15,0; (Don't, Adv) 6,8; (Don't, Don't) 10,2

examQuestions.title: Prisoners' dilemma in trade policy
examQuestions.originalTitle: Formulate the Prisoners' Dilemma in the context of international trade policy (e.g., two nations deciding whether to implement trade protectionism or free trade). Prove that the noncooperative Nash equilibrium yields a suboptimal outcome for both nations, and discuss mechanisms for achieving cooperation.
keyPoints: Protection is each country's dominant strategy
(Protect, Protect) is the Nash equilibrium, worse for both than free trade
Cooperation needs enforceable agreements (WTO), reciprocity, repeated interaction
examQuestions.draw: 2×2 matrix, e.g. (Free, Free) 10,10; (Protect, Free) 20,−5; (Free, Protect) −5,20; (Protect, Protect) 0,0

examQuestions.title: Repeated games and tit-for-tat
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain how infinite repetition transforms the outcome of a Prisoners' Dilemma game. What is the 'tit-for-tat' strategy? Under what conditions (such as the discount rate and credible punishment threats) will cooperation be sustained in indefinitely repeated games?
keyPoints: Tit-for-tat: cooperate first, then copy the rival's last move
Infinite (or uncertain) repetition: the future punishment outweighs the one-off gain from cheating
Needs a low discount rate, quick detection, credible punishment, few players
With a known last round, cooperation unravels by backward induction

examQuestions.title: Sequential games and backward induction
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain how sequential games are modeled using game trees (extensive form). Define subgame perfect equilibrium and explain the technique of backward induction. How does the order of moves dictate the distribution of strategic payoffs?
keyPoints: Extensive form (game tree) shows the order of moves
Backward induction: solve the last move first and work back
Subgame perfect equilibrium: Nash in every subgame; rules out empty threats
Moving first can be an advantage (product-choice game)
examQuestions.draw: Game tree with two stages and payoffs at the end nodes

examQuestions.title: Credible vs empty threats; commitment
examQuestions.originalTitle: What distinguishes an empty threat from a credible threat in commercial bargaining? Explain how making an irreversible investment in specialized plant capacity (e.g., DuPont's strategy in titanium dioxide) serves as a credible commitment that deters potential market entrants.
keyPoints: A threat is credible only if carrying it out is in the threatener's interest
Irreversible investments change your own payoffs and make threats credible
DuPont built titanium dioxide capacity ahead of demand to deter entry
examQuestions.draw: Game tree: entry, then accommodate vs fight, with and without sunk capacity

examQuestions.title: Entry deterrence with extra capacity
examQuestions.originalTitle: Using a 2-stage game, analyze how an incumbent monopoly firm can deter entry by expanding capacity beforehand. Under what cost conditions will entry deterrence be profitable for the incumbent, and when is 'accommodated entry' the rational profit-maximizing strategy?
keyPoints: Stage 1: incumbent decides on capacity; stage 2: entrant decides; then pricing
Extra capacity makes price war the best response after entry, so the threat is credible
Deterrence pays if the capacity cost is below the profit it protects
Otherwise accommodation is the profit-maximising strategy
examQuestions.draw: Payoff matrix or tree with and without the capacity investment

examQuestions.title: Brander–Spencer strategic trade policy (Boeing vs Airbus)
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the Brander-Spencer model of strategic trade policy (the Boeing vs. Airbus commercial aircraft rivalry). Demonstrate using a payoff matrix how a government production subsidy can alter the payoff structure, commit a domestic firm to produce, and successfully capture global market profits from a foreign competitor.
keyPoints: Either firm alone is profitable; if both produce, both lose
Two Nash equilibria: whoever moves first wins
A European subsidy makes producing Airbus's dominant strategy, so Boeing stays out
Caveats: information demands, retaliation, subsidy wars
examQuestions.draw: 2×2 matrix: both produce −10,−10; only one produces 100 for it, 0 for the other; neither 0,0. Then add a subsidy of 20 to Airbus

examQuestions.title: Auctions and the winner's curse
examQuestions.originalTitle: Compare four primary auction formats: English (ascending oral), Dutch (descending oral), first-price sealed-bid, and second-price sealed-bid (Vickrey). Define common-value auctions and explain why the 'winner's curse' causes aggressive bidders to suffer economic losses.
keyPoints: English (ascending), Dutch (descending), first-price sealed, second-price sealed (Vickrey)
Vickrey: bidding your true value is a dominant strategy
Common value: item worth the same to all, but estimates differ (oil tracts)
Winner's curse: the highest bidder usually overestimated, so shade your bid

examQuestions.title: Derived demand; MRP vs VMP
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain why the demand for factor inputs (labor, capital, raw materials) is a derived demand. Define Marginal Revenue Product (MRP_L = MP_L * MR) and distinguish it from the Value of Marginal Product (VMP_L = MP_L * P) when a firm has monopoly power in the output market.
keyPoints: Inputs are demanded for the output they help produce
MRP_L = MP_L × MR; VMP_L = MP_L × P
With output-market power MR < P, so MRP < VMP and the firm hires less
examQuestions.draw: MRP below VMP, both downward sloping

examQuestions.title: Hiring rule MRP = w
examQuestions.originalTitle: Prove that a profit-maximizing firm hiring labor in a competitive labor market will employ workers up to the point where MRP_L = w (the wage rate). Explain why the firm's demand curve for labor is downward sloping even if the output price is constant.
keyPoints: An extra worker adds MRP to revenue and w to cost
Hire while MRP > w; stop at MRP = w
With a constant output price, labour demand slopes down because MP diminishes
examQuestions.draw: MRP curve with horizontal wage lines and the chosen L

examQuestions.title: Industry demand for an input
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain why an industry's demand curve for an input is not simply the horizontal sum of the individual firms' marginal revenue product curves. What feedback effects occur in the output market when input prices fall and all firms simultaneously expand production?
keyPoints: When the input price falls, all firms expand at once
Output price falls, shifting each firm's MRP down
Industry demand is less elastic than the sum of firms' MRPs
examQuestions.draw: Firm MRP curves shifting left; the industry curve steeper than the simple sum

examQuestions.title: Labour–leisure choice and backward-bending supply
examQuestions.originalTitle: Using the consumer model of trade-off between labor and leisure, derive the individual labor supply curve. Explain the opposing effects of a wage increase: the substitution effect (which increases work hours) and the income effect (which decreases work hours). At what point does the curve bend backward?
keyPoints: The wage is the price of leisure: budget line between income and leisure (24 hours)
Substitution effect of a higher wage: more work
Income effect (leisure is normal): less work
Supply bends backward where the income effect dominates (usually at high wages)
examQuestions.draw: Upper panel: income–leisure budget lines; lower panel: the backward-bending supply curve

examQuestions.title: Economic rent vs transfer earnings
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define economic rent and distinguish it from transfer earnings (opportunity cost of input supply). Demonstrate graphically how economic rent is determined in a factor market. Why is all payment received by a completely fixed, perfectly inelastic factor (such as prime commercial real estate or unique human talent) pure economic rent?
keyPoints: Transfer earnings: the minimum needed to keep the input in its current use
Economic rent: payment above that minimum
Graphically: area above the supply curve and below the price
With perfectly inelastic supply (prime land, unique talent) all payment is rent
examQuestions.draw: Upward-sloping supply with rent above it; a vertical supply where the whole rectangle is rent

examQuestions.title: Monopsony in the labour market
examQuestions.originalTitle: Analyze input hiring by a firm with monopsony power in the labor market. Why does the Marginal Expenditure (ME) curve lie above the Average Expenditure (AE) curve? Demonstrate graphically that a monopsonist employs fewer workers and pays a lower wage than a competitive factor market.
keyPoints: ME lies above AE (the labour supply curve)
Hire where MRP = ME; pay the wage from the supply curve
Fewer workers and lower wages than in a competitive market
A minimum wage between wm and wc can raise employment
examQuestions.draw: MRP, AE, ME with Lm, wm and the competitive Lc, wc

examQuestions.title: Union objectives
examQuestions.originalTitle: Analyze the economic objectives of a monopolistic labor union facing a competitive employer demand curve. Contrast the wage and employment outcomes under three alternative union objectives: (a) maximizing total employment; (b) maximizing total wage bill; and (c) maximizing economic rent to union members.
keyPoints: Union as a monopoly seller of labour facing the employers' labour demand
Maximise employment: competitive wage and employment
Maximise the wage bill: employ where MR of labour = 0 (unit-elastic point)
Maximise members' rent: employ where MR of labour = supply — highest wage, fewest jobs
examQuestions.draw: Labour demand, its MR curve and supply, with the three outcomes marked

examQuestions.title: Bilateral monopoly
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define bilateral monopoly (a monopsonistic buyer confronting a monopolistic seller). Show that economic theory cannot definitively predict the unique wage rate in this market structure, explaining why the final outcome depends on the relative bargaining power and strategic threats of the participants.
keyPoints: One buyer with monopsony power faces one seller with monopoly power
The monopsonist wants a low price, the monopolist a high one
The outcome is indeterminate between the two and depends on bargaining power
The two powers tend to offset each other, often pushing the outcome toward the competitive one

examQuestions.title: Stocks and flows
examQuestions.originalTitle: Distinguish rigorously between stock variables and flow variables in microeconomics. Explain why capital equipment and physical factory capacity are stocks, while investment expenditures, depreciation, and corporate revenues are flows.
keyPoints: Stock: measured at a point in time (machines, factory capacity, inventory)
Flow: measured per period (investment, depreciation, revenue, output)
Investment adds to the capital stock; depreciation reduces it

examQuestions.title: Present discounted value
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define Present Discounted Value (PDV). Write the mathematical formula for the present value of a multi-year stream of expected future cash flows (FV_t). Explain why a dollar received in the future is worth less than a dollar received today, even in the complete absence of inflation.
keyPoints: PDV: what a future payment is worth today
A dollar today can earn interest, so future dollars are worth less even without inflation
Higher R cuts PDV, especially for distant payments

examQuestions.title: Perpetuities and bond prices
examQuestions.originalTitle: Derive the formula for the present value of a perpetuity paying a constant annual coupon C at discount rate R (PV = C / R). Explain how the price of a corporate bond relates to its coupon payments, face value, maturity, and effective yield. Why do bond prices fall when market interest rates rise?
keyPoints: Perpetuity: PV = C/R
Bond price = PDV of coupons + PDV of face value
Effective yield: the rate that makes PDV of payments equal the price
Rates up → bond prices down, most for long maturities
formulas: P = Σ C/(1 + R)ᵗ + F/(1 + R)ᵀ
examQuestions.draw: Bond price falling as the interest rate rises

examQuestions.title: NPV rule
examQuestions.originalTitle: State the Net Present Value (NPV) decision rule for capital investment projects. Prove that a firm should undertake an investment project if and only if NPV > 0. How does a company evaluate mutually exclusive investment projects with differing upfront capital requirements?
keyPoints: Invest if NPV > 0
NPV > 0 means the project earns more than the opportunity cost of capital
Mutually exclusive projects: pick the higher NPV
examQuestions.draw: NPV against R: falling curve crossing zero at the IRR

examQuestions.title: Fisher equation and consistent discounting
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the Fisher equation connecting the nominal interest rate (i), the real interest rate (r), and expected inflation (pi). Why is it a critical capital budgeting error to discount nominal cash flows using a real discount rate, or real cash flows using a nominal discount rate?
keyPoints: Nominal rate ≈ real rate + expected inflation
Discount nominal cash flows at a nominal rate, real flows at a real rate
Nominal flows at a real rate overstate NPV; real flows at a nominal rate understate it

examQuestions.title: Diversifiable vs systematic risk; beta
examQuestions.originalTitle: Distinguish between diversifiable (idiosyncratic) risk and nondiversifiable (systematic/market) risk. Explain why investors in international financial markets demand a risk premium only for nondiversifiable risk. What does an asset's Beta (beta) measure in the CAPM?
keyPoints: Diversifiable risk is firm-specific and disappears in a portfolio
Only nondiversifiable (market) risk earns a premium
Beta measures how much an asset moves with the market

examQuestions.title: Human capital and the NPV of a degree
examQuestions.originalTitle: How does an individual apply the NPV criterion to decisions regarding investments in human capital (e.g., pursuing a specialized graduate degree in international commerce vs. immediate workforce entry)? What are the explicit costs, opportunity costs, and expected wage premiums over the working lifespan?
keyPoints: Costs: tuition and forgone earnings while studying
Benefits: wage premium over the working life
Discount the stream; study if NPV > 0
Ignore costs you would pay anyway and sunk past education
formulas: NPV = −Σ (tuition + forgone wages)ₜ/(1 + R)ᵗ + Σ ΔWₜ/(1 + R)ᵗ

examQuestions.title: Hotelling's rule and user cost
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain Hotelling's rule for the extraction of exhaustible natural resources (such as oil or rare minerals). Why must the net price (market price minus marginal extraction cost, P - MC) rise at a rate equal to the rate of interest in a competitive market? Define 'user cost' and explain its role in intertemporal production decisions.
keyPoints: A resource in the ground is an asset: its net price must rise at the rate of interest
Otherwise producers shift extraction earlier or later
User cost: opportunity cost of extracting now rather than later; equals P − MC under competition
In practice user cost is small; discoveries, technology and market power dominate prices

examQuestions.title: Partial vs general equilibrium
examQuestions.originalTitle: Distinguish between partial equilibrium analysis and general equilibrium analysis. Provide a commercial example showing how feedback effects from a supply disruption or import tariff in one market (e.g., ethanol or global shipping) reverberate through related substitute and complement markets.
keyPoints: Partial: one market, others held fixed
General: prices and quantities of related markets determined together, with feedback
Example: an ethanol tariff raises demand for domestic ethanol and corn, then feed and food prices, then feeds back
examQuestions.draw: Two markets side by side with shifts and the feedback arrows

examQuestions.title: Edgeworth box and the contract curve
examQuestions.originalTitle: Construct an Edgeworth box diagram for an exchange economy involving two consumers and two goods. Explain why any allocation where the consumers' marginal rates of substitution are unequal (MRS_A != MRS_B) is Pareto inefficient. What mutually advantageous trades occur until the contract curve is reached?
keyPoints: Box dimensions = total endowments of the two goods; each point is an allocation
If MRS_A ≠ MRS_B, indifference curves cross: trade can help both
Trade continues until tangency; the contract curve links all tangencies
examQuestions.draw: Edgeworth box with endowment point, the lens of mutually better allocations and the contract curve

examQuestions.title: First welfare theorem
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain why a competitive price mechanism automatically guides an exchange economy to a Pareto-efficient allocation on the contract curve. State the First Fundamental Theorem of Welfare Economics and discuss its economic significance for decentralized market economies.
keyPoints: A competitive equilibrium is Pareto efficient
All consumers face the same prices and set MRS = Px/Py, so MRSs are equal
Prices coordinate without central knowledge (invisible hand)
Holds only without market power, externalities, public goods or information problems

examQuestions.title: Utility possibilities frontier; equity vs efficiency
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain how the contract curve maps into the Utility Possibilities Frontier (UPF). Why is an allocation on the UPF not necessarily superior from a social equity standpoint to an inefficient allocation inside the frontier? Discuss the trade-off between equity and efficiency in government redistribution policy.
keyPoints: UPF: utility levels of the two consumers along the contract curve
Points inside are inefficient; beyond are unattainable
An efficient point can be less fair than an inefficient interior point
Redistribution through distorting taxes trades some efficiency for equity
examQuestions.draw: UPF with an inefficient interior point and two frontier points, one very unequal

examQuestions.title: Production efficiency and the PPF
examQuestions.originalTitle: Construct an Edgeworth production box for two goods produced using labor and capital. Prove that technical efficiency in production requires the equalization of marginal rates of technical substitution across both industries (MRTS_LK^X = MRTS_LK^Y). How is the Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF) derived from this condition?
keyPoints: Production Edgeworth box: labour and capital split between industries
Technical efficiency: equal MRTS in both industries
The production contract curve maps into the PPF
The PPF is concave because inputs are not equally suited to both goods
examQuestions.draw: Production box with the contract curve; PPF derived from it

examQuestions.title: MRT and output efficiency
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define the Marginal Rate of Transformation (MRT). Prove that MRT = MC_X / MC_Y. State the condition for overall economic efficiency in output mix (MRS = MRT), explaining why an economy operating at a point where MRS != MRT fails to maximize consumer satisfaction.
keyPoints: MRT: Y given up for one more X — the slope of the PPF
MRT = MCx/MCy
Output efficiency: MRS = MRT; if MRS > MRT produce more X
Competition: MRS = Px/Py = MCx/MCy = MRT
examQuestions.draw: PPF tangent to an indifference curve at the efficient output mix

examQuestions.title: Gains from trade beyond the PPF
examQuestions.originalTitle: Using an expanded Production Possibilities Frontier diagram, demonstrate how free international trade based on comparative advantage enables a country to consume at a bundle strictly outside its domestic production possibilities frontier. Why does trade expand total national utility even if one trading partner has an absolute advantage in all goods?
keyPoints: Specialise where domestic MRT equals the world price ratio
Trade along the world price line to a consumption point outside the PPF
Comparative (not absolute) advantage drives gains: opportunity costs differ
A country less productive in everything still gains
examQuestions.draw: PPF, the world price line tangent at the production point, consumption point outside the PPF

examQuestions.title: Four sources of market failure
examQuestions.originalTitle: Systematically outline the four primary structural reasons why real-world competitive markets fail to achieve economic efficiency: market power, incomplete/asymmetric information, externalities, and public goods. Briefly summarize how each source drives a wedge between private and social optimality.
keyPoints: Market power: P > MC, output too low
Incomplete or asymmetric information: lemons, adverse selection
Externalities: costs or benefits outside prices
Public goods: non-rival and non-excludable, so markets underprovide

examQuestions.title: Negative externalities
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define a negative externality. Distinguish between Marginal Private Cost (MC), Marginal External Cost (MEC), and Marginal Social Cost (MSC = MC + MEC). Demonstrate graphically why a competitive market overproduces goods associated with negative production externalities (such as industrial emissions or plastic waste).
keyPoints: External cost borne by third parties
MSC = MC + MEC lies above private MC
Market produces where D = MC (Q₁), more than the efficient Q* where D = MSC
Deadweight loss between Q* and Q₁
examQuestions.draw: D, MC, MSC, MEC with Q*, Q₁ and the DWL triangle

examQuestions.title: Emissions fees vs standards
examQuestions.originalTitle: Compare an emissions fee (Pigouvian tax) with an emissions standard under conditions of complete information. Prove that an emissions fee set exactly equal to the marginal external damage at the efficient output level induces the firm to produce the socially optimal output. Why do emissions fees provide stronger continuous incentives for technological innovation than command-and-control standards?
keyPoints: Fee = MEC at the efficient output makes the firm produce Q*
With full information, a fee and a standard reach the same level
Fees give continuous incentives to cut more and innovate
With uncertainty: steep damage curve favours standards, steep abatement cost favours fees
examQuestions.draw: Externality diagram with the fee shifting MC up to meet D at Q*

examQuestions.title: Tradable emissions permits (cap-and-trade)
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the economic mechanics of a transferable emissions permit system (cap-and-trade). Why does permit trading across industrial polluters ensure that total emissions abatement is achieved at the minimum aggregate cost to society, regardless of the initial allocation of permits?
keyPoints: The state caps total emissions; firms trade permits
Low-cost abaters cut more and sell; high-cost abaters buy
Marginal abatement costs equalise at the permit price, minimising total cost
Initial allocation affects who pays whom, not efficiency (EU ETS)
examQuestions.draw: Two firms' MCA curves with the permit price and the abatement split

examQuestions.title: Coase theorem
examQuestions.originalTitle: State the Coase Theorem. Explain why, in the absence of transaction costs and with well-defined property rights, private bargaining between affected parties will achieve an economically efficient outcome regardless of who is initially assigned the legal property right. What real-world impediments (free-rider issues, high negotiation costs) limit the applicability of the Coase Theorem?
keyPoints: Clear property rights and no transaction costs: bargaining gives the efficient outcome
Who holds the right affects who pays whom, not the outcome
Obstacles: many parties, free riders, holdouts, hidden information, high bargaining costs
Works best with few parties (factory and fishery)

examQuestions.title: Positive externalities
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define a positive externality and distinguish between Marginal Private Benefit (D) and Marginal Social Benefit (MSB = D + MEB). Demonstrate graphically why private competitive markets underinvest in activities that generate positive external spillovers (such as corporate R&D, green technology adoption, and disease eradication). What policy corrective is required?
keyPoints: External benefit to third parties
MSB = D + MEB lies above private demand
The market underproduces (R&D, vaccines, green technology)
Fix: a subsidy equal to MEB at the efficient output
examQuestions.draw: MC, D, MSB with market Q₁ below efficient Q*

examQuestions.title: Common property and the tragedy of the commons
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define a common property resource (rivalrous but non-excludable, such as ocean fisheries or international commercial shipping corridors). Explain why unrestricted access leads to overutilization and resource depletion ('the tragedy of the commons'). Contrast open-access equilibrium with socially optimal utilization.
keyPoints: Rival but non-excludable (fisheries, crowded shipping lanes)
Each user ignores the cost imposed on others, so the resource is overused
Open-access level exceeds the social optimum where MSC = MB
Fixes: ownership, licences, tradable quotas
examQuestions.draw: Demand (MB), private cost, social cost; open-access F_c beyond the efficient F*

examQuestions.title: Public goods
examQuestions.originalTitle: Define a pure public good in terms of nonrivalry in consumption and nonexcludability. Provide examples relevant to international commerce (such as national defense, maritime navigational aids, or basic scientific research). Explain why private competitive markets fail to provide public goods at socially optimal levels.
keyPoints: Non-rival: one person's use does not reduce others'
Non-excludable: non-payers cannot be kept out
Examples: defence, lighthouses and navigation aids, basic research
Markets underprovide because of free riding

examQuestions.title: Free riders and vertical summation
examQuestions.originalTitle: Explain the 'free-rider problem' and why it prevents voluntary private market provision of public goods. Contrast the vertical summation of individual demand curves used to determine the efficient level of a public good with the horizontal summation used for private consumer goods.
keyPoints: Free rider: benefits without paying, so voluntary provision falls short
Public good: everyone consumes the same quantity, so add marginal benefits vertically
Private good: add quantities horizontally
Efficient level: sum of marginal benefits = marginal cost
examQuestions.draw: Two individual demand curves, their vertical sum and the MC line
